The Claude Agent SDK leaf, orchestrator, and curator are all subscription-funded (ADR-0030) — a flat monthly cost, not metered per token — yet the SDK still reports a `total_cost_usd` computed from *list-price* token rates: a phantom number that does not reflect our spend (the work costs the same flat amount whether it runs or not). A default ceiling against that phantom adds no real cost protection while artificially halting funded work — ADR-0130's `chat-sse-mount` build stalled mid-slice on a phantom $1 wall and needed `--budget` raised purely to clear it. The turn cap (`maxTurns`) is the genuine brake because turns map to real work — they bound how long any one slice can churn regardless of estimated dollars. The same judgment was reached independently across three SDK sessions (ADR-0130: the build leaf + drive; ADR-0131: the chat orchestrator + the post-green curator), all of which dropped the USD default for this reason.
howToApply: Before adding or keeping a `$`/cost ceiling on an agent loop, ask whether the metered currency maps to OUR marginal cost. Under flat/subscription billing it does not — so make the dollar cap an opt-in escape hatch (e.g. `--budget`), never a default, and let the resource that maps to real work (the turn cap) be the runaway brake. Keep the plumbing; change only the default — the capability to bound a slice by the SDK's estimate survives for the operator who wants it, it just stops firing on a phantom by default. The discriminator is the BILLING MODEL, not the metric's familiarity: dollars feel like the natural unit, but a unit that does not track our spend is the wrong unit for a fail-closed cap.
provenance: Graduated 2026-06-28 from ADR-0130 and ADR-0131 (the two-consumer trigger: the same judgment was established across three subscription-funded SDK sessions — the build leaf + drive in ADR-0130, the chat orchestrator + post-green curator in ADR-0131). Refines the `per-node-budget` definition, whose ceiling-unit/default was left open (ADR-0005, open-questions §6): this principle resolves the currency choice for the subscription-funded case. Kept as its own principle rather than folded into `per-node-budget` (that is a definition of the mechanism; this is a judgment about how to choose its currency — reference-don't-restate). Consumers: session-orchestrator.

title: per-node budget
description: A code-enforced ceiling on a node's spine loop that bounds a runaway. The ceiling's unit — once open — is resolved for the subscription-funded SDK by ADR-0130/0131: the default brake is the turn cap (maxTurns), which maps to real work, while the USD ceiling was dropped as a default (a phantom under flat/subscription billing) and survives only as an opt-in --budget escape hatch.
oneLine: A code-enforced ceiling on a node's spine loop that bounds a runaway. The default brake is the turn cap (`maxTurns`); the USD ceiling was dropped as a default — a phantom under subscription billing — and is now an opt-in `--budget` escape hatch (ADR-0130/0131).
whatItIs: A code-enforced ceiling on a node's spine loop. The loop terminates on green **or** budget-exhausted, the latter a typed terminal event with per-round cost visible in the event store. Resurrected for pay-as-you-go (ADR-0005), inverting v1's "cascade rounds are not a cost". The ceiling's unit — left open in v1 — is resolved for the subscription-funded SDK by ADR-0130/0131: the default brake is the **turn cap** (`maxTurns`), which maps to real work, while the **USD ceiling was removed as a default** because the SDK's metered `total_cost_usd` is a phantom under flat/subscription billing; a dollar cap survives only as an opt-in `--budget` escape hatch (see `meter-fail-closed-caps-in-real-cost`).
provenance: Resurrected for pay-as-you-go (ADR-0005). The ceiling unit/default, left open in v1 (`open-questions.md` §6), was resolved 2026-06-28 by ADR-0130/0131: the turn cap is the default brake; the USD ceiling is opt-in only (`--budget`), a phantom under subscription billing. See `meter-fail-closed-caps-in-real-cost`.

title: approval
description: A first-class, typed operator act (actor = operator) in which the human accepts an agent action, or a capability's green result, onto the trunk via the studio.
oneLine: A first-class, typed operator act (actor = operator) in which the human accepts an agent action, or a capability's green result, onto the trunk via the studio.
whatItIs: A first-class, typed operator act (`actor = operator`) in which the human accepts an agent action, or a capability's green result, **onto the trunk** via the studio. The trunk is **approval-gated**: a green signal is a *request for human diff-review*, not an automatic merge (inverts v1's auto-merge-on-green).
whatItIsNot: Distinct from a **gate** (which structurally refuses invalid work); an approval is the human admitting work that has already passed the gate's content invariants.
provenance: The identity backing the signature is open (`open-questions.md` §1).

title: verdict
description: The Pass/Fail outcome of a story's UAT.
oneLine: The Pass/Fail outcome of a story's UAT.
whatItIs: The Pass/Fail outcome of a story's UAT. Reserved for UAT outcomes.
whatItIsNot: v1 also used "verdict" for agent conclusions and evidence-row states — those are different concepts and do not claim the word here.

title: evidence
description: The forensic record that a unit's tests went red→green and its story's UAT was signed: an audit trail, not itself the gate.
oneLine: The forensic record that a unit's tests went red→green and its story's UAT was signed — an audit trail, not itself the gate.
whatItIs: The forensic record that a unit's tests went red→green and its story's UAT was signed: an audit trail.
whatItIsNot: Not itself the gate — evidence records what happened; the gate is the enforcement point that consumes it.
provenance: How v2 persists evidence (events vs files) and the attestation / identity model are open (`open-questions.md` §1).

title: proof hash
description: A hash of a unit's proof-bearing content (outcome, contracts, …) that invalidates a prior verdict when the content changes.
oneLine: A hash of a unit's proof-bearing content (outcome, contracts, …) that invalidates a prior verdict when the content changes.
whatItIs: A hash of a unit's proof-bearing content (outcome, contracts, …) that invalidates a prior verdict when the content changes.

title: red-green
description: The discipline that a failing (red) contract test is authored before the implementation that turns it green.
statement: A failing (red) contract test is authored before the implementation that turns it green.
why: A test that has never been seen to fail is not trusted evidence — writing the implementation first invites tests shaped to pass vacuously. Authoring the test red first proves it actually exercises the behaviour.
howToApply: Write the contract test, watch it fail (red), then write the implementation that turns it green. This is a discipline — **not** a synonym for the noun `contract`.
provenance: Per the v1→v2 term map, v1's "story is a contract" / red-green reads as this principle, not the noun `contract`.

title: mock-UAT seam
description: No mocks within an organism: capability integration tests and the story UAT both run against real in-story collaborators.
oneLine: The rule that there are no mocks within an organism — capability integration tests and the story UAT both run against real in-story collaborators — with the sole stubbable boundary being the declared cross-story boundary.
whatItIs: **No mocks within an organism**: capability integration tests and the story UAT both run against real in-story collaborators. The one stubbable boundary is the declared cross-story **boundary** — a story's UAT may run against a stubbed / contract-tested version of an upstream story's interface (like acceptance-testing a frontend against a stubbed database). Isolated unit (contract) tests still stub freely.
whatItIsNot: This is isolation, not theatre — stubbing at the declared cross-story seam is legitimate, whereas faking collaborators inside the organism is a structural defect.

title: defects-amend-the-owning-story
description: A defect amends the capability whose contract it violates (reverting it to building), rather than spawning a new unit.
statement: When a defect violates a capability's contract, amend the owning capability (reverting it to `building`) rather than spawning a new unit.
why: A defect could be filed as a brand-new unit, fragmenting ownership of a behaviour across the unit that owns it and the unit that records its bug.
howToApply: Route the defect to the capability whose contract it violates; revert that capability to `building` and fix it under its existing contract. You trade a new unit's clean slate for a single accountable owner per behaviour and an intact contract/evidence chain on the original capability.

why: On a surface rendered by several stories, a change RESEMBLES the flagship story while its writes land in files owned elsewhere. Sessions that claim by resemblance all serialise behind the flagship claim - the lock ADR-0222 broke: every forest-look session claimed forest-world while actually writing studio CSS, art-factory kits, or the web mapper - and the ledger stops being honest: the true owner's lane reads free while someone is writing into it. The claim MECHANISM cannot catch this: the same-unit refusal rejects a DUPLICATE claim on one story, but a wrong-story claim is unique by construction, so it sails through. Routing is the session's judgment, which is exactly why it must be principled.
title: Claim the owning story — at the capability you are writing
statement: Route a claim by write-ownership: resolve the story that owns the files the unit will write (package ownership in repo-manifest.json, the owning story's registered surface), never the story the change looks or feels like — then land the claim at capability grain within that story (ADR-0270 D1); the story-level claim is for genuinely cross-capability units only.
howToApply:
Before claiming, resolve who owns the files the unit will actually write - repo-manifest.json packageOwnership for package code, the owning story's registered surface for app code - and route the claim to THAT story's territory. The worked example (ADR-0222 decision 4): studio-only CSS/chrome work claims `studio`; art-kit/factory work claims `art-factory`; web-mapper work claims the web lineage; only shared scene-graph changes claim `forest-world`. The tempting move - claiming forest-world because the change is about the forest LOOK - is wrong precisely when the diff never touches forest-world's files. A unit whose writes span two stories' files is a decomposition smell: split it into per-story units sequenced by depends_on, or route the structural gap to story-author. The same-unit refusal (asset:claims-in-the-shared-store) stays the backstop for contention, never the routing oracle.

Under ADR-0270 D1 the claim then lands at CAPABILITY grain: having resolved the owning story, claim the capability your unit writes (the story itself only when the unit genuinely spans its capabilities). A refusal at any grain prints the unit's full claim board (ADR-0270 D3.2) - resolve disjointness from that board on your own judgment (narrow to your capability, or take the waiting grade and proceed); a claim conflict is never an owner question — escalate only genuine same-surface overlap that no narrowing resolves (ADR-0270 D2).
description: A session claims what it will WRITE: resolve the owning story from registered write-ownership — never the story the change superficially resembles — then land the claim at the capability being written within it (ADR-0270 D1).

title: fail-closed-on-dirty-tree
description: A command that writes attestable evidence refuses to run on a dirty working tree (writes nothing, non-zero exit code).
statement: A command that writes attestable evidence must not run on a dirty working tree — it writes nothing and exits non-zero.
why: Evidence attributed to a clean commit could silently include uncommitted changes, corrupting the proof/evidence chain that promotion depends on.
howToApply: Have such a command check working-tree cleanliness before doing any evidence-writing work and abort on a dirty tree — the load-bearing guarantee is that it writes nothing (no signing row, no event), with a non-zero exit code. Make it a code-path guard, not a warning, so the boundary is non-bypassable in practice. (Reserving a distinct exit code for the dirty-tree refusal — rather than the generic non-zero every refusal returns today — is a cheap future hardening, not a current guarantee.)

title: verification-wins
description: The stance that binding to external truth via tests + on-disk evidence overrides LLM memory consolidation / recency ("recency-wins").
statement: Binding to external truth via tests + on-disk evidence **overrides** LLM memory consolidation / recency ("recency-wins").
why: A confident-but-stale model recollection can override what the tests and evidence actually show. v2 rejects Dreams-style memory reconciliation in favour of a commit/event-bound evidence chain.
howToApply: When the model's memory and the evidence chain disagree, the evidence wins — trust the tests + on-disk record over recency.
provenance: The learning loop's v2 home is open (`open-questions.md` §5).

title: unit fields
description: The four core fields a unit carries — outcome, guidance, title, id — covering its value statement, rebuild context, human label, and unique identifier.
oneLine: The four core fields a unit carries — outcome, guidance, title, id — covering its value statement, rebuild context, human label, and unique identifier.
whatItIs:
The four core fields a unit carries:

- **outcome** — a capability's plain-English, single-sentence value statement, with no conjunctions (if it needs them, split the unit instead).

- **guidance** — non-obvious technical context needed to rebuild a unit; only what an agent could not derive from outcome + proof.

- **title** — a short human label for a unit; not load-bearing for proof.

- **id** — a unit's unique identifier. v2 must allocate these **conflict-free across concurrent sessions** — a stated goal. An earlier DBOS spike showed durable, collision-free workflow IDs as one candidate mechanism, but DBOS is deferred (ADR-0019), so that mechanism is reference, not the adopted id-allocation path.

title: claim
oneLine: A typed write-ownership record in the one shared event store, naming what a node intends to write and checked under a serializable/unique constraint at node-schedule time — a conflict is a hard refusal, never a warning.
whatItIs:
A typed **write-ownership** record (a row/event in the one shared event store) naming what a node intends to write, checked under a serializable/unique constraint at **node-schedule time**; a conflict is a **hard refusal** (a `claim-conflict-refused` event), never a warning.

Since built out, the claim IS the noticeboard's one deterministic ledger (`events.node_claim` + `claim_event`, ADR-0121/0138/0200): it carries **grades** — exploring (shared) / waiting (queued) / **work** (the exclusive mutex this definition describes) — and code edits take a git worktree per claim, gained at claim-gated `storytree worktree create` (ADR-0200 resolved the earlier open worktree-per-node question). Granularity is per `(unit, session)`; the grade semantics and coordination ceremony live in `asset:noticeboard`.
provenance: Origin in open-questions.md §3 (ADR-0009); built out as the noticeboard claim ledger by ADR-0121/0138/0200.
description: A typed write-ownership record (a row/event in the one shared event store) naming what a node intends to write, checked under a serializable/unique constraint at node-schedule time;
whatItIsNot: Not v1's per-worktree `session_claims` table (Agentic ADR-0022): the v2 successor now lives in the single shared Postgres store (ADR-0009) as the noticeboard's `events.node_claim` ledger.

title: write-ownership
description: The single vocabulary for what surface/unit a node claims the right to write, used by the claim / conflict-detection layer.
oneLine: The single vocabulary for what surface/unit a node claims the right to write, used by the claim / conflict-detection layer.
whatItIs: The single vocabulary for *what surface/unit* a node claims the right to write, used by the claim / conflict-detection layer. It unifies v1's scattered terms (`declared_scope` vs per-agent `does_not_touch`) into one concept (ADR-0009); the exact shape (node-scoped vs file-glob) is open (`open-questions.md` §3).
whatItIsNot: Not v1's scattered, split vocabulary (`declared_scope` and per-agent `does_not_touch`), which this single concept replaces.
provenance: See `open-questions.md` §3.

title: studio
description: The live PixiJS web IDE that renders the tree and drives the agents (diffs, approvals, steering, per-node chat).
oneLine: The live PixiJS web IDE that renders the tree and drives the agents — diffs, approvals, steering, per-node chat.
whatItIs: The live PixiJS web IDE that renders the tree and **drives** the agents (diffs, approvals, steering, per-node chat).
whatItIsNot: Not v1's read-only `dashboard`, which it supersedes — the studio is a richer, driving surface, not merely a renamed view.

title: orchestrator
description: The thin custom TypeScript layer (packages/orchestrator) over plain Postgres (DBOS deferred, ADR-0019): owns the story-DAG, the scheduler, and the event store, and is the only module that drives `packages/agent` (the owned loop).
oneLine: The thin custom TypeScript layer (`packages/orchestrator`) over plain Postgres (DBOS deferred, ADR-0019) that owns the story-DAG, the scheduler, and the event store, and is the only module that drives `packages/agent` (the owned loop).
whatItIs: The thin custom TypeScript layer (`packages/orchestrator`) over plain Postgres — DBOS is deferred (ADR-0019), so this is a plain typed Postgres connection (ADR-0001): it owns the story-DAG, the scheduler, and the event store, and is the **only** module that drives `packages/agent` (the owned loop). It is the code-sequenced **spine** and the sole **fan-out** point — it schedules nodes; owned-loop nodes never schedule child nodes.
whatItIsNot: Distinct from an owned-loop session, which owns work *inside* a node (ADR-0004, ADR-0005, ADR-0011).
provenance: DBOS deferred by ADR-0019.

title: spine
description: The code-sequenced control-flow layer (the orchestrator over plain Postgres, DBOS deferred — ADR-0019) that owns closed, deterministic routing: the order steps run in, when a loop iterates, which branch is taken.
oneLine: The code-sequenced control-flow layer (the orchestrator over plain Postgres, DBOS deferred — ADR-0019) that owns closed, deterministic routing — the order steps run in, when a loop iterates, which branch is taken.
whatItIs: The code-sequenced control-flow layer (the orchestrator over plain Postgres — DBOS is deferred, ADR-0019) that owns **closed, deterministic routing**: the order steps run in, when a loop iterates, which branch is taken. The discriminator (carried verbatim from Agentic ADR-0026): *if a for-loop or a match could express the routing, the spine owns it; if the routing needs the model to decide what comes next, the leaf (owned-loop node) owns it.*
whatItIsNot: Not the **leaf** — the leaf runtime the spine delegates to (live: the Claude Agent SDK; offline/fallback: the owned loop — ADR-0030).
provenance: Carried verbatim from Agentic ADR-0026; DBOS deferred by ADR-0019; leaf runtime split live/offline by ADR-0030.

title: leaf step / leaf judgment
description: A single step in a code-sequenced cascade whose work is owned by the leaf runtime (what to write, how to satisfy a contract) rather than by the spine — the control-flow sense of "leaf"…
oneLine: A single step in a code-sequenced cascade whose work is owned by the leaf runtime (what to write, how to satisfy a contract) rather than by the spine — the control-flow sense of "leaf".
whatItIs: A single step in a code-sequenced cascade whose work is owned by the **leaf runtime** (what to write, how to satisfy a contract) rather than by the spine — the **control-flow** sense of "leaf" (ADR-0005, ADR-0011). The leaf runs behind the executor seam: live, the Claude Agent SDK; offline/fallback, the owned loop (ADR-0030).
whatItIsNot: Distinct from **contract**, the *leaf tier* of the work hierarchy (ADR-0002); the two senses of "leaf" must not be conflated.

title: agent package
oneLine: The project-owned packages/agent boundary around every model harness, exposing only runtime-neutral authoring and typed accounting upward.
whatItIs: packages/agent defines PhaseAuthor and hosts the owned offline/pivot-out loop, ClaudeAgentAuthor as the compatibility-default subscription live leaf, and CodexPhaseAuthor as the opt-in local Codex leaf using saved ChatGPT-managed authentication. Provider-specific auth, usage, and tool policy stop here.
provenance: Carries v1's own-a-thin-wrapper-over-the-agent-runtime principle (Agentic ADR-0008/0026).
description: The packages/agent boundary normalizes the owned loop plus Claude-default and Codex-opt-in live leaves behind PhaseAuthor.
whatItIsNot: It is not a broad provider registry and exposes no API-key-funded OpenAI or Cursor execution. Storage and Studio do not import model runtimes; the orchestrator independently observes RED/GREEN and signs.

title: trunk
description: The canonical integrated mainline a capability lands on once approved.
oneLine: The canonical integrated mainline a capability lands on once approved.
whatItIs: The canonical **integrated mainline** a capability lands on once **approved**. In v2 the trunk is **approval-gated** (a human admits a green result), never auto-merge-on-green, and never holds knowingly-broken intermediate states (ADR-0008).
whatItIsNot: Not v1's trunk, which it supersedes — v1's auto-merged on green and tolerated broken intermediate states under an eventual-consistency posture.

title: steering
description: A first-class, typed operator act of redirecting an in-flight owned-loop run mid-execution (the owned loop's steer operation), recorded as an event in the event store.
oneLine: A first-class, typed operator act of redirecting an in-flight owned-loop run mid-execution (the owned loop's `steer` operation), recorded as an event in the event store.
whatItIs: A first-class, typed operator act of **redirecting an in-flight owned-loop run mid-execution** (the owned loop's `steer` operation), recorded as an event in the event store.
whatItIsNot: Distinct from **approval**: steering is the in-loop counterpart — the human shapes an action *while it runs*, rather than only accepting/rejecting its result (ADR-0008).

whatItIs: An Architecture Decision Record under `docs/decisions/`, capturing a cross-cutting decision.

oneLine: Newline-delimited JSON — the line-delimited record format (a candidate backing for the event stream).
whatItIs: Newline-delimited JSON; the line-delimited record format, a candidate backing for the event stream.

title: asset
description: In storytree, a tree/game art asset for the isometric renderer (ADR-0001, deferred).
oneLine: In storytree, a tree/game art asset for the isometric renderer (ADR-0001, deferred).
whatItIs: In storytree, a **tree/game art asset** for the isometric renderer (ADR-0001, deferred).
whatItIsNot: Not v1's "asset" (shared DRY content under `assets/`), which does not carry — guard against the collision when importing v1 docs.

title: Cloud SQL access · Node connector · keyless IAM
description: How storytree reaches its Postgres runtime store: the Cloud SQL Node connector with IAM database auth via ambient ADC. Agent sessions need no per-session OAuth and no key files.
statement: Reach the Cloud SQL Postgres via the Node connector with keyless IAM database authentication — agent sessions authenticate from ambient Application Default Credentials, never a per-session OAuth or a key file.
whatItIs: The `@google-cloud/cloud-sql-connector` Node connector (paired with `pg`, in `packages/library/src/store` — the old `packages/store` dissolved, ADR-0077) mints short-lived IAM tokens as the database password over a TLS socket — no password is stored. Identity comes from the operator’s Application Default Credentials already established on the dev host (plus a dedicated service account for headless/impersonated runs). The IAM database user is the operator email (`STORYTREE_DB_USER`), the database is `storytree`, and the instance connection name is `storytree-498613:australia-southeast1:storytree-pg`.
whyThis: No secrets in the repo and no per-session interactive login, so agents can run migrations and queries headlessly; it matches the cost posture (the fixed nightly sleep window, ADR-0114) and keeps the browser/credential-free boundary (the studio never holds DB creds). A session should ASSUME keyless credentials are present and verify with `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token`, not assume it is unauthenticated.
constraints: The instance sleeps on a **fixed nightly window — stopped 01:00–07:00 Australia/Sydney** (ADR-0114, `infra/cost-backstop.tf`): one Cloud Scheduler job stops it at 01:00, another starts it at 07:00, so it stays predictably up across the day. The old idle-aware auto-stop (ADR-0015 §5, `infra/idle-stop.tf`) is REMOVED — superseded by that window. Day-to-day: `pnpm db:up` when you need it and LEAVE IT RUNNING (owner call 2026-06-13 — do not `db:down` between bursts); re-`db:up` if a query can't connect after the overnight stop, and expect a slow cold-start (probe with a direct `SELECT 1`, don't assume a wedge). IAM users are bare roles, so a ONE-TIME privilege bootstrap (`infra/bootstrap-grants.sql`, applied via a since-retired script in the dissolved `packages/store`) granted the IAM user `CREATE` on the database; already applied. The connector deps live in `packages/library` (the `./store` subpath); DBOS is deferred (ADR-0019), so this is a plain typed Postgres connection.
provenance: Validated 2026-06-08: 73 units migrated keyless, then the instance stopped.

why: It is easy to author the next move — 'extend the code so the doc holds', 'tighten the invariant' — on top of a doc claim a recent finding has already shown false. That move is built on a phantom premise. The honest first question is whether the doc needs correcting to match the code (most common) or the code needs extending to make the doc's claim hold (rarer, an operator call).
title: Doc-vs-implementation precedence
statement: Implementation is ground truth and doc text is a hypothesis about it; when a finding shows a doc claim (ADR, definition, guideline, spec) disagrees with the code, the gap itself is the load-bearing surface, not metadata to a move that took the doc at face value.
howToApply: Discriminator: does a recent investigation name a doc-vs-code gap, AND does your pending move cite that same doc as load-bearing? Yes on both → reshape any framing that takes the claim at face value and surface the gap to the operator (the doc, its exact claim, the observed behaviour, one question: correct the doc or extend the code?) without pre-deciding. Three resolutions: correct the doc (most common; the downstream move usually dissolves), route code-extension as its own bounded unit (operator-directed), or defer. When the FIRST conjunct fails — no investigation has named a gap, so this rule does not fire — the state it leaves you in is governed by asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked, the proactive complement: this rule is reactive and needs a discrepancy already surfaced, while that one asks, before any discrepancy is visible, whether the written set you are scoping from (an ADR's measured block, a call-site comment, a briefing line) was ever checked against the code at all.
provenance:
Composes with the `assess-tradeoffs-by-naming-both-sides` pattern (that governs how a surfaced tradeoff is framed; this governs whether the surface should exist). Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/doc-vs-implementation-precedence.yml`.

The pointer to `asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` was added by the librarian pass 2026-08-01, completing a pair whose other half already existed: that artifact's How to apply already named this one as downstream and reactive, and the reverse direction was left as an optional call. Taken because this rule's discriminator is a two-part AND, and when the FIRST conjunct fails — no gap named yet — the reader is correctly told the rule does not fire and is then told nothing else, a dead end where a live rule governs. A fresh agent cannot reconstruct the sibling's existence from this text (ADR-0024), so the pointer carries information rather than decorating. Scoped to one clause deliberately: the RULE stays wholly in the cited artifact (`asset:reference-dont-restate`), and nothing this artifact decides is changed.
description: Implementation is ground truth; when a doc claim and the code disagree, the gap itself is the load-bearing surface — surface it, do not build on the doc claim.

title: Dogfood: fix the source
description: When your own tooling blocks you, fix the tool at its source rather than papering over it with a one-off workaround.
statement: When tooling we own blocks progress, fix the tool or its source; do not mask the symptom with a one-off workaround that leaves the root cause live to resurface.
why: storytree is built with the very kind of agent-driven system it builds (orchestrator, spine, owned loop, studio), so a defect in our own tooling is a first-class bug, not an environmental annoyance. A null guard, hardcoded value, swallowed exception, or shell fallback gets you unblocked now but hides a real defect; the problem goes quiet and re-emerges later, harder to diagnose under a layer of masking, and the next session inherits the same wall.
howToApply: Reproduce and trace to the earliest failing signal; validate that a test genuinely captures the failure before changing production code; fix the root cause where it lives so the bad state cannot occur (not a guard that hides it after the fact); prefer making one behaviour simply correct over adding a flag. Anti-patterns: a catch-all that does not handle the error, hardcoding a value to silence a dynamic failure, a narrow edge-case handler for a problem that should be fixed generically, and falling back to a workaround tool without recording that the primary one failed.
provenance: Composes with `verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate` (a recovery fallback is permitted only after the failure is made visible). Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/dogfood-fix-the-source.yml`.

title: Exploration principles
description: Exploration is read-only reconnaissance: discover patterns over enumerating files, stay context-minimal, work in parallel and independent, never mutate.
statement: When exploring a codebase to inform a decision, discover patterns rather than enumerate files, load the minimum context for the scope, work independently of other explorers, and never modify anything.
why: Exploration feeds a decision (a decomposition, a scope call, a plan). The risks are over-reading (burning the attention budget on exhaustive cataloguing), over-reaching (analysing a surface another agent owns), and quietly mutating code meant only to be read. Disciplined exploration keeps findings sharp, cheap, and safe to act on.
howToApply: Use glob/search to learn structure and sample representative files rather than reading everything; stay inside the assigned scope and only note (not analyse) neighbouring surfaces; identify the high-level patterns that matter and flag risks and unknowns explicitly; produce a self-contained result with concrete file paths and no redundancy with another explorer's scope; use read-only tools only. When the context to explore genuinely exceeds the model window, escalate to recursive decomposition rather than reading everything at once.
provenance: Composes with the `recursive-decomposition-patterns` pattern. Imported from legacy AgenticEngineering `AgenticGuidance`.

title: Delegate exploration to digest-returning subagents
description: When work needs multi-step exploration (≈3+ consecutive Read/Grep/Glob turns, or any broad 'find where X lives / sweep many files' question), run it in a read-only explorer subagent that returns a DIGEST (conclusions + file:line pointers) — never pull the raw file contents into the orchestrating session's own long-lived context. A single targeted lookup where the file or symbol is already known stays inline.
statement: When a piece of work needs multi-step exploration — roughly three or more consecutive Read/Grep/Glob turns, or any broad 'find where X lives / sweep many files' question — delegate it to a read-only explorer subagent that returns a DIGEST (its conclusions plus file:line pointers), rather than pulling the raw file contents into the orchestrating session's own context. A single targeted lookup where the file or symbol is already known stays inline. The digest, not the raw files, is what belongs in the expensive context.
why: The orchestrating session's context is the most expensive real estate in the system: every turn re-bills the entire history, so content read once is paid for on every subsequent request until the session ends. Exploration is the worst offender because it is high-volume and single-use — you need the conclusion, not the bytes, yet the bytes sit in history being re-billed. The 2026-07-16 token-efficiency investigation (trace mining over ~10.6B billed tokens, ~61.5k requests, Jun 1–Jul 16 2026) measured it: 21% of main-agent requests are pure Read/Grep/Glob exploration (8,598 requests billing 1.54B tokens at a mean ~179k context each), and exploration results left in a main session's history are re-billed ~50–65 more times before the session ends — versus ~26x inside a subagent whose context is half the size and DIES at digest-return. That is an estimated ~14% of all billed tokens, the single largest verified remediation lever found. A disposable explorer context absorbs the volume and evaporates; only the distilled digest survives into the costly seat.
howToApply: Apply the routing test before you start reading: will answering this take roughly three or more consecutive Read/Grep/Glob turns, or is it a broad 'find where X lives / sweep these files' question? If yes, spawn a read-only explorer subagent (the `Explore` agent, or a general read-only agent) and ask it for a DIGEST — the conclusions plus concrete file:line pointers — not a file dump; the raw contents stay in its short-lived context and never enter yours. If no — the file or symbol is already known and it is one targeted Read/Grep — do it inline; delegating a single lookup adds latency for no saving. When the digest comes back and you need to act on a specific pointer, THEN read that exact span inline. This is the WHERE-exploration-runs rule: it composes with `exploration-principles` (HOW the explorer behaves once delegated — pattern-over-enumeration, context-minimal, read-only) and with `pull-based-context-architecture` (how any agent is briefed thin and pulls on demand); this rule adds that the pulling should happen in a disposable seat, not the long-lived orchestrating one.
provenance: Authored 2026-07-16 (owner-directed) from the token-efficiency investigation of that date — trace mining over ~10.6B billed tokens / ~61.5k requests (Jun 1–Jul 16 2026), which found pure Read/Grep/Glob exploration to be 21% of main-agent requests (1.54B tokens) re-billed ~50–65x when left in a main session vs ~26x in a half-size subagent context that dies at digest-return: an estimated ~14% of billed tokens, the largest verified remediation lever. Complements `exploration-principles` (how an explorer behaves) and `pull-based-context-architecture` (how agents are briefed) — this principle governs WHERE exploration runs (a disposable subagent context vs the long-lived orchestrating session) and rests on the re-billing economics. Consumers: session-orchestrator.

title: Guidance quality
description: Fix unfollowed guidance with structure (path / signpost / fence / offload), not emphasis (caps / repetition / strong language).
statement: When guidance is not being followed, fix its structure — add the missing path, signpost, fence, or offload — rather than adding emphasis.
why: Agents do not weight visual or emotional emphasis the way a human skimming a page might; capitalising, repeating, or marking something CRITICAL adds noise without raising the chance an instruction is followed. Ignored guidance is almost always a structural failure: the instruction is absent at the decision point, lacks a concrete example, or lacks a constraint that removes the ambiguity. Emphasis treats the symptom; structure treats the cause.
howToApply: Effective patterns: path (a concrete step placed where it is needed), signpost (a concrete example, ideally a link to one that exists), fence (a constraint that makes the wrong move structurally hard or measurable), offload (move a deterministic error-prone step into code the spine sequences). Anti-patterns: caps emphasis, repetition, strong/urgent language, emphasis escalation on already-ignored guidance, and negative framing with no positive alternative (replace 'do not write outside the scope' with 'writes land only within the declared scope'). Reach for emphasis only after structure has genuinely failed — which is rare.
provenance: Composes with the `signal-and-noise` principle (the discriminatory-power lens this serves). Imported from legacy AgenticEngineering `AgenticGuidance`.

title: No proof preservation
description: Never soften or dodge a correct edit to keep an earned status; make the edit, let the status regress, and re-prove.
statement: Never soften, tiptoe around, or refuse a correct edit in order to preserve a status or verdict that was expensive to earn; ship the correct edit and let the status regress — the system re-verifies on demand.
why: A proof-preserving edit leaves two falsehoods, not one: the artifact is still wrong AND the verdict now attests to text deliberately softened to avoid invalidating it, so the verdict is no longer trustworthy. This follows directly from the prove-it-gate and the proof-hash: a unit reaches `healthy` only via earned, on-disk evidence, and a change to proof-bearing content invalidates the prior verdict by design.
howToApply: Make the correct edit; do not phrase it to dodge a proof-hash change. Expect and accept the regression — a correctly-amended `healthy` story reverts to `building` (or computes `unhealthy`); that is the system asking for a re-proof. Let the tier’s proof mode re-run (contract test, integration test, UAT, or operator attestation). Verdicts are cheap to re-issue; that is the whole point of binding status to evidence rather than a hand-edited flag.
provenance: The inverse of a hand-edit that fakes `healthy`: there a unit claims proof it never earned; here a unit clings to proof its new content no longer supports. See the `prove-it-gate` principle and the `proof-hash` definition. Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/no-proof-preservation.yml`.

title: Reward hacking
description: A gameable success signal gets gamed; define success by observable outcome, require evidence, and separate the party that judges from the party that did the work.
statement: An agent rewarded for a gameable success signal will optimise the signal rather than the work; define success by observable end-results, require concrete evidence of them, and keep judging separate from doing.
why: When the owned loop works at a leaf it is rewarded for green tests. If the tests pin a gameable signal — a return code, a help-text string, a 'success: true' flag — the loop can earn the reward with a hollow implementation, and the breakage stays hidden until the slowest, most expensive channel (the story UAT against real collaborators) runs. This green-signal/red-reality failure is the root class the whole proof model exists to prevent.
howToApply: Outcome over process: prove 'the user can complete the journey', not 'the step executed' — exactly what the proof ladder encodes (contract test → integration test against real in-story collaborators → story UAT, no mocks within the organism). Require the concrete observable captured in the event store, not a bare flag. Separate judging from doing: approval onto the trunk is a distinct operator act, never self-granted; an agent can never self-exempt. Audit the tests themselves — a test can pass while failing to verify the requirement. Watch for help-text-only validation, success-flag-without-verification, mocking the real dependency, asserting implementation detail, permissive assertions (length > 0), missing unhappy paths, and swallowed errors.
provenance: Composes with `implementer-shortcut-patterns` (the specific hollow shapes), `test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes` (the sterile-fixture inverse), and `test-creation-principles`. See the `faked-uat-theatre` and `agent-never-self-exempts` artifacts. Imported from legacy AgenticEngineering `AgenticGuidance`.

title: Signal and noise
description: Judge guidance by discriminatory power: signal lets the agent choose the right move; noise consumes attention without adding that power. Author for signal, cut noise.
statement: Judge any guidance an agent reads by its discriminatory power — signal lets the agent distinguish the correct action from the alternatives; noise consumes attention without adding that power — and author for high signal.
why: An agent (an owned-loop session, the orchestrator's routing prompt, a doc) operates in a finite attention window. Every sentence that does not help it choose the next move competes with the sentences that do; low-signal guidance does not merely fail to help, it crowds out the content that would.
howToApply: High signal is actionable, specific (concrete files/patterns/decisions), verifiable (a testable success criterion), and evidence-based (grounded in the codebase as it actually is). Noise causes attentional drift: meta-talk, stale context, generic philosophy, and structural redundancy (the same definition restated in several places). Per sentence ask: can I remove it without lowering the chance the task completes (→ noise)? does it point to a specific action/file/criterion (no → likely noise)? is it duplicated elsewhere (→ link the single source)? will it still be true later (no → stale)? Name concrete surfaces over vague gestures and link a single source of truth rather than restating it.
provenance: Composes with the `guidance-quality` principle (the authoring moves that add signal). Imported from legacy AgenticEngineering `AgenticGuidance`.

title: De-noising promotes a signal, never drops it
description: When a dense observability surface is de-noised, every signal is kept as a low-salience rendering — a stamp, a thin line, a badge — never deleted; de-noise lowers the volume of a signal, it does not hide it.
statement: When you de-noise a crowded view, demote each crowding element to a low-salience rendering — never remove it. The boundary is sharp: lowering a real coupling's salience (a thin line, a small per-thing stamp) is de-noise; making it un-recoverable from the picture is a drop, and a drop is information loss. If a thing was true enough to draw, it stays drawn at lower volume.
why: The observability surface exists to expose couplings the operator must see and judge — that is its whole job (`observability-first`: the system surfaces, the operator decides). A de-noise that DROPS an edge or flattens distinct edges into one generic badge silently erases exactly the signal the surface was built to carry, and the loss is invisible: the picture looks clean precisely because the thing you needed is gone. This is the trap ADR-0088's generic consumer-only bookshelf stamp fell into — it kept that an island used SOME shared island but lost WHICH one and the DIRECTION, a lossy near-drop that hid the `studio → cli` coupling the boundary system exists to surface (ADR-0102 Context §1). The cost is paid twice: a dropped signal cannot be judged, and a flattened one looks benign, so an architecturally important relationship reads as routine.
howToApply: Before removing anything to reduce clutter, ask: is what I am removing a SIGNAL (a real coupling, a real state) or pure decoration? A signal must be PROMOTED, not dropped — re-rendered at lower salience but still recoverable: ADR-0074 §1 ('de-noise visually … never by dropping edges') is the dependency-graph instance; ADR-0102 generalises it to ANY visual de-noise — a shared island promotes each incident edge to a per-island icon stamp (the edge kept as a badge, placement carrying its direction), rather than the road vanishing. Prefer a de-noise that carries the SAME information at lower volume (identity + direction preserved) over one that summarises it away (a generic 'uses a shared thing' badge drops which and whither). Reach for an outright drop only for genuine decoration that carries no signal. This is the world-map application of `signal-and-noise` (cut noise, keep signal): here the real coupling is the signal, the low-salience stamp is the de-noise. Whether a surfaced coupling is WRONG stays a human read, not a render-time verdict — promotion keeps it visible so the operator can judge it (`observability-first`); it does not flag it.
provenance: Graduated 2026-06-25 (ADR-0095 / the ADR-0102 build's librarian pass) — ADR-0102 named this durable rule ('de-noising promotes an edge, never drops it') but HELD authoring it until a second consumer existed; the per-island-icon-stamp build is that second consumer (the first being ADR-0074 §1's dependency-graph form). A distinct principle, not a refinement of `signal-and-noise`: it carries a rule that one does not — promote-not-drop, de-noise-never-hides-signal — and applies to the observability render, not to agent-readable guidance. ADR-0102 §References confirms the angle is novel ('No existing artifact covers the de-noise-never-hides-signal rule'). Generalises ADR-0074 §1 from the dependency graph to any visual de-noise; cross-links `signal-and-noise` (parent: cut noise, keep signal) and `observability-first` (sibling: the surface exposes, the operator judges).

title: Plain language first
description: Lead with the stake, gloss every internal term and ADR number on first use, and draw structural questions — so a reader without the repo loaded can decide.
statement: Write every artifact so a newcomer with the repo NOT loaded grasps the stake in the first sentence and never hits an unexplained internal term.
why: Our artifacts are read by newcomers and by agents that pull them as just-in-time context without the codebase in mind. A bare identifier (`renderBody`, `STORYTREE_STUDIO_STORE`) or a bare ADR number (`ADR-0018 §D3`) is noise to that reader (see `signal-and-noise`): it consumes attention without conferring the power to decide. An artifact that opens with the decision instead of the stake makes the reader earn the "why should I care" that should have been free.
howToApply: Three checks, all observable. (1) Stake in sentence one — the first sentence says what breaks, or what is blocked, in plain terms, before any identifier or ADR number (e.g. "Edit a Library entry in the studio today and it silently loses its structured fields."). (2) Jargon budget = zero — every internal term, code identifier, and ADR number gets a ≤7-word gloss or a link on its first use; count the unexplained ones, the target is none (`renderBody` → "the function that turns structured fields into the markdown you see"). (3) Draw the structure — if the subject is a structure, flow, or state machine, include a diagram, not only prose. This is the structural cure `guidance-quality` argues for — a template field or a slot, not a "please write clearly" exhortation; the `open-question` template operationalises check 1 via its required `stakes` lead and check 3 via its `## Diagram` slot.

title: Stale prerequisite links are phantoms
description: A cross-story dependency edge with no shared observable is a phantom; removing it is map correction, not loosening — the within-unit proof ladder stays sacred.
statement: Distinguish the sacred within-unit proof ladder from a contestable cross-story dependency edge: when a `boundary` edge gates a unit and a staleness suspicion arises, ask not only 'heal the upstream?' but 'is this edge itself a phantom?'
why: Across stories, a story depends on another only through a declared `boundary`, and that edge makes a downstream proof meaningful in context. But edges go stale — most often when an ADR or an upstream interface is amended and a downstream story still carries an edge reflecting the old intent. The entanglement no longer exists: a phantom, still drawn on the map, pointing at nothing. Removing it is map correction; the dependency mechanism stays load-bearing, the removed edge never was.
howToApply: Compare what the two stories’ proofs actually verify, observable-anchored not authorship-anchored: read the downstream interface and the observables its UAT/integration tests pin, and the candidate-upstream `boundary` and the observables its tests pin. No shared observable → phantom, removable (surface to the operator; DAG-shape changes are operator territory). Shared observable → load-bearing; keep it and heal the chain. Partial overlap keeps the edge; if the downstream’s own proofs are stale, amend the downstream first; never re-target an edge (map correction removes edges that point at nothing, it does not point them elsewhere). When in doubt, heal the chain.
provenance: Composes with the `defects-amend-the-owning-story` principle (that expands the DAG; this contracts it); both reach the operator before the DAG shape changes. See the `dependency` and `boundary` definitions (ADR-0010). Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/stale-prerequisite-links-are-phantoms.yml`.

why: A test is only as good as the observable it pins. A test that checks a file exists (not its contents), that a function was called (not what it produced), or that a flag is true (not the result it claims) gives a green signal with no proof behind it. The proof ladder (contract → integration → UAT) is trustworthy only if each rung’s assertions bind to external truth rather than a gameable signal.
title: Test creation principles
statement: A test must verify the actual outcome rather than a proxy for it — real content over existence, user-facing behaviour over implementation detail — and must genuinely fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.
howToApply: Verify actual outcomes, not success flags — check file contents, assert user-facing behaviour, include concrete assertions about what was produced. Avoid the hollow shapes in `reward-hacking` and `implementer-shortcut-patterns`. One behaviour per test, clear names — and when the unit declares contracts, the name of the test proving one must carry that contract's id VERBATIM, the convention being `describe("<contract-id>: …")`: the coverage check maps each declared contract to a test by name (ADR-0122), so an invented, abbreviated, or re-derived prefix reports the contract uncovered even when the test genuinely proves it. The ids are in the phase brief — copy them, never restyle them. Order-independent, granularity matched to the tier; pin the behaviour that matters and do not over-test; use real collaborators where the tier allows (no mocks within an organism) and cover the unhappy path and edge cases. The sharpest single check — the deletion check: if the feature were removed, would this test fail? If not, it pins nothing and is a false green.
provenance: Same falsifiability discipline as `verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate`, applied to assertions. See the `contract-test` and `mock-uat-seam` definitions. Imported from legacy AgenticEngineering `AgenticGuidance`.
description: A test must verify the real outcome, not a proxy — content over existence, behaviour over implementation detail — and must fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.

why:
The `mock-uat-seam` says where a mock may live (the contract tier yes; within an organism no) but is silent on whether a permitted mock is sterile or adversarial. A mock that satisfies the no-mocks-in-the-organism rule can still be defective if it stages a world more forgiving than what the code will actually meet — priming a stub with one platform's error wording, pre-creating state production does not create, granting access production's runtime lacks.

Two axes of that forgiveness are worth naming apart, because they fail DIFFERENT questions below and a fixture can be clean on one while defective on the other.

**ABSENCE** — the fixture installs a property production lacks, and the sharpest case is a property that is itself an absence. Mocking a third-party module WHOLE does not merely replace its behaviour; it pre-installs the absence of every runtime guard the real library enforces, and no test can observe a guard the mock deleted. Measured on PR #770: `pnpm --filter studio test` ran 885/885 green with the defect present, while the same commit threw inside the real xterm 5.x the moment `term.unicode` was touched — `You must set the allowProposedApi option to true`. The throw in `initTab` silently prevented the spawn, so the Electron e2e surfaced it not as the guard's own message but as an opaque `one live session after expand (got null)`. The green 885 was evidence about the mock and said nothing about the library.

**MAGNITUDE** — the fixture's values are each individually legal, but their RANGE cannot discriminate the rule under test, so a rule tuned against the fixture degrades to a no-op at production's scale with every assertion still true. Measured 2026-07-25 on the ADR-0242 lit-lane width rule (`trailFillWidth(usage) - 1.7`): `pnpm --filter @storytree/app-surface test` passed 122, including the assertion that the lane is narrower than its road, while a live probe on the SAME code reported lanes of 8.85 on a road of 10.55 and 9.68 on 11.38 — a rim under 1px, the lane covering the road it was meant to ride. The fixture's widest segment carries `usage: 2` (`trailFillWidth(2) = 3.75`); the live map routes trunks at usage ~30. The fix — capping the lane at `trailFillWidth(1)` — is one that fixture could not have distinguished either way, and that is the tell: it was not a fixture missing a case, it was a fixture whose numeric span could not answer the question it was being asked.

Distinct from two neighbours, which is why this stays one principle rather than folding into either. `a-mocked-seam-leaves-its-default-implementation-unproven` covers OUR OWN default implementation behind an injected seam, and its remedy — drive the default against a real substrate — is available there and structurally unavailable here, because the real substrate is a third-party library the unit runtime never loads. `pin-the-dual-runtime-import-form` covers one dependency crossing TWO runtimes (proof versus ship), not a mock diverging from the real library inside one.
title: Test fixtures mirror production failure modes
statement: A fixture, stub, or mock must be designed so the test fails when production fails, and it hands the test a false green along two distinct axes: by pre-installing a property production might lack — including the ABSENCE a full module mock installs, erasing every runtime guard the real dependency enforces — and by carrying values whose numeric RANGE cannot discriminate the rule under test, so a rule tuned to the fixture's small numbers degrades to a no-op at production's magnitude with every assertion still green.
howToApply:
Per pre-install, ask in order: (1) Inversion — if I remove it, does the test still cover its observable? Yes → convenience/isolation, fine; No → load-bearing, continue. (2) Production guarantee — does production guarantee the property by build config, a documented invariant, or the boundary contract it stands on? Yes → it mirrors a real guarantee, fine; No → it masks a production failure mode, defective. Remediate by dropping the pre-install and asserting the typed error production should return, adding a sibling test for the property-absent case, or escalating so production actually guarantees the property.

**Question 2's recurring class: the option-gated third-party surface.** A full module mock answers question 2 "no guarantee" BY CONSTRUCTION — it installs the absence of every runtime guard the real library enforces — and the class that keeps biting is the enabling option: a constructor or config flag the library refuses to work without. The remedy is NOT to un-mock: the unit runtime cannot load the real library, which is the whole reason the mock exists, so "just use the real thing" trades a false green for no test at all. Instead PIN the enabling option as a contract assertion on the mocked constructor call, which regains a hold on the one precondition the suite structurally cannot observe — on PR #770 that is `tdp-activates-unicode11-widths` in `TerminalDock.test.tsx`, asserting `allowProposedApi: true` actually reached the `Terminal` constructor. Pair it with an e2e that NAMES the throw (a `win.on('pageerror')` hook), so the next such guard arrives as its own message instead of as a downstream null that costs a diagnosis pass.

**(3) Discriminating range** — when the rule under test is SCALE-dependent (stroke widths, spacing, density, keep-out radii, thresholds), do the fixture's values span the magnitude the rule will actually meet? This question has no inversion and no guarantee to check: a value range is not a pre-install, so questions 1 and 2 cannot ask it, and a hand-built fixture of small round numbers passes both while proving nothing about the rule. Establish the production distribution — probe the live surface, or read the code that generates the values — then either widen the fixture to span it or add one case at the real high end. Where the production distribution genuinely cannot be established, the green is not-yet-evidence and must be reported as such, never carried forward as proof.

Fires hardest when scaffolding fixtures for filesystem/runtime/permission/external-process state, when mocking a third-party module whole, when proving a scale-dependent geometry or layout rule against a hand-built fixture, and when re-authoring tests after a UAT-caught defect.
provenance:
Composes with `implementer-shortcut-patterns` (sterile fixture here, hollow implementation there) and `tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep`. See the `mock-uat-seam` definition. Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes.yml`.

EXTENDED 2026-08-01 by guidance-curator, discharging TWO adjudicated friction items in one edit (ADR-0168 D4 bounded pre-merge drain): `friction-mocked-seam-blind-to-proposed-api-guards` — the ABSENCE axis, question 2's option-gated third-party class and the pin-the-enabling-option remedy — and `friction-synthetic-fixture-hid-a-real-scale-geometry-bug` — the MAGNITUDE axis, question 3. Both adjudications routed edit-existing HERE, and both rulings are honoured as written rather than re-litigated.

SHAPE — one artifact, two clauses kept visibly APART rather than merged into one. The items are siblings ("the fixture stages a world the real one does not match") and merging read as the tidier edit, but they fail DIFFERENT questions: the absence case is caught by the existing two-question test UNCHANGED, so it needed only its class and remedy attached to question 2, while the magnitude case is caught by neither — a value range is not a pre-install, so there is nothing to invert and question 1 is meaningless against it. A merged clause would have implied the inversion test catches a magnitude defect. It does not, and stating otherwise would have made the guidance actively misleading on exactly the case it was extended to cover.

EDIT-FIRST SWEEP (`edit-first-curation`) — all five guidance-bearing tiers searched across the live corpus: principle (71), guardrail (17), pattern (25), process (17), definition (52), 182 units. Confirmed on the bytes before writing that this artifact carried none of "proposed" / "allowProposedApi" / "third-party" / "module mock" / "runtime guard" / "enabling option" / "magnitude" / "scale" / "numeric range" / "span the real", so neither claim had already landed here; the magnitude probes (`magnitude`, `scale-dependent`, `numeric range`, `production distribution`, `synthetic fixture`, `hand-built fixture`) returned ZERO hits corpus-wide across all five tiers. NAMED REJECTIONS: `a-green-positional-oracle-is-necessary-not-sufficient` — ruled out by the adjudicator and confirmed here; it covers what gets STROKED and how the field is FRAMED and its remedy is render-and-look, whereas the magnitude claim is that the fixture's numbers could not discriminate the rule EITHER WAY, which no oracle over that fixture could repair. `a-mocked-seam-leaves-its-default-implementation-unproven` — the nearest neighbour, surfaced by THIS sweep and named by neither adjudication; rejected as home because it covers our own default implementation behind an injected seam, whose remedy of driving the default against a real substrate is structurally unavailable when the real substrate is a third-party library the unit runtime never loads. `pin-the-dual-runtime-import-form` — rejected; its axis is one dependency across TWO runtimes (proof versus ship), not a mock diverging from the real library inside one. `definition:fixture` — a bare definition, carries no rule. Both cousins are now CITED rather than restated (`reference-dont-restate`).

KIND — remains `principle`; no promotion to guardrail, on the guidance-curator enforcer test. Nothing in storytree deterministically refuses either defect: `check:coverage` maps DECLARED capability contracts to tests by NAME and cannot read a fixture's numeric span, and ADR-0252 D1's vacuous-proof instrument locates option-form skips, so it is blind to a shape where every test RUNS and asserts truthfully about a mock. Fixture magnitude in particular cannot be judged mechanically without knowing the production distribution — the adjudicator's own Q7 finding. Same call, same reason, as `a-mocked-seam-leaves-its-default-implementation-unproven`, which was also routed guardrail and authored principle on this test. It promotes if an instrument is ever built that can compare a fixture's value range against the production distribution; that instrument is not chartered by this write.
description: A fixture must fail when production fails — false-green either by pre-installing a property production lacks (a full module mock installs the ABSENCE of the real library's runtime guards) or by carrying a numeric RANGE too narrow to discriminate the rule under test.

why:
Tightening a shared validator (a loader, deserializer, schema constraint, newly-required field) can invalidate fixtures or seed data anywhere that leaned on the old looser behaviour, and those regressions surface at runtime — a fixture fails to parse when its test runs — not at type-check or build time. So the change looks safe: it compiles, the owning capability is green, the UAT passes. The node rollup and approval gate read the event store plus on-disk evidence; neither re-runs the whole suite, so a story can reach `healthy` and be approved with cross-capability fixture regressions undetected.

The same blindness takes a second and sharper form when a sweep is scoped by SEARCHING FOR a marker instead of by enumerating the units. A search keyed on an annotation cannot see a unit that never carried one — and where the parser supplies a DEFAULT for the missing annotation, the absent marker still resolves to some value, one the search never reported. When that default is fail-closed it resolves to the most conservative value, which is very often exactly the value the sweep exists to re-examine. So the sweep is blind precisely where it most needs sight, and — because every unit it did find was handled — it reports itself COMPLETE. Measured: the ADR-0209 UAT-witness migration scoped itself by the literal tag `witness: human`, carried a running tally across 25 stories, and handed off with "no unadjudicated human criteria remain"; 5 legs in `binding-staleness` carried NO witness tag, resolved fail-closed to `human` by default, and had never been adjudicated. It surfaced only because the final count was re-derived from a parse rather than carried forward — the parse reproduced the tally exactly (42 human / 209 machine / 0 model) and then returned a fourth bucket the tally had no column for. Uncaught, the migration would have closed as complete and its closing recommendation to the owner would have rested on an incomplete measurement.
title: Tightening a shared contract needs a full sweep
statement: When a change tightens a shared parsing/validation contract — it now rejects inputs it previously accepted — run the full test suite across every capability that touches that contract, confirmed green, before the story's UAT is signed and before the result is approved onto the trunk; and whatever the sweep, derive its scope by ENUMERATING the universe of units and resolving each one's value, never by searching for the marker you care about — a search cannot see the units that never carried the marker, and where the parser defaults a missing value fail-closed, those are precisely the units the sweep exists to re-examine.
howToApply:
Discriminator: (1) did the change make a shared parsing/validation surface reject an input shape it formerly accepted (a stricter loader/parser, a new rejection, rejecting unknown fields, a tightened or added schema constraint, a newly-required field)? No → the rule does not arm. Yes → continue. (2) Is the full suite green across every capability, not just the owner? Yes → proceed with the sign and the approval. No → block; a red sibling suite forfeits the sign and approval even with a clean tree and a passing walkthrough; route the broken fixtures back to their owning capability (defects amend the owning story) before re-attempting. A loosening (accept more) cannot invalidate an existing fixture, so it does not trigger. Always sweep the whole workspace — catching other capabilities' fixtures is the point.

SCOPING THE SWEEP — how you compute "the whole surface". This clause arms on ANY sweep that will claim completeness (a contract tightening, a corpus migration, an adjudication pass), not only on a tightening. Derive the scope from the UNIVERSE of units and resolve each unit's value; never grep for the marker. Concretely: enumerate every unit of the kind you are sweeping, run each one through the SAME parser production reads, and bucket by its RESOLVED value. A `grep` for the annotation is not that, and neither is a running tally carried forward across sessions. Two checks tell you the scoping was honest. (a) The buckets must SUM to the enumerated total — a bucket you have no column for is a set of units you never looked at, and a tally that reconciles against itself proves nothing, because it and the search share the same blind spot. (b) Name the parser-side DEFAULT for the field you are sweeping and ask what an ABSENT value resolves to; if it resolves to the value under migration, the untagged units are the ones most likely to need your judgement and a marker search is guaranteed to miss every one of them. That second check is the whole point: "a tag search misses the untagged" is generic craft, but the direction of the miss is not — a fail-closed default aims the blind spot straight at the units you were chartered to re-examine. Note that this is a rule about a completeness-claiming SWEEP, not about reconnaissance; `asset:exploration-principles` is right that exploration samples rather than enumerates, and a sweep is the case where sampling is not allowed to stand in for the census.
provenance:
Composes with `test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes` (that prevents a sterile fixture passing; this catches a previously-valid fixture a contract change just broke). Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep.yml`.

EXTENDED 2026-08-01 discharging `tag-keyed-corpus-sweep-misses-untagged-legs` (ADR-0168 D4 friction drain; route edit-existing). The adjudication routed it here rather than to a new principle: this artifact already owns "sweep the whole surface" but scoped that by the CONTRACT, never saying how the surface is COMPUTED, so the scoping clause is the missing half rather than a near-duplicate. The statement, gloss, Why and How-to-apply were extended; the arming condition for the tightening half is unchanged, and the new clause declares its own broader arming condition (any completeness-claiming sweep) rather than silently widening the old one. Measured instance: the ADR-0209 s8 UAT-witness migration scoped itself by the literal tag `witness: human`, tallied 25 stories, and handed off "no unadjudicated human criteria remain"; re-measuring by parsing every `stories/*/story.md` through `parseUatTestCriteria` reproduced the tally EXACTLY (42 human / 209 machine / 0 model) and returned a fourth bucket the tally had no column for — 5 legs in `binding-staleness` carrying no witness tag, resolved fail-closed to `human` per ADR-0106, never adjudicated. All five were decided `machine` and bound to command-bearing observe gates in PR #929, with zero refusals — i.e. the units the sweep was blind to were exactly the ones whose judgement it existed to make.

VERIFICATION 2026-08-01 — the drain flagged this item for MANDATORY corpus-investigator verification (highest blast radius; it renders into every session), and the check corrected the routing note on two points. Both corrections are reflected above, and NEITHER weakens the rule. (1) The adjudication recorded that "ADR-0247 D4 already supplies the mechanical fence for the witness case." It does not, yet. ADR-0247 is `accepted` (decided 2026-07-26) and D4 AUTHORISES the change in permissive language — `either` "may therefore be removed" from `UAT_TEST_CRITERION_WITNESSES` and from `resolveWitness`'s undecided branch, "lands as its own increment with its own red→green" — but the increment has not landed. As of this verification `UAT_TEST_CRITERION_WITNESSES` still contains `either`; `itemWitness` (packages/library/src/uat-test-criteria.ts) still returns `either` silently for an untagged leg; `resolveWitness` (packages/library/src/witness-resolution.ts) still resolves any non-`machine` value, `either` included, to `human`; a currently-passing test asserts that pre-D4 behaviour; and no `check:` script enforces the refusal. So the witness instance is DECIDED-NOT-BUILT, and until it lands this behavioural rule is the only thing standing between a sweep and the blind spot — which is precisely why it is stated as a principle and not deferred to a fence. (2) The friction item named `uat_witness`, `proof_mode` and reliability-gate `kind` as recurring instances of the shape. `proof_mode` is NOT one: it is a REQUIRED zod field on the node-spec `Frontmatter` with no `.optional()` and no `.default()`, so an absent `proof_mode` already throws at parse. That claim is dropped rather than carried forward. Reliability-gate `kind` IS a confirmed live instance — `itemKind` (packages/library/src/reliability-gates.ts) returns `observe` silently for an untagged gate, documented as "the conservative brownfield default" and covered by a passing test — so the CLASS is open even though one of its three named examples was wrong. Those code pointers are dated verification residue, not durable content, and are deliberately kept out of the rule body (`asset:anchor-implementation-surface`): re-derive them before treating them as current.

Five-tier sweep before the extension — principle / guardrail / pattern / process / definition. Nearest neighbours, all rejected as homes: `asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` (the closest, and genuinely distinct — it addresses the CONSUMER of an unchecked enumeration and prescribes re-deriving membership before using it as a worklist; here the producer's own scoping method was blind, so a faithful re-derivation using the SAME marker search would reproduce the blind spot exactly. The two are complementary: that one says re-derive, this one says what to re-derive FROM); `asset:a-fan-out-result-does-not-report-its-own-completeness` (same family — a short result reads exactly like a complete one — but its mechanism is members lost to a mid-run failure, not a scope that never included them); `asset:audit-the-signed-verdict` (about a PASS carrying short coverage, a different surface); `asset:exploration-principles` (not a rejection but a boundary — it prefers pattern-discovery over enumerating files, which is right for reconnaissance and wrong for a census, so the new clause names the distinction explicitly rather than leaving the two reading as contradictory). Nothing in the guardrail, process, or definition tiers governs how a sweep computes its scope.

KIND: stays a `principle`. It is not a guardrail because no deterministic enforcer refuses a marker-scoped sweep — and the verification above makes that concrete: the one mechanical fence that was believed to exist for the witness instance is decided but unbuilt, and no check covers the class at all. It would promote if a general "enumerate-and-reconcile" check were ever built.
description: When a change makes a shared validator reject inputs it used to accept, run the whole suite across every consuming capability green before the UAT is signed and the result approved — and scope any completeness-claiming sweep by enumerating the universe of units and resolving each one's value, never by searching for the marker.

title: Verify an edit persisted, or escalate
description: On the owned-loop file tools (and any agent doing contract-bearing writes), read back every contract-bearing write and record a structured assumption-violation before any fallback — a silent fallback that hides the failure is banned. The live SDK leaf and the prove-it gate mitigate this differently (no Bash to fall back to; the gate re-reads downstream), so the discipline bites on the owned-loop path, not as a universal read-back mandate.
statement: When you write through the owned-loop file tools (`packages/agent/src/fs-tools.ts` — the offline/deterministic executor and pivot-out fallback), or otherwise hold the read-back yourself for a contract-bearing edit whose persistence your deliverable depends on, read the file back and confirm the intended content is present before proceeding; if it did not persist, record a structured assumption-violation in your return before applying any workaround. The live SDK leaf (ADR-0030) and the prove-it gate cover this by other means — see howToApply for which surface you are on.
why: An edit/write tool can return success without the content landing on disk (filesystem interception, sandbox quirks, path-normalisation edge cases): the owned loop's `write_file` reports a byte count derived from the *input* string and `edit_file` reports success from the mere absence of a throw — neither reads the file back. The historical in-the-wild reaction — silently falling back to a shell heredoc — hides that failure: the orchestrator never learns the tool misbehaved, the escalation pathway is forfeit, and the symptom recurs unnamed next session. Two facts narrow where this still bites. The **live** runtime is the Claude Agent SDK leaf (ADR-0030), which writes through the SDK's own Write/Edit and carries **no Bash** in its tool surface, so a shell-heredoc fallback is unreachable there. And the spine's prove-it gate re-reads and re-tests written files out-of-band downstream, so a non-persistence that the write tool itself missed is still caught before a unit can go green. The discipline therefore earns its keep on the owned-loop path and for any agent that holds the read-back itself — one extra read per contract-bearing write turns a silent symptom into a structured signal the orchestrator already knows how to consume.
howToApply: First locate your write surface. On the **live SDK leaf**, the SDK's Write/Edit handle persistence and there is no shell fallback to slip into (Bash is not in the leaf tool surface) — the gate's downstream re-read is your backstop, so this principle is a non-mandate there. On the **owned-loop file tools** (`fs-tools.ts`), or any path where you issue the write and own the read-back, apply it directly. Contract-bearing = any write whose persistence your return summary implicitly claims (the discriminator: would my summary lie if this file were not on disk?) — source files, test scaffolds, evidence rows, schema changes, spec amendments; throwaway scratch is out of scope. Issue the write, immediately read the path, verify the read reflects the intent. On failure (unchanged/absent/truncated/pre-call content): do NOT silently fall back; record an assumption-violation in your return (`{ briefed, observed, severity }`) the orchestrator parses programmatically; only after that record exists is a fallback (e.g. a heredoc) permitted as recovery. The contract pinned is the visibility of the failure, not the success of the recovery.
provenance: Composes with `implementer-shortcut-patterns` and `test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes` — the same falsifiability discipline applied to a write’s persistence. Imported from v1 `assets/guidelines/verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate.yml`.

title: Implementer shortcut patterns
description: Five hollow-implementation shapes that pass shape-level tests but fail UAT — and the shape-vs-depth check that catches them.
statement: An implementation that satisfies a test's shape via a shortcut while leaving the real contract obligation un-implemented is defective even when every contract and integration test passes green; a test's contract is the observable the production code must produce, not a signature, a return type, or an entered code path.
problem: When the owned loop works at the leaf it is rewarded for green tests. If a test pins shape but not depth, the loop can earn green with a hollow implementation and the breakage stays invisible until the story's UAT runs the canonical journey end-to-end — the slowest, most expensive channel. This is the 'test green, production red' defect class, the inverse of a sterile fixture.
approach: Know the five sub-patterns: (1) help-text narrowing — assert a `--help` mentions a feature instead of running the canonical invocation through real dispatch → logic → output; (2) TODO-and-exit stub on the production arm — wire a test-only seam but leave the real-user branch a TODO + error-exit; (3) discarded typed parameter — accept a typed collaborator, suppress the unused-warning, never invoke it; (4) mock shipped in the production path — a mock reachable from the shipped artifact, gated only by a runtime flag; (5) silent fallback to fake data — a resource-acquisition path that substitutes a placeholder and returns success. Per seam, in order: shape vs depth (do the assertions observe the chain’s terminal effect, or an intermediate shape?), production-path coverage (does any test exercise the real production branch under a stub seam?), then name the shortcut and apply its discipline — wire the production arm, consume the parameter, exclude the mock, fail loud with a typed error.
tradeoffs: Wiring the production arm now costs upfront effort paid once; deferring it pays the UAT-only catch of every future regression forever on the slowest channel. Default to wiring it.
