Measured: a session was briefed that the `process` artifact ADR-0252 D4 mandates "does not exist", and an offline `library artifact list process` agreed, returning 13; live `--pg` returned 15, including the very artifact the brief's whole mandate was to author. The offline seed is an export that lags live edits, and the brief's enumeration was taken from that same pre-move state — so the two were one reading counted twice, not two witnesses. Before scoring a second read as corroboration, ask whether it is downstream of the first; if it is, you still have one observation. `asset:capture-the-oracle-for-a-convention-you-dont-own` is this same shape in the test-authoring setting — a test that computes its expected value the way the code does proves only that two copies of one belief agree.

**Any reading of a moving shared surface is a state claim, and it expires — a COUNT no less than an absence.** "X does not exist", "nothing covers this", "the prerequisite has not landed" are the obvious shape; so are "there are 9 open capabilities", "the tier holds one row", "the drain is RED at 14 open". All of them are readings of a moving shared surface, timestamped at the moment they were taken and silently false afterwards — and that holds whether the claim reached you in a brief or you made the observation yourself early in the session. Cardinality has to be named rather than left implied, because a positive count does not READ as an existence claim to someone applying the negative wording, and it is not falsified the way one is: an absence dies to a single counterexample, while a count dies to the number simply MOVING — no counterexample anywhere, and nothing on the page that looks wrong. On a store many sessions mutate concurrently (ADR-0009/0023) the window is minutes, not days. Re-read the premise against the enforced source immediately before acting on it, and hardest when acting on it IS the mandate: authoring the thing said not to exist, PUBLISHING the figure into an ADR, a plan, a decision document or a report, or escalating a block (`asset:escalate-up-when-blocked-or-out-of-scope` carries that precondition at the escalation moment). One `--pg` query is the whole cost. Measured three times, and the third is the rule's own consumer. (1) The `process` case above — a brief and an offline `list process` both said 13, live `--pg` said 15. (2) 2026-08-02: a brief asserted the live open-question tier was EMPTY; it held exactly one row, `oq-public-live-forest-on-the-website`. Its CONCLUSION survived and its stated REASON did not — the tier is UNHOMED, not empty, because ADR-0267 D4 stores the containment edge on the CHILD and derives an arc's question view by query, and that row carries no `arcRef`. The same brief's other limb was an arc count; the live figure that day was 17. (3) 2026-08-03: a board-drain brief asserted the friction drain was "RED at 14 open / 13 routable" and the live measure was "WARN — 12 open". Two sibling routings had landed in between, so the stale figure named the wrong BAND rather than merely the wrong magnitude — it reported a ceiling breached that was not. Cost was zero only because the brief instructed a re-measure and it was taken before any verdict rested on it. Distinguish this from `asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked`, which governs a set nobody ever checked: here the enumeration WAS checked and was correct when made, which is why re-deriving it with a different idiom would not have saved the session and re-reading the live source would. Distinguish it too from `asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted`: the offline read genuinely ran and genuinely returned not-found — false corroboration, not an unrun check. And from `asset:a-handoff-claim-that-work-landed-is-unverified-state`, which is deliberately NOT widened to meet this: its scope is anchored to git branch and merge state in its statement, in its worked examples and in its own test, so a live-store tier fact has a different authoritative source and a different enforcement mechanism; the two cross-reference rather than converge.

WHY ONE EDIT AND NOT TWO: read separately they are a grep-hygiene note and a briefing-staleness note with nothing in common. Read together they are one defect in this artifact's TRIGGER. The rule fires "when sources disagree", which presupposes both sources were consulted and the conflict is visible — and neither incident ever reached that state. They are the two silent halves of one rule, and as two separate bullets each would have had to cross-reference the other on its only load-bearing line. EVIDENCE, with the two worked instances kept INLINE rather than pushed here, because `asset:example-carries-the-discriminator` makes them decoration without their rationale: grep — `@storytree/cli` matched prose in a comment at `apps/studio/server/codeStamp.ts:82` while being absent from `apps/studio/package.json` (the studio dropped it in ADR-0112), briefly scoping the ADR-0267 arc-rollup join to `packages/cli` until a package.json read corrected it to `packages/drive`; brief — an offline `list process` returned 13 and agreed with the brief, live `--pg` returned 15 including `verification-decay-detection`, the artifact the brief existed to author, and the item reproduced itself inside its own adjudication, whose corpus search found the seed 11 artifacts behind live. KIND: an edit to an existing principle, so the enforcer test does not arise, and no guardrail was minted because none would be honest — no deterministic mechanism can read an arbitrary prose brief's corpus-state premises, nor judge whether a scan answers the question it was asked. STATEMENT DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED: both routing rulings fenced the edit to `howToApply`, and the opening line already reaches past "disagree" with "not the one that merely mentions the fact"; widening the statement itself is a separate call and not this seat's to take unasked. EDIT-FIRST (`asset:edit-first-curation`) — all five guidance-bearing tiers swept live: principle (71), guardrail (17), pattern (25), process (17), definition (52). Named rejections. `asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` (principle, the nearest neighbour by far and NOT named at adjudication — it excludes both cases by its own fence, governing a set nobody ever checked and stating explicitly that staleness is not its axis; the brief's enumeration was checked and correct when made, and the grep genuinely ran and answered its own question correctly). `asset:an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` (principle, the real second candidate for the grep instance and it does own "a text scan sees occurrence, not dependency" — rejected on remedy: it REPLACES a mis-chosen observable inside a check you are authoring, where the remedy here is a PRECEDENCE move to the source that enforces, which is this artifact's own sentence). `asset:capture-the-oracle-for-a-convention-you-dont-own` (principle, states the non-independence shape exactly but in the test-authoring setting — cited as sibling, not folded, per this corpus's habit of growing that family by narrow siblings). `asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted` (principle, nearest sibling for the brief case but covers a checker that could not RUN; ruled out at adjudication and re-confirmed here). `asset:pull-based-context-architecture` (pattern — the briefer-side answer, brief thinly and pull just-in-time; this is the briefed reader's side, and this artifact already cites it). `asset:library-edit-ceremony`, `asset:friction-adjudication` (process — procedures, not source-precedence rules). The `definition` tier holds terminology only; `asset:plan`'s freshness check (ADR-0183 D2) is the right reflex with the wrong instrument, since it git-logs PATHS and passes clean on a false corpus-state assertion. Nothing in the corpus becomes redundant; this is a pure addition. Consumers unchanged, plus any session handed a brief asserting what does not exist, and any agent deriving a dependency or boundary set from a text scan.
Widened 2026-08-03 by guidance-curator in the ADR-0168 D4 board drain, discharging friction `friction-brief-asserted-stale-live-tier-state` (routed edit-existing by graduation-synthesist, corpus-investigator-verified). WHAT CHANGED, and only this: the 2026-08-01 expiring-state-claim passage, from NEGATIVE EXISTENCE to any reading of a moving shared surface, with CARDINALITY named explicitly. The rule was stated narrower than its OWN evidence — its worked example is already a count (offline `list process` returned 13, live returned 15) while the lead sentence and all three of its listed shapes were framed as non-existence, so an agent holding "there are 16 active arcs" would not recognise the passage as addressed to them. A count is also falsified differently, which is why the widening carries a reason rather than just a longer list: an absence dies to one counterexample, a count dies to the number moving, with nothing on the page that looks wrong. EVIDENCE ADDED, live-verified rather than taken from the item's prose: the open-question tier held exactly one row, `oq-public-live-forest-on-the-website`, carrying no `arcRef` — confirmed through the mechanism ADR-0267 D4 itself specifies, since a dangling arcRef is refused at write time so any stamp would have surfaced under exactly one arc; and 17 arcs were live that day, internally cross-checked as 32 total = 17 active + 15 closed. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED: the "16 vs 17" delta. That the brief said 16 is the filer's self-report and the original brief text is not in the corpus; the rule rests on the confirmed facts instead. ALSO RECORDED: the third instance is this rule's own consumer failing at it — the brief for the board-drain session that adjudicated this item asserted the friction drain was RED at 14 open when the live measure was WARN at 12, which is a wrong BAND and not merely a wrong magnitude. It is disclosed as a reinforcement observed at the adjudicating seat, and the item's own impact paragraph had predicted exactly that consumer ("arc counts, artifact counts, drain ceilings"). The illustration now names an unrelated shape ("there are 9 open capabilities"); the confirmed evidence below it is unchanged.
description: When sources disagree, resolve to the one the system enforces — the live projection beats the seed, the schema beats prose, the event log beats hand-written status.

title: No claim without evidence
description: A claim is admissible only with the evidence that proves it — verbatim output, a citable path/line, an event id — never a paraphrase or an impression.
statement: A claim is admissible only with the evidence that proves it — a verbatim runner summary, a citable path and line, a named command and field, an event id — never a paraphrase, an impression, or a guess.
why: The f53caac lesson: "all tests pass", reported without the verbatim final summary line, was falsified by an empirical re-run. Paraphrase is the smell — it is where optimism, hallucination, and reward-hacking hide. The same failure generalises: a finding asserted from impression fabricates state, and an "environment / OS / flaky" framing dodges falsification entirely.
howToApply: Test claims: run the canonical command end-to-end on the post-change tree, read its output, attach the verbatim final summary line. Findings: every one carries an evidence path that names a real source proving it — path:line, command + field, or an event-store query; when the corpus is silent, return "could not determine", never a guess. Environment/flaky framings are inadmissible without three-run determinism evidence, an authoritative citation, or an in-corpus counter-example check — search the workspace for a working idiom first.
provenance: Harvested from V1 `build-rust` (the f53caac lesson) + `system-investigator` + `trace-explorer`; graduated for v2 (owner call, 2026-06-14). Consumers: corpus-investigator, friction-analyst, leaf-* (escalation).

title: story-author
description: The dedicated author of the disk-canonical work hierarchy (story › capability › contract): it bounds one provable journey per story and writes only frontmatter-markdown under `stories/**`, through a fail-closed spawned/native subagent file-tool fence.
oneLine: The dedicated author of the disk-canonical work hierarchy: one provable journey per story, the dependency graph between them, authored only as frontmatter-markdown under `stories/**`.
role: story-author owns WHAT gets built: the work DAG of stories, capabilities, and contracts. It reads the current hierarchy from the disk-canonical `stories/**` frontmatter-markdown files, bounds each story to one complete user journey, decides whether and how to split, drafts the proof-walkthrough that sizes a unit before its prose, and wires the `depends_on` graph from real prerequisites. It authors only that surface, through the sanctioned spawned/native subagent file tools whose fail-closed fence permits `stories/**` and denies every other write. It does NOT author Library knowledge, use a live DB write boundary, implement, run the gate, prove, sign, or promote: a unit EXISTS when its file is authored; green-ness is the gate's later, separate verdict.
outcome: Each authored story states one journey whose outcome needs no conjunctions and whose proof is a single coherent UAT walkthrough; every capability/contract under it has a writable proof at its tier; the dependency graph is acyclic and re-derivable from real prerequisites. Every changed frontmatter-markdown file is under `stories/**`, is read back after writing, and is visible through the existing corpus validators and read-only work-hierarchy CLI surfaces. A denied or non-persisting write is reported to the caller — a silent no-op is a failure.
tools: Read / Grep / Glob plus Write / Edit only inside `stories/**`, supplied by the spawned/native subagent file-tool surface. The spawned runtime enforces that scope fail-closed and exposes no Bash, so a shell cannot bypass the fence. Read-only work-hierarchy inspection uses the existing `storytree tree [<story-id>]` and `storytree tree spec <node-id>` surfaces when the caller/native surface exposes them; after a spawned write, the caller runs those projections and the existing corpus validators. Least-authority: no Library artifact write, no DB/`--pg`, no gate, no build/promotion/signing verb, no implementation.
workflow:
**session_start:** read the target brief and the current work hierarchy from disk under `stories/**`; search tier rules just-in-time, never preload them. Use the read-only `storytree tree [<story-id>]` / `storytree tree spec <node-id>` projections when available; they inspect the disk hierarchy, not a Library write store.

1. Bound the journey (one journey per story); apply the splitting-rule only on its two falsifiable triggers.
2. Draft the proof-walkthrough FIRST at each tier — if no coherent walkthrough exists, re-tier before authoring.
3. Author or amend only `stories/**` frontmatter-markdown through the fenced Write/Edit tools; wire `depends_on` from real prerequisites only. Never use a Library artifact command for a work unit.
4. Read every changed file back and confirm the intended frontmatter and markdown persisted. Return the changed node ids so the caller can run the existing corpus validators plus `storytree tree <story-id>` / `storytree tree spec <node-id>` as the post-spawn parse/readback check. Escalate a denied or non-persisting write. Stop — never implement, run the gate, prove, sign, or promote.
escalation: Story-shape calls that outlive the unit (a new tier boundary, a cross-cutting split, a decision worth an ADR) are surfaced to the human outer loop, never decided unilaterally — but a call the owner already DIRECTED in conversation is recorded, not re-asked: author its ADR born `accepted` (`adr new --decided`, ADR-0110), not hedged `proposed`. A write that won't persist is reported, not worked around.
provenance: Evolved from V1 `legacy/Agentic/agents/planner/story-writer` (disposition: evolve). The dedicated story author the owner asked for (2026-06-14) after seeing stories improvised by the leaf mechanics or the orchestrator session. Re-tiered to v2's story › capability › contract. Corrected 2026-07-10 against ADR-0039 d.2 and ADR-0137 d.1: work units are disk-canonical `stories/**` frontmatter-markdown written through the spawned/native subagent's fail-closed file-tool fence, not live Library artifacts; the DB-only write guidance was removed. Distinct from guidance-curator (rule content) and librarian-curator (corpus structure). No ADRs injected — searched just-in-time. Owner extension (2026-06-26, ADR-0110): a story-shape ADR the owner DIRECTED in conversation is authored `accepted` (the `adr new --decided` path), not hedged `proposed` for a redundant end-of-flow ratification.

title: glue-worker
description: The spawned write-scoped leaf that makes ONE minimal scoped edit — un-asserted connective code within a story (wiring, composition, a few routes) — inside a caller-declared path fence, then stops. The desktop chat's scoped-glue actuator (ADR-0160): it honours a task prompt, signs nothing, and lands through the existing gate→PR path.
oneLine: The spawned leaf that makes ONE minimal, scoped glue edit inside a caller-declared path fence and stops — the connective code a story needs but no contract can pin, honoured from a task prompt and never self-signed.
role: glue-worker is the write-scoped subagent the session-orchestrator spawns (via `spawn_glue_worker`) to make a SINGLE minimal scoped edit to un-asserted glue — the connective code that binds a story's proven capabilities into a running whole but declares no capability of its own (no isolatable red→green): wiring, composition, a dependency thread, a few routes in a sidecar file (ADR-0158 D1). It edits ONLY within the caller-declared `paths` (a write outside them is denied fail-closed by the spawn fence — the wall is the runtime's, not a request it can waive), does exactly what the task prompt asks and no more, and returns a plain summary. It does NOT drive a red→green (that is the builder leaf), author the work hierarchy (that is story-author), judge or sign a verdict (the spine signs; ADR-0091), or land anything (the orchestrator lands through run_gate + open_landing_pr; CI re-proves the owning story transitively). Like a maintenance electrician sent to connect three wires in one panel: it does the named join cleanly and leaves the rest of the building untouched.
outcome: The named scoped edit is made inside the declared path fence and nothing outside it is touched; the change is the minimum that satisfies the task (no speculative refactor, no widened scope); any real logic discovered hiding in the wiring is SURFACED for extraction into a contract rather than silently buried; and the result is a plain summary carrying no verdict — the orchestrator runs the gate and lands it, CI re-proves the owning story. A write the fence denied is reported, never worked around.
tools: Read / Grep / Glob for the repo, and Write / Edit fenced fail-closed to the caller-declared `paths` (a write outside them is denied BEFORE it lands and recorded as a violation). NO Bash (a shell write would bypass the fence), NO gate, NO promotion or landing verb, NO signing — least-authority: it edits the declared surface and stops. Landing is the orchestrator's (run_gate + open_landing_pr), the sole signer is the spine.
workflow:
**session_start:** read the task prompt and the declared `paths`; read the target file(s) and just enough around them to make the edit correctly — do not preload the corpus.

1. Confirm the edit is genuinely glue — before touching a line, check it is not hiding an extractable pure function (ADR-0158 D1). If real logic is buried in the wiring, STOP and surface it: it earns a contract (route back to the orchestrator / builder), it is not glue.
2. Make the MINIMUM edit the task describes, only within the declared `paths` — no speculative abstraction, no widened scope, no drive-by refactor.
3. Keep every write inside the fence — a denied write is reported, never re-attempted from another angle.
4. Return a plain summary of what changed. Stop — do not run the gate, open a PR, or sign anything.
escalation: Real logic discovered hiding in the wiring (glue that is actually an extractable pure function) is SURFACED for extraction into a contract, never buried in the edit. A write the fence denied — an edit the task needs but the declared `paths` do not cover — is reported to the orchestrator (widen the scope or re-route), never worked around. It signs and lands nothing: the gate and the merge are the orchestrator's, the verdict is the spine's.
provenance: New in v2 (2026-07-05), authored for ADR-0160 (the desktop chat's scoped glue actuator) resolving ADR-0158 D4. The spawned role behind `spawn_glue_worker` — the runtime equivalent of the terminal's Agent/Task tool the desktop chat lacked, so a scoped glue intent ('add 3 routes to backend-entry.ts') is delegated to a path-fenced worker instead of over-routing into a whole-story `story build --real`. Rendered from this one artifact (ADR-0051/0055): the terminal `storytree agents glue-worker` and the spawned glue-worker move together. Distinct from the builder leaf (which drives a red→green) and story-author (which authors the work hierarchy). Should cite the `glue` definition (ADR-0158 D1) once it is migrated into the seed — a librarian follow-on.

title: Orchestrate, route, supplement: the inner loop is one tool
problem: Treating `node/story build --real` as 'the job' force-fits work a machine can't cleanly sign — GLUE with nothing worth asserting (SQL/DB adapters, dependency additions, pure config or wiring) — into a proof that can't pin it, or silently skips it. The routing filter that actually works is 'does this piece have an isolatable red→green test?', NOT package boundaries: one package can hold both an algorithm the leaf proves and glue it can't, and a provable algorithm can straddle packages. (Glue is one of TWO orthogonal reasons a machine can't sign a unit; the other is operator-attested work — look/feel/live/spend (ADR-0070), where the output is only judgeable by a human — routed to the frontend-builder / an operator-attested leg, NOT folded into the glue bucket. ADR-0158 D2.)
approach:
1. DECOMPOSE into provable units — the filter is 'does this piece have an isolatable red→green test?', not package boundaries. The provable units carry the algorithm; the rest is integration/wiring.
2. ROUTE the provable units to the inner loop, chained in dependency order: either `story build --real` (a story's capabilities, ordered by `depends_on`, stack in one worktree and promote once, ADR-0031) or sequenced individual `node build --real` runs across merges (each fresh worktree is cut from current main, so a landed piece is visible to the next). Cross-package work is SEQUENCED via `depends_on`, never done atomically. A complex driver-composition / multi-surface --real build can exhaust the per-slice turn ceiling (--max-turns, default 16) even after the leaf reaches green (run_proof=green) — it fails to TERMINATE, surfacing as `Reached maximum number of turns`. This is orthogonal to --budget (the USD ceiling): a build well under budget still hits it, so READ the failure — a turn-exhaustion is not a real red. Give such a build headroom — size the turn budget by what the leaf must produce, not by file size (`turn-budget-keys-on-assert-surface`); the default 16 is independently known-tight for orientation too (storytree orchestrate). When the routed unit is an editsExisting re-drive — its behaviour already partly at HEAD — scope its brief to ONE behaviour with a mechanically-pinned red and freeze what is already built (`mechanical-red-redrive-brief`), else the gated leaf silently ships one-of-N behaviours or reds a different, still-uncovered contract.
3. SUPPLEMENT the non-leaf glue — SQL/DB adapters, dependency additions, pure config/wiring with nothing to assert — with the orchestrator's OWN subagents (the Agent tool); do it yourself only as a last resort. (Visual/UI is NOT glue: it is operator-attested work — look/feel/live/spend (ADR-0070) — a SEPARATE orthogonal axis routed to the frontend-builder / an operator-attested leg, not folded in here. ADR-0158 D2.) When a dependency addition instead feeds a capability the leaf DOES prove but that SHIPS through a different runtime (e.g. `node:test`-proved, esbuild-bundled), it is not pure glue: pin its surviving import form in the spec — a form green in the proof runtime routinely crashes the ship runtime (`pin-the-dual-runtime-import-form`).
Through-line: the inner loop carries the ALGORITHM load; the orchestrator carries the INTEGRATION/WIRING load. When the inner loop genuinely can't prove a piece — it needs a DB-backed proof, a new dependency, or a browser/visual proof it lacks — that is a capability gap to RAISE and EXPAND; in the meantime route the piece to a subagent. Never force-fit it into a hollow proof and never silently skip it.
statement: The inner loop — the leaf prove-it-gate → signed verdict (`storytree node|story build --real`) — is ONE tool the session-orchestrator wields, not the whole job. The orchestrator's job is to DECOMPOSE work into provable units, ROUTE those to the inner loop chained in dependency order, and SUPPLEMENT the non-leaf glue with its own subagents — doing the glue itself only as a last resort.
tradeoffs: Routing costs something: deciding provable-vs-glue per piece and sequencing cross-package work over several merges is slower than one atomic change — but an atomic cross-package edit can't be proven unit-by-unit, and a hollow `--real` proof over un-isolatable glue is worse than no proof. The standing risk is the orchestrator quietly absorbing glue it should have delegated, or force-fitting glue into the inner loop instead of naming the capability gap. Composes with `slow-growth-minimum-to-green` (the leaf's discipline INSIDE a provable unit) and `cross-story-dependency` (the `depends_on` direction rule that orders the routing).
description: The leaf prove-it-gate is one tool the orchestrator wields, not the whole job: decompose work into provable units, route those to the inner loop in dependency order, and supplement the non-leaf glue with the orchestrator's own subagents.

title: The --real turn budget keys on the assert surface, not file size
description: Size a `--real` unit's turn budget by its assert surface — the files the leaf must author times the contracts it must cover, plus a brownfield-rework premium — not by the size of any file it touches.
statement: Size a `--real` unit's turn budget by its ASSERT SURFACE — the number of files the leaf must author times the number of contracts/asserts it must cover, plus a premium for brownfield rework — never by the size of the largest file it touches: the default 16 turns fits a one-file, few-assert unit; a multi-file or multi-assert unit wants `--max-turns 45`; a brownfield studio-component rework wants 45 to 50 (ADR-0130).
problem: A plan or planner that budgets turns by file size — 'this touches a 4000-line file, give it 45; nothing big in scope, so the default 16 stands' — under-budgets the units that actually blow the cap. The turn cap (ADR-0130; default 16, raisable to 45) is enforced per authoring slice: a unit that exceeds it fails CLOSED at AUTHOR_TEST or IMPLEMENT with `Reached maximum number of turns`, wasting a full ~4-minute round-trip before the retry. The units that exhaust it are not the ones with a big file in scope — they are the ones with a large assert surface: several small net-new files, or one small file with many asserts, or a brownfield rework. File size is the wrong predictor.
approach:
Count what the leaf must PRODUCE, not what it must read:
1. FILES THE LEAF MUST AUTHOR — the source files plus the test file. Several net-new files, even small ones, each cost turns; one file costs fewer.
2. CONTRACTS/ASSERTS IT MUST COVER — a test with N contracts is N red→green cycles the leaf drives; a many-assert contract is expensive even in one small file.
3. BROWNFIELD-REWORK PREMIUM — reworking an existing component (understand → change → keep the rest green) costs more than the same surface net-new.
Map it: one file and a few asserts → the default 16; multi-file OR multi-assert → `--max-turns 45`; brownfield studio-component rework → 45-50. Over-budgeting costs nothing — ADR-0130 made the turn cap a ceiling, not a metered spend — while under-budgeting costs a failed-closed round-trip, so round UP when unsure.

Why file size misleads (the discriminating cases):
- A net-new studio capability of three small files — a component, a pure module, and a 6-contract jsdom test — touches NO large file, yet the default 16 failed closed at AUTHOR_TEST; the retry at `--max-turns 45` authored in 18 turns and passed 6/6. File-size keying budgeted 16 and was wrong; the assert surface (3 files × 6 contracts) explains the 45.
- A one-file, two-direction pure rule with a 7-assert contract is small by file size, yet the default 16 failed closed; the pass needed 42 turns at IMPLEMENT. One small file, large assert surface.
- A brownfield studio-component rework failed closed at `--max-turns 30` with no verdict; 50 succeeded.
tradeoffs: Counting the assert surface up front is slightly more work than eyeballing file size, and the numbers are heuristics, not measurements — a unit budgeted 45 may author in 18. But the asymmetry favours rounding up: over-budget wastes nothing (ADR-0130 made the turn cap a ceiling, not a spend), while under-budget wastes a full failed-closed round-trip and a re-launch. Composes with `slow-growth-minimum-to-green` (fewer asserts per unit is the cheaper unit); consumed by the `planner` (its Budget step) and the plan `budgets` field, and cited by `orchestrate-route-supplement` for its turn-ceiling headroom.
provenance: New in v2 (2026-07-14), consolidating a turn-budget heuristic that was duplicated across the `planner` agent's Budget step and the plan `budgets` field placeholder — both keyed on file size ('a fiddly module'), which the evidence refutes; a third variant lived in `orchestrate-route-supplement`. Distilled from friction items `friction-realbuild-turn-budget-keyed-on-file-size-not-file-count` (reinforced ×2) and the archived `friction-studio-component-rework-needs-45-turns-not-the-plans-30`. Runs: `real-mrga153y` (3 small net-new files + a 6-contract jsdom test → failed closed at AUTHOR_TEST on the default 16) vs `real-mrga73eq` (same scope at `--max-turns 45` → AUTHOR_TEST 18 turns, PASS 6/6); `real-mrj9v5xd` (one-file 7-assert pure rule → failed closed on 16) vs `real-mrja2qgq` (→ IMPLEMENT 42 turns, PASS); and a brownfield studio rework that failed at `--max-turns 30` and succeeded at 50. Generalises the `real-build-turn-ceiling-vs-budget` memory from 'a fiddly module' to the assert-surface driver.

why: The prove-it-gate's guarantee is real but narrow: spine-observed red→green on the AUTHORED test. It is silent on test COMPLETENESS — the leaf chooses what to assert, and under turn pressure (the --max-turns ceiling, see orchestrate-route-supplement) it reliably drops the trickiest robustness/concurrency contract while still signing green. Trust the green alone and you land a unit that looks proven but under-covers its spec: an arc once signed a `shared-forest-connection` capability green while dropping a `bounded-never-hangs` contract (no timeout — a hanging connector hangs forever), caught only by a later audit. The mirror failure is over-eager auditing — calling a contract dropped because the unit's OWN test does not assert it, when the behaviour is INHERITED from a collaborator: a single-session guard once looked dropped from a stream adapter but was effective transitively through the runner's module-level in-flight flag; the adapter being stateless did not make the behaviour absent (a false gap-call). So even WITH the gate, a green's COVERAGE is a claim, not a proof — audit it, and audit your audit: both checks read the actual code, never its surface.
title: Audit the signed verdict against the spec
statement: A signed GREEN verdict is a coverage CLAIM to audit, not a coverage GUARANTEE — and the verdict can report its OWN shortfall while still saying PASS, so read the coverage figure and the touched-file set before you read the word PASS, run `storytree coverage <cap>` to mechanically catch a contract with no test, read the authored test against the spec's contract list, and confirm a suspected gap in the code (inherited ≠ absent) before raising it.
howToApply: After a --real signed green on a multi-contract unit: (0) READ THE VERDICT ITSELF, before running anything. A signed PASS carries its own per-contract coverage figure (ADR-0127), and a PASS whose figure falls short of the unit's declared contracts is an already-reported shortfall — the machine has told you, in the same line, that the green covers less than the node claims. Nothing refuses that PASS today, so the refusal is yours: a green that reports covering fewer contracts than the node declares is not a landing. Then cross-check the DIFF against the DECLARED SURFACE — on a node whose contracts span several files, read the touched-file set and confirm every declared file was actually authored, because the recurring shape is a leaf that authors one spotlight pair (the implementation and its test) and leaves the rest of its declared surface untouched while the spine honestly signs the red→green it did observe. Both reads are cheap, come before any tool, and are the only place the multi-FILE drop is visible at all: the coverage check below reasons about contracts and tests, not about which files the diff touched. (1) run `storytree coverage <capability-id>` — the offline check maps each declared `## Contracts` behaviour to an OBSERVED test by the naming convention and exits non-zero on an uncovered contract (the mechanical form of the manual sweep; ADR-0122). A non-zero exit is a SUSPECTED gap to confirm, not a confirmed one — the check now reads the test's assertions structurally (ADR-0126) — a test that is skipped (`.skip`/`.todo`) or asserts nothing substantive (a constant-only `assert(true)`) no longer counts as covered — but it still cannot judge RELEVANCE: a test that asserts something substantive yet unrelated to its contract still reads covered (the deferred semantic-reviewer follow-on, ADR-0126). It also maps at CONTRACT granularity: a single contract that enumerates several assert bullets reads covered the moment its crux case exists, so on a multi-assert contract descend past the check to confirm EACH asserted bullet has a covering case — the leaf implements every branch but authors only the spotlight case (the multi-ASSERT sibling of the multi-FILE spotlight drop that step 0 catches; same leaf economics, one level down). (2) For each flagged (or suspected) gap, trace the behaviour through the unit's collaborators — the runner it calls, a shared/base module, a dependency default — before concluding it is absent; a 'stateless' adapter often inherits a guard one level down (inherited ≠ absent). (3) When a gap is REAL and LATENT (no live consumer yet), land the core and raise a tracked capability gap — do NOT hand-author the missing proof (that forges the coverage the gate exists to earn) and do NOT silently skip it. This is the post-proof companion to orchestrate-route-supplement (which routes the unit in) and a sibling of verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate in the verify-the-claim family. It is also the DETECTION half of a family whose other members act earlier: `asset:a-spec-body-describes-only-what-it-contracts` removes what tempts the leaf off-target, and `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` narrows what it can author on a re-drive — this rule is what catches the occurrence neither prevented.
provenance: Graduated 2026-06-27 (ADR-0095) from session agent-memory (leaf-drops-trickiest-contract): an inner-loop QA lesson the outer loop learned on the ADR-0113 thick-client arc — a signed green under-covered its spec (fr-bounded-never-hangs dropped from shared-forest-connection, gap-closed in a later PR) and a suspected gap was a false positive because the behaviour was inherited (the chat-session-stream single-session guard, corrected). The manual contract→test sweep gained a deterministic tool 2026-06-27 — `storytree coverage <cap>` (ADR-0122, amends ADR-0020) — folded into step (1) here. Durable essence extracted; the event-record (PR numbers, dates) stays in git (ADR-0095 D5). Refines prove-it-gate (the gate proves the test passed, not that it covers the spec); composes with orchestrate-route-supplement (the routing it follows post-proof) and verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate (the verify-the-claim family). Consumers: session-orchestrator. AMENDED 2026-08-01 by guidance-curator, discharging the GUIDANCE half of `friction-inner-loop-multifile-spotlight`, which was routed to the behavioural floor and came back PARTIAL rather than unauthored — this artifact already carried the detection principle and already NAMED the multi-file spotlight drop, but only as the sibling of the multi-assert case it taught, so the named face was never taught. Step (0) is that missing half: read the verdict's own per-contract coverage figure, and cross-check the diff's touched-file set against the declared surface. The measured occurrence is what makes the addition specific rather than decorative: a multi-file node signed PASS with a coverage figure of zero of three declared contracts, on a diff containing only the spotlight implementation-and-test pair while every other declared file was untouched. Note what that says — the machine had ALREADY reported the shortfall on the verdict line and the PASS stood anyway, so the failure was not a missing measurement but an unread one, which is why the remedy is a reading step and not another tool. EDITED rather than authored as a new artifact, per `asset:edit-first-curation` (five-tier sweep — principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition): the only content a separate artifact could add is the assertion that a multi-file PASS must not sign while its declared contracts are uncovered, and the party that signs is the deterministic SPINE, not an agent — a floor rule addressed to an agent cannot stop it, so the sibling artifact would have carried one genuinely new sentence, a mechanism that does not exist, and would otherwise have restated this one. The GATE half stays open and is correctly NOT authored here: a fail-closed multi-file coverage floor at signing time is TOOL work, separately routed and still owed, and `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief`'s provenance already records it as the gate-side lever of this family. Authoring a guardrail asserting that floor would name an enforcer that does not exist, which is the specific falsehood the enforcer test prevents; whoever builds it should amend step (0) to point at the mechanism rather than at the reader. Two stale ADR citations were corrected in place on the same edit (`asset:accepted-adrs-carry-no-stale-prose`, applied to a Library body): step (1)'s structural-assertion reading and its deferred semantic-reviewer follow-on both cited ADR-0123, which is the WebGL forest-world renderer decision; the decision that made a contract covered only by a substantively-asserting test is ADR-0126, verified against `docs/decisions/` at the time of this edit. Family cross-references added on the same edit: `asset:a-spec-body-describes-only-what-it-contracts` (the spec-body lever, authored 2026-08-01) and `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` (the brief lever) are the two PREVENTION members whose detection half this is.
description: A signed green --real verdict proves the leaf's authored test went red→green under the spine's eye — not that the test covers every contract the spec enumerates, and not that every declared file was authored: a PASS can carry a short coverage figure on its own line while the diff holds only a spotlight pair. Read the verdict's own coverage figure and file set first, run `storytree coverage <cap>` to mechanically flag the dropped contract, then audit the authored test against the spec's contract list; and because the audit can err, confirm a suspected gap in the code (inherited ≠ absent) before raising it.

title: Scope the edits-existing re-drive brief: one behaviour, mechanical red, frozen build
problem:
An editsExisting re-drive re-runs `node`/`story build --real` to add or re-tense behaviour on a unit that ALREADY exists at HEAD. The prove-it-gate proves the leaf's AUTHORED test went red→green under the spine's eye — NOT that every briefed behaviour was authored, and NOT that the red pins the BRIEFED behaviour rather than some other uncovered one. Two dodges recur, and the spine signs a PASS on BOTH.

Multi-behaviour under-delivery: a brief naming N behaviours reliably lands the FIRST and silently skips the rest, and the spine signs on the one authored red→green. In one increment this hit twice in a row — a drive briefed for two contracts shipped only the scrollback ring (no `list()`, no test), and a drive briefed for the restore path plus an unmount reversal shipped only the restore — each a signed PASS whose core behaviour was still missing, caught only by the coverage report plus hand-inspection of the authored bytes.

Coverage-frame steering: an editsExisting target that keeps its contract id reads 'covered' to the gate-time coverage-by-title axis (ADR-0126/0127), so the leaf's AUTHOR_TEST gravitates to whatever reads UNCOVERED and writes its red against a DIFFERENT contract — the drive signs honestly on that other red→green while the briefed re-tense stays unbuilt, and the coverage axis is BLIND to the miss because the retained id still reads green. Two consecutive drives signed off-target this way; the rewrite landed only once the brief was hardened to the mechanical-red form.

The generic editsExisting brief arm (`realPrompts` in `packages/orchestrator/src/resolve-prove-spec.ts`, ADR-0057 §3) steers the leaf to 'a regression test that fails against current behaviour' but does not pin WHICH test, forbid new blocks, or freeze built work — and `spec.guidance` is threaded into the leaf prompt un-validated — so removing the leaf's room to dodge is entirely the per-node brief's job.
approach:
1. ONE behaviour per re-drive. Never brief N behaviours in a single editsExisting drive; when a re-tense or increment needs several, SEQUENCE them one drive each and freeze the earlier ones as built. Focused single-behaviour briefs landed clean on the first attempt, 11–14 turns, each time they were tried — the countermeasure that actually works.

2. Make the red MECHANICAL in `spec.guidance`. Name the EXACT existing test whose BODY may be rewritten, its `test()`/`it()` title and contract id UNCHANGED byte-for-byte (renaming it to an invented prefix is a separate leaf-side miss); FORBID adding any new `test()`/`it()` block; and spell the setup/mock change plus the ORDERED assertions that must fail at HEAD. This converts an invisible kept-id re-tense — which coverage-by-title reads as already covered — into an observable HEAD-failing assertion the spine sees at CONFIRM_RED. It composes with `right-kind-red`: this rule pins the brief's red SPEC (what the author writes), while `right-kind-red` governs the OBSERVED red's KIND (what the spine will accept).

3. FREEZE everything already built. The brief NAMES what exists and must not be touched; the working form is literal — 'contract 6 is BUILT, do not touch; THIS drive adds only X'. A leaf that cannot see the fence re-touches or regresses built work.

Through-line: narrow the brief until the only thing the leaf CAN author is the one behaviour you named. The goal is to make the dodge IMPOSSIBLE in practice, not merely detectable after signing — because the detector that would otherwise catch it is partial (see Tradeoffs).
statement: When you re-drive an editsExisting `--real` unit whose behaviour already partly exists, author the node's brief (`spec.guidance`) for exactly ONE behaviour, pin its red MECHANICALLY — name the single existing test whose BODY is rewritten (its `test()`/`it()` title and the contract id byte-for-byte UNCHANGED), FORBID adding any new `test()`/`it()` block, and spell the setup/mock change plus the ORDERED assertions that must fail at HEAD — and FREEZE everything already built by naming it untouchable; a brief this narrow leaves the gated leaf no room to silently ship one-of-N behaviours or to write its red against a different, still-uncovered contract.
tradeoffs:
More drives, honestly. Sequencing N behaviours as N drives costs more subscription spend and wall-clock than one omnibus re-drive — but the omnibus reliably under-delivers AND signs a PASS that LOOKS complete, which is worse than slower-but-honest: the miss surfaced only under hand-inspection plus the coverage report, after wasted spine drives.

Why this is a pattern, not a guardrail (the enforcer boundary). Nothing deterministically reads a brief and rejects a bad one — `spec.guidance` is threaded into the leaf prompt un-validated (`resolve-prove-spec.ts`). The nearest deterministic mechanism, the gate-time per-contract coverage axis (`computeContractCoverage`, ADR-0126/0127), is a partial DOWNSTREAM DETECTOR, not an enforcer of the brief: it flags a declared contract with no vouching test (the multi-behaviour drop shows on the verdict line as 'uncovered: …'), but it is BLIND to the kept-id re-tense because the retained id reads covered, so it never fires on that miss. With no honest deterministic enforcer to name, the honest kind is PATTERN — a spec-authoring discipline that keeps a re-drive inside what the partial detector CAN catch and removes the leaf's room to dodge, not a boundary a mechanism fails closed on.

One lever of a family. This is the SPEC-AUTHORING lever, for whoever writes the brief (the session-orchestrator or the planner). Two sibling levers in the same false-green family act elsewhere and are separate rules: a LEAF-side floor (name each test for its contract id, not an invented prefix) and a GATE-side coverage floor at signing (block a multi-file or multi-assert PASS while declared contracts are uncovered). The post-proof companion is `audit-the-signed-verdict` — audit the coverage CLAIM rather than trusting the green.
provenance: Graduated 2026-07-14 (ADR-0168 D5 friction drain) from two reinforced friction items: `friction-multi-contract-redrive-briefs-underdeliver` (reinforced ×2; runs real-mrhxlfy8 coverage 0/7 with `list()` missing, real-mrhxzx4o a signed PASS while the unmount-reversal test it was told to reverse still stood, and focused follow-ups real-mrhxvdak 7/7 and real-mrhycnse 6/6 landing clean first try) and `friction-coverage-frame-steers-leaf-off-retensed-contracts` (runs real-mrj0zx7o and real-mrj1ibmu signed off-target, real-mrj2mlj0 landing the rewrite only after the brief was hardened to the mechanical-red form at commit ec0ff203). CONSOLIDATES both into this one spec-authoring lever. Two SIBLING levers in the same false-green family route separately: `friction-inner-loop-multifile-spotlight` → a gate-side multi-file coverage floor at signing; `sdk-leaf-drops-contract-id-test-names` (reinforced ×6) → a leaf-side test-naming floor. The multi-ASSERT sibling `friction-signed-pass-covers-many-asserts-with-one-crux-test` folds into `audit-the-signed-verdict`. Raw friction event-records (PR numbers, dates) stay in git per ADR-0095 D5; the durable essence lives here. Consumers: session-orchestrator, planner.
description: When you re-drive an editsExisting `--real` unit, author its brief for exactly ONE behaviour with a mechanical red — name the existing test whose body is rewritten, forbid new test blocks, spell the HEAD-failing assertions — and freeze everything already built, so the gated leaf cannot silently ship one-of-N or red a different contract.

title: The published surface is not evidence of runtime shape -- probe, then pin
problem:
The published surface of a dependency -- its typings, its README, the import form it documents -- is a CLAIM about the artifact, not the artifact. For a split-era or 0.x package the two come apart, in two distinct shapes, and both fail SILENTLY.

SHAPE 1, the runtime split: a dependency's import mechanism is not portable across runtimes, and the runtime that PROVES a capability is not the runtime that SHIPS it. A UMD/CJS package rejects a named ESM import under `node --import tsx --test` -- cjs-module-lexer cannot see the named export through the UMD wrapper, so the proof crashes with `SyntaxError: ... does not provide an export named '...'`. The obvious workaround, `createRequire(import.meta.url)`, greens `node:test` -- but throws once esbuild bundles the module to CJS, where `import.meta.url` is undefined (`ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` at app load). The two runtimes are two worlds of differing forgiveness; a leaf optimising for a green under the one it can see silently lands a form that crashes the one it cannot. The asymmetry is the trap: the tsx-side crash at least fails the drive closed at CONFIRM_GREEN -- costly but visible -- whereas the ship-side form signs a PASS under `node:test` and surfaces only at load, caught (if at all) by a scoped survival e2e, so it can reach the owner's walk as a crash-at-launch.

SHAPE 2, the surface/runtime disagreement, which needs no runtime split at all: a package's published TYPINGS can simply not describe the constructor it ships. `@xterm/addon-clipboard` 0.1.0 declared `constructor(provider?: IClipboardProvider)` -- ONE parameter -- while its shipped `lib/addon-clipboard.js` ran `constructor(base64 = new Base64(), provider = new BrowserClipboardProvider())`, provider SECOND. A caller obeying the typings binds its provider to the BASE64 slot and leaves the default second-slot provider in place -- and that default, `BrowserClipboardProvider`, implements `readText` as `navigator.clipboard.readText()`: precisely the clipboard-READ vector an OSC 52 write-only intent exists to close. It type-checks (the call is valid against the typings), it passes a naively-mocked test (a mock accepts either arity), and no lint can help, because no linter knows which argument slot carries a security boundary. The security intent is undone with nothing red anywhere.

Shape 1 is the test-green/production-red family (`asset:implementer-shortcut-patterns`) with the proof runtime staging a more-forgiving world than production (`asset:test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes`). Shape 2 is the same root reached without a second runtime: the surface described something the artifact does not do.
approach:
PROBE, then PIN, then FORBID -- in the spec, not at the leaf -- and date what you learned.

(1) PROBE THE ARTIFACT YOU ACTUALLY RESOLVE, never the surface that describes it. For a runtime split: a ~30-second `node --import tsx --test` probe of the bare import, plus a ship-side check that the `--format=cjs` bundle actually loads (build and run it, or grep the emitted `dist/*.cjs` for the runtime-fragile call). For an argument shape: read the SHIPPED `lib/*.js` / `lib/*.mjs` under the RESOLVED path (`node_modules/.pnpm/<pkg>@<version>/node_modules/<pkg>/`) -- minified is fine, parameter order and its defaults stay legible -- and read the `.d.ts` beside it as a second, independent claim to be compared, never as the answer. Resolve the version first: the surface you are checking belongs to a specific resolved version, not to the package.

(2) PIN WHAT YOU FOUND, in the artifact that will still be read when you are gone. The surviving IMPORT FORM goes in the SPEC as the REQUIRED mechanism -- for a UMD/CJS package that is the static default import then destructure (`import Pkg from 'pkg'; const { Thing } = Pkg;`), which both cjs-module-lexer and esbuild-cjs accept. An ARGUMENT SHAPE goes in a CONTRACT TEST, not a comment and not a cast: capture the constructor and assert the security-bearing argument lands in the slot you verified (e.g. the provider is the SECOND captured argument), so the placement is re-proved on every run rather than trusted. Pin the shape whenever a slot carries a security or correctness boundary; a purely cosmetic argument does not earn a contract.

(3) NAME AND FORBID each tempting alternative WITH its discriminating rationale, so the fence teaches why and not merely what: the named ESM import (`import { Thing } from 'pkg'`) is forbidden because it crashes the tsx proof runtime (cjs-module-lexer cannot resolve the named export through the UMD wrapper); `createRequire(import.meta.url)` is forbidden because it signs PASS under `node:test` yet crashes the esbuild-cjs ship bundle at load (`import.meta.url` is undefined once bundled). The spec owns the choice precisely because the leaf, judging by whichever green it can reach, will otherwise pick a runtime-specific form.

(4) TREAT THE FINDING AS VERSION-SCOPED, and keep the CONTRACT rather than the WORKAROUND. A 0.x surface-vs-runtime defect expires at the next bump, in EITHER direction: it can be fixed as readily as it was introduced, and a defensive cast written against it silently becomes dead weight -- or worse, a comment asserting a mismatch that no longer exists. So the durable residue is the contract test, which keeps guarding the boundary across the bump, while the workaround is retired the moment the probe says it is no longer needed. Re-probe on a version bump; never carry a version-specific finding forward as a standing fact. This is `asset:anchor-implementation-surface` applied to a dependency: the finding is anchored implementation detail with a shelf life, the pinned boundary is the durable part.

Applies to any dependency whose published surface you would otherwise take on trust -- most sharply a 0.x or split-era line, and any dependency added to a capability proved in one runtime and shipped through another (the `asset:launch-desktop` main is exactly that shape: `node:test`-proved, esbuild to `apps/desktop/dist/*.cjs`).
statement: When a capability leans on a SPLIT-ERA or 0.x dependency -- one whose published surface can disagree with the artifact it actually ships, or whose surface behaves differently under the runtime that PROVES the capability than under the runtime that SHIPS it -- read the SHIPPED artifact you actually resolve before trusting the surface that describes it, PIN what you found (the surviving import form in the spec; the argument SHAPE in a contract test wherever a slot carries a security or correctness boundary), NAME-AND-FORBID the tempting alternatives each with its discriminating rationale, and treat the finding as VERSION-SCOPED; both failure shapes are SILENT -- they compile clean and pass a naively-mocked test -- so an unpinned choice signs a PASS the shipped artifact does not honour.
tradeoffs: The probe plus one spec paragraph cost a few minutes, paid once per new dependency; reading a shipped `lib/*.js` is a single file read, and the contract test that pins a slot is a handful of lines. Skipping it pays two different ways. On shape 1 it pays in signed-but-ship-broken drives: the originating capability burned four of six `--real` drives (~$2.50 of subscription-billed leaf time) on import mechanics and produced a signed PASS whose shipped bundle crashed at launch -- a defect that reaches the owner's walk, the slowest and most expensive channel. On shape 2 it pays in a security regression that is invisible until exploited: nothing anywhere goes red, so the read and the pinned slot are the ONLY things standing between the intent and the defect. Step 4 carries its own recurring cost, and it is a real one -- you re-probe on every version bump, and you must actually RETIRE a workaround when the probe says the defect is gone, or the codebase accretes casts and comments defending against a bug that upstream fixed, which read to the next agent as current facts. Pay it anyway; a stale finding read as current is the more expensive failure. Default to probing the artifact and pinning the boundary.
provenance:
Distilled 2026-07-14 from friction item `friction-new-dep-import-form-two-runtimes` (ADR-0168 D5 friction drain), filed driving the ADR-0190 pty-session-manager re-prove when the capability's `@xterm/headless` / `@xterm/addon-serialize` dependencies hit both walls. Evidence: `--real` drives real-mrj0nf05 and real-mrj17fnu failed closed at CONFIRM_GREEN on `does not provide an export named 'Terminal'` under `node --import tsx --test` (reproduced in a 30s probe); after the spec pinned default-import-then-destructure, drive real-mrj1w14e signed PASS at 431c125 but the leaf used `createRequire(import.meta.url)`, and the desktop survival e2e caught the shipped bundle crashing at load (`ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`, `apps/desktop/dist/main.cjs`) -- fixed by an ADR-0158 glue-worker swap to a static default import (commit 4d9fabb4; `dist/main.cjs` createRequire count 1 to 0). Sibling of `test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes` (the proof runtime as the more-forgiving world) and `a-live-only-guarantee-is-an-honesty-gap` (a ship-side failure caught only by a scoped live e2e is the honesty gap); composes with `implementer-shortcut-patterns` in the test-green/production-red family; grounds on the `launch-desktop` surface. Run and commit ids are the durable event-record residue (ADR-0095 D5); git history holds the rest.

BROADENED 2026-08-01 discharging `friction-addon-typings-runtime-ctor-mismatch` (ADR-0168 D4 friction drain; route edit-existing). That item's adjudication routed it HERE rather than to a new artifact: its own Impact names the SAME defect class as `friction-new-dep-import-form-two-runtimes` -- the friction this artifact was distilled from -- so a second, near-duplicate rule about 0.x dependency surfaces is exactly the corpus duplication `asset:edit-first-curation` forbids. The artifact was therefore broadened from its narrow original framing (the import FORM must survive both runtimes) to the general rule the second instance supports: the published surface is not evidence of runtime shape. The id stays `pin-the-dual-runtime-import-form` so existing `asset:` citations keep resolving; title, gloss, and statement now match the broadened scope, and the original framing survives intact as Shape 1. Second instance, from PR #774: `@xterm/addon-clipboard` 0.1.0's `typings/addon-clipboard.d.ts` declared `constructor(provider?: IClipboardProvider)` while `lib/addon-clipboard.js` shipped `constructor(t = new i, e = new o)` -- provider SECOND, defaulting to `BrowserClipboardProvider`, whose `readText` calls `navigator.clipboard.readText()` -- so a typings-conformant provider would have bound to the base64 slot and left clipboard READ enabled against an OSC 52 write-only intent. Caught pre-red by reading the shipped lib; pinned by the `tdp-clipboard-osc52-write-only` contract in `apps/studio/src/components/TerminalDock.test.tsx`, which asserts the provider sits in the SECOND captured constructor slot.

VERIFICATION 2026-08-01 -- the drain's MANDATORY corpus-investigator check, required precisely because the rule turned on a 0.x runtime detail that can change under us. It did change, and that outcome is why step 4 of the Approach exists. The repo now pins `@xterm/addon-clipboard` 0.2.0 (`apps/studio/package.json`), whose `typings/addon-clipboard.d.ts` declares `constructor(base64?: IBase64, provider?: IClipboardProvider)` -- TWO parameters, in the SAME order as the runtime. The 0.1.0 typings mismatch is FIXED and is no longer live in this repo. What still holds at 0.2.0, both re-verified: the shipped constructor order (base64 first, provider second, in `lib/addon-clipboard.js` and `lib/addon-clipboard.mjs` alike) and `BrowserClipboardProvider.readText` calling `navigator.clipboard.readText()`. The repository's own history is the worked example for step 4: commit 3757292f introduced a defensive `ClipboardAddonCtor` cast whose doc-comment stated the 0.1.0 mismatch verbatim, and commit a371a880 ("xterm 6 renderer upgrade") bumped to 0.2.0 and DELETED that cast because the typings had been fixed -- while the `tdp-clipboard-osc52-write-only` contract SURVIVED the bump and still pins the provider to the second slot. The workaround expired; the contract did not. The rule is stated so that it does NOT rest on the version-specific fact: it asserts that a 0.x published surface is not evidence and that any such finding is version-scoped, never that a particular version is currently mismatched. The 0.1.0 case is carried as dated history, which is what it now is.

Five-tier sweep before the broadening -- principle / guardrail / pattern / process / definition. No artifact in any tier addresses a dependency's published surface versus its shipped runtime. Nearest neighbours: `asset:test-fixtures-mirror-production-failure-modes` and `asset:a-live-only-guarantee-is-an-honesty-gap` (already this artifact's sources -- both about the PROOF environment being more forgiving than production, not about the dependency lying); `asset:a-mocked-seam-leaves-its-default-implementation-unproven` (rejected -- genuinely adjacent, in that a mock leaves the real implementation unexercised, but it governs an injected seam of OUR OWN code, and its remedy is to test the default implementation, not to read a third-party artifact); `asset:anchor-implementation-surface` (rejected as a HOME, adopted as a SOURCE -- it governs where rotting implementation detail may live, which is exactly the rule step 4 applies to a dependency finding, so it is cited rather than restated). Nothing in the process or definition tiers touches dependency surfaces.

KIND: stays a `pattern`. It is NOT promoted to the `guardrail` the original drain routed, and this second instance does not change that -- it strengthens the case against promotion. The enforcer test is unmet in both directions: nothing deterministic refuses an under-pinned spec (CONFIRM_GREEN catches only the tsx-side crash; the ship-side form reached signed-PASS, and the `dist/*.cjs` bundle-grep check the first drain flagged still does not exist), and no lint can know which argument SLOT carries a security boundary, which is the second instance's whole point. The only real enforcer is the per-case contract test this pattern tells you to write -- a discipline, not a fence. It promotes to a guardrail if and when a general check exists.
description: For a split-era or 0.x dependency the published surface -- typings, README, the documented import form -- is not evidence of the runtime shape you will actually get: read the artifact you resolve, pin the surviving import form in the spec and the argument shape in a contract test wherever a slot carries a security or correctness boundary, name-and-forbid the tempting alternatives, and treat the finding as version-scoped.

why: A live-registration step was once skipped on a LAPTOP session (direct network, DB confirmed RUNNABLE, every probe connecting) because the agent reasoned '443-only egress blocks port 3307' — CLAUDE.md's remote-web/VM caveat mis-applied to a session where it did not hold. The story was authored to disk but the live `--pg` registration never ran, for a reason that was not real. Two facts make an assumed-false reachability unsafe. First, the remote fence is genuinely REMOTE-only, and its real mechanism is narrower than the port story that caused this failure: the sandbox's proxy CONNECT-tunnels arbitrary ports, so it was never a blocked port (ADR-0250 corrected that framing) — what it cannot carry is the Cloud SQL CONNECTOR, because client-mTLS is definitionally incompatible with a TLS-terminating middlebox, and ordinary HTTPS on 443 is unaffected (ADR-0258 D2 narrowed 'no database access' to 'no connector'). Meanwhile `gcloud` is no longer required for the REST control plane (ADR-0063) and DB auth is keyless Cloud SQL IAM over ambient ADC (ADR-0021) — so on a laptop/direct-network session the data plane is reachable and the caveat is inapplicable. Second, a timeout at RUNNABLE is almost always a slow cold-start, not a wedge: the instance stops nightly (asleep 01:00–07:00 Australia/Sydney, ADR-0114) and after an overnight stop the first connection can exceed `db:up`'s whole readiness poll (ADR-0060 owns that budget — 600 s since 2026-07-30) — a direct `createPool` `SELECT 1` connected in ~340 ms once warm while the poll was still timing out, and a cold-start of ~21 min has been seen. Inferring 'unreachable' from either signal skips a write that would have persisted; the probe is cheap and definitive.
title: Probe DB reachability, never infer it
statement: Before concluding the DB is unreachable — and especially before skipping a live `--pg` write for that reason — PROBE it: open a direct connector and run `SELECT 1` via `@storytree/library/store` `createPool`. Never INFER unreachability from the environment or session type. A `db:up`/preflight `unreachable within Ns` while the instance status is RUNNABLE is a slow cold-start to wait out and re-probe, not a wedge. The remote-web/VM fence is REMOTE-SESSION-ONLY and is narrower than it sounds: what cannot work there is the Cloud SQL CONNECTOR — client-mTLS is definitionally incompatible with that sandbox's TLS-terminating proxy (ADR-0250 D1, narrowed by ADR-0258 D2) — not database access in general. On a laptop/direct-network session none of it is in play, so it is never a reason to declare the store unreachable there.
howToApply: When any preflight, `db:up`, or tool reports the DB unreachable — or you are tempted to skip a live `--pg` write because you believe it is — do NOT reason from the session/environment type. Open a direct connector and run `SELECT 1` via `@storytree/library/store` `createPool` (keyless IAM, ADR-0021); a fast connect (sub-second once warm) is the definitive proof the store is reachable and the write should proceed. If the probe itself times out while the instance status is RUNNABLE, treat it as a slow cold-start: `db:up` (a no-op if already up), wait, and re-probe — the poll can time out before the instance finishes waking (up to ~21 min after the overnight stop, ADR-0114). Only conclude 'unreachable' when a direct probe genuinely fails to connect after a warm-up window. And invoke the remote-sandbox explanation only on a confirmed remote-web/VM session, never on a laptop/direct-network one — and state it as what it is: the Cloud SQL CONNECTOR cannot cross a TLS-terminating proxy (ADR-0250 / ADR-0258), which is not the same as 'no database access' and never a port to work around. This is the DB-reachability member of the verify-the-claim family alongside `verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate`: the failure it prevents is skipping a live `--pg` write because reachability was assumed-false rather than probed.
provenance: Authored 2026-07-03 after a live UAT walk where a spawned story-author agent on a LAPTOP session (direct network, DB RUNNABLE, probes connecting) skipped a live `--pg` node registration, concluding '443-only egress blocks port 3307' — CLAUDE.md's remote-web/VM caveat mis-applied to a direct-network session. Owner directive: DB-reachability is probe-not-assume. Sibling of `verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate` in the verify-the-claim family. Consumers: story-author.
description: Never conclude the shared Cloud SQL store is unreachable by inferring it from the environment or session type — verify with a direct connector `SELECT 1` (`@storytree/library/store` `createPool`). A `db:up`/preflight timeout at status RUNNABLE is a slow cold-start to wait out and re-probe, not a wedge; and the remote-web/VM fence is the Cloud SQL CONNECTOR rather than database access — client-mTLS cannot survive that sandbox's TLS-terminating proxy (ADR-0250 / ADR-0258) — which is remote-session-only and says nothing about a laptop/direct-network session.

title: Deterministic, parameterised geometry
description: Author the forest world's visual geometry as pure deterministic generators driven by meaningful parameters over a render-agnostic world-model→render seam — an aesthetic change is a parameter or generator tweak, never a hand-placed coordinate edit.
statement: Author the forest world's visual geometry as pure, deterministic generators driven by a few meaningful parameters over a render-agnostic world-model→render seam: an aesthetic change is a parameter or generator tweak, never a hand-placed coordinate edit; geometry is emitted as point arrays (Vec2[]) and stringified to SVG only at the edge; output is a pure function of the data (hash/rand01, no Math.random, no wall-clock). Stay on SVG; Konva is named-deferred behind the seam.
why: Hand-specified per-feature vector paths are a local-minimum trap: every aesthetic change becomes a coordinate edit with invariants to preserve (start on the dock, end on the mouth, no self-intersection, stay deterministic), so the geometry is rigid and resists redesign — the river network paid for this over ~6 iteration rounds. Pushing the look behind parameters and pure generators makes a change a knob tweak the inner loop can prove, keeps the renderer swappable behind the seam, and keeps the render pixel-stable (a non-deterministic render breaks the deep-link-renders-identically-on-first-paint contract the visual proof depends on). It does NOT eliminate taste rounds — appearance has no compiler — only shortens them.
howToApply: Express a visual change as a parameter or generator adjustment, not a coordinate edit (riverGeometry.ts is the model: MST → drainage → confluence → route-around → meander are already pure parameterised functions). Emit Vec2[] into the world model from buildWorld(); let the SVG layer stringify d-strings at the edge — never store a d-string in the model. Keep generators a pure function of the data (no Math.random, no Date.now / new Date()). Keep parameters few, meaningful, and named — resist a knob per pixel. Stay on SVG; a substrate swap (Konva) is owner-gated behind the trigger fence (ADR-0069 §3), never reached for to 'make rivers easier'.
provenance: Authored 2026-06-17 (ADR-0070) as the pullable form of ADR-0069, mirroring how one-element-per-signal is the pullable form of ADR-0062. Consumers: frontend-builder.

title: Render and witness a flag-guarded surface
description: The visual leaf's self-QA is feedback, never a verdict: push machine-checkable facts down into Stage-1 assertions, witness the irreducible look with the committed Playwright harness + preview_* MCP (not a per-run script), and hand the owner a deep-link to attest.
statement: A visual leaf checks its own work by witnessing a flag-guarded surface — but the witness is FEEDBACK, never the proof: first push every machine-checkable visual fact DOWN into a Stage-1 assertion, then witness only the irreducible look, reusing the committed harness rather than reinventing a capture script per run, and STOP for the owner's operator-attested nod.
problem: A visual surface has a real check the pure red-green loop doesn't cover — someone has to LOOK. Two failure modes follow. (1) The leaf reaches for a screenshot where a machine assertion would do: 'the river starts on the dock and ends at the mouth, no self-intersection' is a Vec2[] assertion, and 'the panel shows X given these props' is a jsdom assertion — both belong in the Stage-1 --real proof, not an eyeballed image. A screenshot is not a substitute for an assertion you can write. (2) For the part that genuinely needs an eye, the leaf hand-writes a throwaway capture script each run (.roads-qa.mjs, chrome --headless --screenshot), re-hitting the same traps every time — notably the occluded-tab trap (preview_screenshot hangs on a hidden tab) — and producing inconsistent, unrepeatable evidence. A per-run script is not a capability.
approach:
1. PUSH MACHINE-FACTS DOWN FIRST. Before capturing anything, ask which 'visual' facts are actually assertions: geometry invariants become Vec2[] assertions over the generator output; render/behaviour facts become jsdom component assertions. Use preview_inspect (computed CSS / colour / spacing) and preview_snapshot (a11y tree / text / roles) to TURN an eyeballed fact into a written assertion, then land it in the cap's Stage-1 --real proof (asset:orchestrate-route-supplement). What remains after this is the irreducible look.
2. WITNESS THE LOOK WITH THE COMMITTED HARNESS, not a fresh script. Reuse the repo's Playwright harness — apps/desktop/e2e/harness.mjs (offline API stubs + DETERMINISTIC settle-polling + real-click) and apps/studio/playwright.config.ts (a real dev server pinned to the offline json store) — or the preview_* MCP for interactive checks. Drive a headless capture (the harness's own, not preview_screenshot on a hidden tab) so the occluded-tab trap can't bite. The render must be deterministic for the witness to be repeatable (asset:deterministic-parameterised-geometry).
3. KEEP IT FEEDBACK-ONLY, THEN HAND OFF. The capture is the artifact the OWNER attests against, not a self-granted pass: build the look behind a flag, witness it, surface the hosted deep-link (#/tree/<id>) and STOP. The look earns an operator-attested verdict the human signs (ADR-0070 §3 / ADR-0007) — the leaf never self-signs it (asset:agent-never-self-exempts), and the orchestrator stands the experience up for the owner to judge (asset:stage-the-attestation-experience).
tradeoffs: A committed harness is less nimble than a bespoke script for a one-off exotic capture — but reinventing the capture per run burns tokens, re-encounters the same traps (the occluded tab), and yields evidence no two runs agree on; the harness pays for itself by the second use. The sharper standing risk is the inverse over-reach: treating a green self-QA screenshot as if it PROVED the look. It never does — only the owner's operator-attested nod moves the look to healthy, exactly as only the spine's observation (not the leaf's feedback tool) counts for red/green. Composes with asset:deterministic-parameterised-geometry (a stable render is what makes a witness repeatable) and asset:stage-the-attestation-experience (the orchestrator-side counterpart that puts the confirmed experience in front of the owner).
provenance: Graduated 2026-07-05 at the owner's direction (ADR-0159 — the frontend-builder process re-authoring) as the pullable form of the leaf's visual self-QA. First-classes what frontend-builder used to improvise per run: standardise on the committed Playwright harness (apps/desktop/e2e/harness.mjs, apps/studio/playwright.config.ts) + the preview_* MCP, push machine-checkable facts down into Stage-1 assertions, and keep the capture feedback-only (the look is operator-attested, never self-signed). The inner-loop counterpart of stage-the-attestation-experience (that one is the orchestrator standing the experience up for the owner; this one is the leaf witnessing its own surface before the handoff). Consumers: frontend-builder.

title: A green positional oracle is necessary, not sufficient
description: A positional/geometry checker can only judge where geometry sits, so it is structurally blind to a whole class of visual defect — stroke and subdivision-seam artifacts, and fit-to-view framing — that lives in what gets stroked and how the field is framed; a geometry or whole-canvas render that lands on a green oracle alone is under-proven, so render a before/after and look.
statement: A positional or geometry oracle can only judge WHERE geometry sits, so it is structurally blind to the defects that live in what gets STROKED — seam and outline artifacts from subdividing a shape — and in how the field is FRAMED — fit-to-view / viewBox: a green such oracle is NECESSARY but never SUFFICIENT, so any geometry pass, subdivision, or whole-canvas render is under-proven until a before/after has been rendered and LOOKED at, no matter how green its unit tests.
why: Three times in one art-machinery arc a checker reported zero violations on a visibly broken render, because each defect sat outside what a positional oracle can see. ADR-0217 increment 4: findDepthConflicts returned [] and all 76 tests passed while the render carried a heavy dark X across a door — a door pane split into four fragments (indices 10/12/14/20) each stroking its OWN cut edges, four seam strokes that no depth or physics oracle can catch because every fragment is in the right place and the right draw order. The facade-subdivision seams found earlier the same session — visible bands across every wall above and below each window — were the same root cause. And PR #704: a whole-canvas LibraryOverview SVG signed GREEN on 8/8 contracts while rendering mostly offscreen, because it carried no viewBox and nothing positional was wrong. The generalisable cost each pays for: any pass that SUBDIVIDES geometry must also decide what stops being an outline, and any whole-canvas surface must decide its frame — and no positional checker can catch getting either wrong. The failure is not a lost taste round (appearance has no compiler); it is a FALSE GREEN — a defect one look from shipping to the owner as finished evidence that the machinery works, at roughly an hour of diagnosis plus a redesign of the split path once it is caught. The machinery that catches LOOK is not built, so treating a green positional oracle as proof of the look is trusting a checker for a class of defect it was never able to see.
howToApply: Treat a green positional or geometry oracle as a necessary GATE, never as proof of the look. Before landing a geometry pass, a subdivision/split, or a whole-canvas render, ask the discriminating question: does this change what gets STROKED, or how the field is FRAMED? For a subdivision the answer is almost always yes (new cut edges become new outlines); for any full-canvas SVG it is almost always yes (viewBox / fit decides what is on screen). When it is, RENDER a before/after and look — the checker being green tells you nothing about that defect class. Two concrete guards fall out: when you subdivide a shape, carry per-edge provenance so a fragment outlines only the edges it inherited (the door-X fix); when you emit a whole-canvas surface, set an explicit viewBox / fit rather than trusting the default. This is ADR-0070 stage 2 (geometry is machine-proven, the look is operator-attested) and ADR-0217 station 4 (render, look, refine) being load-bearing rather than a nicety. The render-and-look governs when the AGENT must look before it trusts green; the look VERDICT stays the owner's operator-attested call, and the agent never self-signs it (asset:render-and-witness-a-flag-guarded-surface, asset:agent-never-self-exempts).
provenance: Graduated 2026-07-20 (ADR-0168 friction adjudication, routed=principle) from the friction geometry-checker-green-while-the-render-was-visibly-broken, reconciling in the same edit the never-executed sibling graduation friction-svg-cap-fit-to-view-framing-falls-in-the-geometry-look-gap (routed to principle ~9 days earlier to fold into render-and-witness, but never written — corpus-investigator confirmed zero viewBox/fit language across the floor). Names the blind spot ADR-0070 and ADR-0217 imply but never state in words: a positional / geometry oracle cannot see stroke, subdivision-seam, or fit-to-view-framing defects.
