Nothing in the corpus becomes redundant; this is a pure addition. Consumers: every agent that can spawn or start background work — session-orchestrator, graduation-synthesist, librarian-curator, guidance-curator, planner, frontend-builder, story-author.
description: An agent never ends its turn waiting for a notification from work it dispatched — the report may be routed to a session that did not ask for it, the child may already be dead, or the work may simply outlast the turn, and all three are indistinguishable from inside the wait. Poll in-turn, then finish on your own judgment and name what could not be learned.

why: The leaf's entire world is the spec plus the brief, and the two are not equally actionable. A brief points at a contract identifier; a body paragraph describes a behaviour in enough detail to write. When the two compete, specificity wins, and the drive then signs an honest PASS on the contract the leaf chose — the gate proves red-to-green on the AUTHORED test, and it did go red to green, so nothing anywhere is false. What surfaces instead is the briefed contract sitting in the verdict's own uncovered list, which is easy to read as an ordinary coverage shortfall rather than as the leaf having been steered. The sharp fact, and the reason this needs stating at all, is that the explicit disclaimer does not help: the measured case carried a plain not-yet-contracted label directly on the passage and the leaf built it anyway, three times on one capability before anyone traced the cause to the spec rather than to the brief. The countermeasure is proven by removal rather than by argument — deleting the later-slice prose and re-driving the same node built the briefed contract to full coverage on the first attempt. Each wasted occurrence costs a whole metered drive plus the forensics to work out why the wrong thing arrived, and it recurs silently as long as the bait sits in the body.
title: A spec body describes only what it contracts
statement: A capability spec body is read by the gated leaf as instruction, not as narrative. Any behaviour described in it concretely enough to implement is buildable, and a described-but-uncontracted behaviour reliably outweighs the frontmatter drive brief, because it is the more specific and more actionable thing in the leaf's context. So the body carries only behaviour that is under contract. Marking a passage as a later slice or as not yet contracted does not defuse it — that disclaimer is prose the leaf reads alongside the description, not a fence around it. Direction, future slices, and intentions belong in the story doc or an arc plan; the capability body the leaf reads carries the contracts and nothing else.
howToApply: Before a `--real` drive, read the capability body the way the leaf will: as a list of things it is being asked to build. Strike anything that describes a behaviour concretely enough to implement but does not appear in the contracts. Do not settle for labelling it deferred — a disclaimer is not a fence, and the measured failure had one. Two homes are legitimate for what you strike: the story doc, for durable intent about where the capability is going, and an arc plan, for anchored disposable sequencing (`asset:anchor-implementation-surface` governs which artifacts may carry that class of content at all). When a leaf HAS already built an uncontracted slice, close the loop in both directions: adopt the built behaviour as a real contract so the work is not thrown away, AND remove every remaining mention of it from the body, so the next drive is not re-baited by the same prose. This is the SPEC-BODY lever in the family of ways a gated leaf builds the wrong thing while signing honestly. `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` is the BRIEF lever and is scoped to editsExisting re-drives of behaviour already partly at HEAD — it narrows what the leaf can author; this rule removes what tempts it, and the two compose on a re-drive. `asset:audit-the-signed-verdict` is the post-proof detector for the same family, which is what catches an occurrence you did not prevent. `asset:slow-growth-minimum-to-green` is the sizing rule this serves — a body that names only its contracts is a body that cannot ask for more than the minimum.
provenance: Authored 2026-08-01 by guidance-curator, discharging `friction-spec-named-unbuilt-slice-baits-the-leaf`, routed to `principle` and never authored. EVIDENCE (kept here per `asset:reference-dont-restate`, out of the rule text): three wrong-contract drives on a single capability, each an honest signed PASS on a contract other than the briefed one, the third with the briefed contract named explicitly in the verdict's own uncovered list while the authored diff added a behaviour the spec described only as a later slice, not yet contracted. The countermeasure was proven by removal — the later-slice prose was deleted and the re-drive built the briefed contract at full coverage — which is what makes the causal claim a controlled one rather than a correlation, and clears `asset:friction-justification-bar`. Per-occurrence cost was roughly a metered drive plus half an hour of forensics, three times. The specific run and commit identifiers stay in git and in the capability's own story file per ADR-0095 D5; the durable essence lives here. KIND — principle, as routed, and correct on this seat's enforcer test: nothing reads a spec body and refuses uncontracted prose, and `spec.guidance` reaches the leaf prompt unvalidated, so no deterministic mechanism exists to name. The nearest mechanism, the gate-time per-contract coverage axis, is a partial DOWNSTREAM DETECTOR rather than an enforcer — it did surface the miss here, as the uncovered contract on the verdict line, but it is structurally blind to the neighbouring case where the leaf retains a contract identifier, which is why `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` records the same limitation in its own tradeoffs. Principle rather than pattern because the content is a truth about what a spec body IS in the leaf's context — an instruction surface for an unsupervised builder rather than a design narrative for a human reader — and the relocation it asks for is not a tradeoff between comparable options but the removal of a hazard. EDIT-FIRST (`asset:edit-first-curation`, under its 2026-08-01 five-tier amendment): all five guidance-bearing tiers were swept — principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition — verdict UNAUTHORED. Named rejections: `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` (pattern, the closest neighbour; scoped in its own statement to editsExisting RE-DRIVES of behaviour already partly at HEAD and acting on the BRIEF, where this is a fresh spec body naming a not-yet-built future slice — its provenance already treats sibling levers in this family as separate rules); `asset:anchor-implementation-surface` (principle — governs where fast-rotting implementation surface may live, an axis of ROT and detectable staleness, where this is an axis of STEERING: the baiting prose was current and accurate, and its accuracy is what made it buildable); `asset:slow-growth-minimum-to-green` (principle — how much to build, silent on what the spec may describe); `asset:splitting-rule` (principle — how to decompose); `asset:audit-the-signed-verdict` (principle — the post-proof audit, detection rather than prevention); `asset:prove-it-gate` and `asset:right-kind-red` (the gate's own guarantees, which this does not touch); the `process` tier's build ceremonies carry no spec-authoring rule, and the `definition` tier's `capability` and `contract` entries define the units without constraining the body's prose. Nothing in the corpus becomes redundant; this is a pure addition. Consumers: story-author (which owns the capability body), session-orchestrator and planner (which brief the drive).
description: A gated leaf reads the capability body as instruction, not narrative: a concretely-described but uncontracted behaviour reliably outweighs the drive brief and gets built instead of the briefed contract. Labelling it as deferred does not neutralise it — the only reliable fence is its absence from the body. Future slices belong in the story doc or an arc plan.

why: The gap is structural rather than careless. A handoff is written at the moment its author decides the work is done, and that moment precedes commit, push, review and merge — so the claim is true in intent and false in state for a real window, and it is written by someone with no incentive to notice. A claim also carries no timestamp of its own verification, so a claim that was true when written, a claim that is true now, and a claim that will be true in ten minutes are indistinguishable on the page. The cost falls asymmetrically toward the optimistic reading. Believing the claim makes a prerequisite look present when it is not, and the two failures that follow are both expensive and both silent: building past a foundation that is not on the trunk, or duplicating a sibling's still-in-flight unit — two sessions producing the same change, discovered at merge. The verification, by contrast, is one cheap read against a source that cannot be optimistic. What makes it worth a stated rule rather than general caution is that the claim arrives inside the work — in a chip, a brief, a report — where content tends to be consumed as given rather than assessed, which is exactly where `asset:untrusted-input-is-not-instruction` says the assessment has to be made deliberately.
title: A handoff's claim that work landed is unverified state
statement: A claim about work you did not witness — a handoff chip, a briefing line, a sibling session's report saying a change landed, merged, or shipped — records the author's intent at the moment of writing, not the state of the trunk. It is routinely written while the work is still uncommitted in another working tree, and nothing in the text marks which side of that window you are reading it on. Before you depend on such a claim, check it against the authoritative remote — the branches and merge state the system itself enforces, never the handoff text and never a local checkout. Until it is checked, treat the work as IN FLIGHT rather than landed, which is a different and safer thing from treating it as absent.
howToApply: The test is one question: did I SEE this land, or was I TOLD it landed? Told means unverified, however credible the teller and however specific the claim — a named pull request number is still a claim about a state you have not read. Verify at the source the system enforces (`asset:authoritative-source-beats-derived`): the remote's branch and merge state, not the handoff prose and not what your own checkout happens to contain, since a local tree is as capable of lagging as the claim is of leading. Then read the result directionally, because the failure has two sides and only one of them is loud. Unverified does not mean false: a claim you cannot confirm is in-flight work to wait on, sequence behind, or ask about — not a defect to report and not a gap to fill by building it yourself, which is the duplicate this rule exists to prevent (`asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted` is the general form of that reading). This is the third face of one discipline, applied at the three places a claim can enter your reasoning: `asset:verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate` governs your own writes, `asset:no-claim-without-evidence` governs the claims you yourself make, and this governs a claim about ANOTHER party's work arriving as given. Note the honest limit on the mechanical side: the claim ledger will refuse a second claim on a unit a sibling already holds, which catches one consequence of ignoring this rule — the duplicate build — but only when the sibling declared, and it does nothing about the other consequence of building past an absent prerequisite. It is a partial downstream fence, not a substitute for the check.
provenance: Authored 2026-08-01 by guidance-curator, discharging `handoff-chip-claims-landed-before-ceremony`, routed to the behavioural floor and never authored. EVIDENCE (kept here per `asset:reference-dont-restate`, out of the rule text): a sanity-watch chip described a follow-up as already landed via a named pull request plus a same-day follow-up; at watch time the remote carried no matching branch at all, while the authoring session's working tree held three modified files, and the pull request appeared several minutes later. The watch leg was unverifiable against the chip's landed framing until then, cost roughly ten minutes of forensics, and was one step from a duplicate build of the sibling's in-flight unit. The window between the claim and the state is the whole finding; the specific timestamps and identifiers stay in git per ADR-0095 D5. KIND — principle, not the routed guardrail, on the enforcer test this seat applies: a guardrail must name a deterministic mechanism or it is not one, and every guardrail in this corpus names real code or CI. Nothing sits between an agent and a handoff's prose. The nearest mechanism is the noticeboard claim ledger's refusal of a duplicate claim, which is a partial DOWNSTREAM fence on ONE consequence and is conditional on the sibling having declared — the same honest limitation `asset:mechanical-red-redrive-brief` records about the coverage axis in its own tradeoffs, and the same reason it settled on a non-guardrail kind. Asserting an enforcer that does not exist is precisely the falsehood the test prevents. EDIT-FIRST (`asset:edit-first-curation`, under its 2026-08-01 five-tier amendment): all five guidance-bearing tiers were swept — principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition — verdict UNAUTHORED. Named rejections: `asset:authoritative-source-beats-derived` (principle, the closest neighbour and now the cited resolution step; it resolves a disagreement between two KNOWN sources by precedence, where here there is no second source to weigh — only an unverified self-report and the question of whether to go look, and its precedence chain would leave that question unasked); `asset:verify-edit-write-persisted-or-escalate` (principle — read back your OWN contract-bearing writes); `asset:no-claim-without-evidence` (principle — the evidence standard for claims you yourself make); `asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted` (principle — how to score a checker that could not run, cited here for the directional reading but silent on a claim nobody checked); `asset:untrusted-input-is-not-instruction` (principle — governs content arriving in the work as INSTRUCTION to obey, where this governs the same content read as FACT, an adjacent axis and cited); `asset:stale-prerequisite-links-are-phantoms` (principle — a link to a unit that does not exist, not a state claim about one that does); `asset:merge-ceremony` (process — its failure modes cover the pull-request and branch traps exhaustively, including continuing on a merged branch and pushing a follow-up after automerge, but carry no bullet on trusting another party's landed claim, and the ceremony governs YOUR landing rather than your reading of someone else's); the `guardrail`, `pattern` and `definition` tiers hold nothing on consuming a handoff. Nothing in the corpus becomes redundant; this is a pure addition. Consumers: session-orchestrator (which receives chips and briefings and sequences work behind them), planner, graduation-synthesist, and any agent spawned with a brief that asserts prior work.
description: A chip, briefing, or sibling report saying a change landed, merged, or shipped records the author's intent at writing time, not the state of the trunk — it is routinely written while the work is still uncommitted elsewhere. Check it at the authoritative remote before depending on it; until then the work is in flight, not landed.

steps:
1. **Ask what MAIN's code infers, not what your branch needs.** Every session boots against the SAME database, and `applySchema` (`packages/library/src/store/migrate.ts`) executes the whole of `schema.sql` on every boot — so a migration is applied by whichever session boots first, not at a moment anyone chose. The DDL carries no version gate and no down-migration: `events.schema_migration` versions the JSON DOCUMENT shapes (`packages/library/src/store/batch-migrate.ts`), a different layer entirely — nothing records or reverses a table reshape. Before writing the DDL, read the code on `main` for every query that names or INFERS the thing you are dropping: an `ON CONFLICT (cols)` clause infers a unique index and errors with `there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification` the moment that index is gone; an FK target, a partial-index predicate, and an insert relying on a `NOT NULL` default are the same shape. If nothing on `main` touches it, the change is one-sided and the rest of this ceremony does not arm.

2. **Split the swap — it is never one edit.** A constraint swap looks atomic in the DDL and is not. `DROP CONSTRAINT` + `ADD CONSTRAINT` in a single landing has no safe apply moment in either direction: apply it before your branch merges and every session still running `main` errors on the dropped target; don't apply it and your own live smoke stays red against a store that lacks the new shape. No ordering rescues a one-shot swap — that is why the split is the technique and not a nicety.

3. **EXPAND — add the new shape alongside the old, and move the writers, in a landing of its own.** The expand step is TWO layers and the second is the one that gets missed: (a) additive DDL only — create the new column/index/constraint while the OLD one still stands, accepting a redundant-but-valid overlap; (b) change every writer to name the NEW target, and land that on `main`. Once the expand is on `main`, both constraints exist and no live query infers the doomed one — which is the precondition the contract step needs.

   *Worked example, and the discriminator.* The ADR-0200 `events.node_claim` change swaps a single-column PK `(unit_id)` for a composite PK `(unit_id, session_id)` plus a partial unique `(unit_id) WHERE grade = 'work'`. Attempted as one swap it has no safe window, because `main`'s claim write was `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (unit_id) DO NOTHING` — whose conflict target is the very PK the migration drops. Expanded it is unremarkable: add the `grade` column and the partial unique index while `PRIMARY KEY (unit_id)` still stands (the old PK makes the new index trivially satisfiable, so the addition touches no data), move the writers onto `ON CONFLICT (unit_id) WHERE grade = 'work'` and `ON CONFLICT (unit_id, session_id)`, land THAT — and only then, in a later landing, swap the PK. The tempting alternative is the one that shipped: write the whole swap into `schema.sql` behind a `pg_constraint` catalog guard so it is idempotent. Idempotence is the wrong property. The guarded `DO $$` block is correct, re-runnable DDL and it still breaks every pre-expand writer the instant it first runs — safe-to-re-run is not the same claim as safe-for-the-code-already-running.

4. **MIGRATE the data in the expand landing, guarded.** Backfill new columns with a value that is correct for the rows that already exist (`grade TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'work'` correctly recast yesterday's exclusive claims), and keep every statement a no-op on re-run. Because `applySchema` runs on every boot, the fresh-install `CREATE` path and the in-place `ALTER` path must converge on exactly the same shape — if they diverge, two live sessions disagree about what the table is.

5. **CONTRACT — drop the old constraint in a LATER landing, never the one that expanded.** Nothing in this system reports when the last pre-expand session dies. The only honest signal is structural: a session's worktree holds the code it started with, and a branch dies at its merge (ADR-0271), so the contract waits until the expand has been on `main` long enough that no live session predates it. When you cannot establish that, leave the overlap in place — a redundant index is cheap, a shared store that refuses half the fleet's writes is not.

6. **If no compatible overlap exists, NAME the break window and hand it UP — never take a silent one.** Some changes genuinely have no expand step. Who is broken, for how long, and what has to re-run afterwards is a rollout decision above the unit: state the window and escalate rather than applying at merge and hoping (asset:escalate-up-when-blocked-or-out-of-scope). If what is needed is a standing rollout POLICY rather than a one-off call, that is an ADR, not a paragraph in the unit.
title: Migrate the shared store's schema
trigger: You are about to edit `packages/library/src/store/schema.sql` in a way that DROPS or NARROWS something existing code depends on — a primary key, a unique constraint, an index an `ON CONFLICT` target infers, an FK target, a column, a NOT NULL. A purely additive change (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` with a default) does not arm this ceremony. The tell that you have already crossed it without noticing: a live smoke on your branch is red against the shared store and the only way to green it is to apply the migration NOW, before the branch merges.
surfaces:
- **The shared Cloud SQL store** — one database shared by every session; reached with `pnpm db:up` / `pnpm db:status` (asset:db-control). This ceremony WRITES its schema, which db-control never does.
- **The DDL and its applier** — `packages/library/src/store/schema.sql`, executed by `applySchema` in `packages/library/src/store/migrate.ts` on every boot. The DDL is ungated and unreversible — `events.schema_migration` versions the JSON document shapes, not the tables — so the file must be idempotent AND compatible with the code already running.
- **The writers** — every store module whose SQL names a constraint (`ON CONFLICT` targets, FKs, partial-index predicates): `packages/library/src/store`, `packages/notice-board/src/store`, `packages/studio-members/src/store`.
- **The landings** — expand and contract are separate pull requests through the merge ceremony (asset:merge-ceremony). What proves each one is a live smoke against the shared store — a `--pg` command such as `pnpm storytree noticeboard claims <unit> --pg` or `pnpm storytree library artifact <id> --pg` — never the offline gate.
statement: Land a change to the shared store's schema as EXPAND then MIGRATE then CONTRACT, across SEPARATE landings — add the new shape alongside the old and move every writer onto it first, and drop the old constraint only once no running code still infers it — because `applySchema` runs on every boot against ONE database that your branch's code and main's code are both already using.
provenance:
Authored 2026-08-01 by the guidance-curator drain pass, discharging `friction-constraint-swap-migration-has-no-safe-premerge-window` — the oldest routable item on the worklist (filed 2026-07-16 from the ADR-0200 `node_claim` PK swap, whose live smoke failed against the shared store and whose build agent refused to apply the migration pre-merge and escalated the rollout ordering rather than working around it).

NET-NEW rather than an edit, against the edit-first default (asset:edit-first-curation). All five guidance-bearing tiers were swept — principle, guardrail, pattern, process, definition — for `expand-migrate-contract`, `constraint swap`, `PK swap`, `ON CONFLICT`, `pre-merge window`, `shared DB migration`, `schema change`, `rollout`, `breaking change`, `backward compatible` and `DDL`. No artifact in any tier mentioned expand-migrate-contract, a constraint swap, or `ON CONFLICT`. Named rejections: **principle:tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep** is the nearest neighbour and is NOT the home — it governs a shared PARSING/validation contract tightened at test time, and its remedy is a full-suite sweep before the sign, whereas this is a shared MUTABLE RESOURCE two code versions use at once, which no suite can observe; **guardrail:claims-in-the-shared-store** names the same store and the same table but asserts write-OWNERSHIP semantics, not how the schema beneath them changes; **process:db-control** owns reaching the instance, never reshaping it; **process:library-edit-ceremony**'s "migration" is the seed-to-live corpus sync, a different sense of the word; **process:merge-ceremony** owns the landing but is silent on what a landing does to shared state.

Authored as `process`, the kind the route named: it is an ordered operational recipe with an observable trigger and a stated verification. It is NOT a guardrail — nothing deterministic refuses a two-sided migration (the gate and CI are DB-free), so claiming an enforcer would be false. Tier note for the librarian: the process tier is normally the librarian's standing projection of the decision log (ADR-0154), and this process projects no ADR, because the corpus holds no ratified rollout policy. The friction's own routeReason flagged that a ratified policy would be an ADR escalation; that escalation is SURFACED here, not taken.

The step-3 worked example is a design reading of the shipped `schema.sql` — the catalog-guarded `DO $$` PK swap and the partial unique index the new writers infer — offered as the discriminator between idempotent and compatible. It is not a claim about what the 2026-07-16 session was told at the time; that session's refusal-and-escalate was the correct move available to it.

LIBRARIAN RULING on the tier note above, 2026-08-01 — the artifact STANDS AS AUTHORED in the `process` tier; no re-homing and no ADR is required, and the surfaced escalation is CLOSED rather than left open. Three findings. (1) ADR-0154 D1's obligation is ONE-WAY: a load-bearing ADR that changes a way-of-working must have a current `process` deriving from it. It creates no converse duty that every process project an ADR, so "projects no ADR" is not a defect. (2) ADR-0034 §2 admits GUARDRAILS as sources alongside ADRs, and the binding constraint it does impose — a process makes no new policy — is satisfied here. This artifact's authority derives from a MECHANICAL property of the substrate, not from a policy choice: `applySchema` executes the whole of `schema.sql` on every boot against one shared database, with no version gate and no down-migration, and `events.schema_migration` versions JSON document shapes rather than tables. Expand-migrate-contract is what that substrate forces, not a rule anyone elected; the artifact correctly refuses to make the policy it would need an ADR for, escalating the break-window call at step 6 and saying so explicitly. (3) The bijection ADR-0154 D2 actually gates is process↔ENTRYPOINT, not process↔ADR, and it was verified GREEN with this artifact live: `check:surface-coverage` reported OK across 18 processes and 67 entrypoints at exit 0, with both drain axes still at zero.

The ADR escalation is therefore NOT taken, and the reason is that there is nothing yet to ratify: a standing rollout POLICY would need a break window someone actually has to take, and none has been. If a future change genuinely has no expand step, step 6 routes it up — and THAT is the moment an ADR is owed, not this one. Recorded here so the next librarian pass does not re-derive it.
description: How a schema change reaches the shared Cloud SQL store without breaking the sessions still running main's code: expand, migrate, then contract across separate landings — never a one-shot constraint swap.
failureModes:
- **Treating a constraint swap as one atomic DDL edit.** Measured 2026-07-16 on the ADR-0200 `node_claim` PK swap: the branch's live smoke `pnpm storytree noticeboard claims notice-board --pg` failed with `column "grade" does not exist` because the shared store had not been migrated, while migrating it would have broken `main`'s `ON CONFLICT (unit_id)` claim writes for every other running session. The build agent correctly refused to apply it pre-merge and escalated the rollout ordering; the unit's last verification step had to be deferred past the merge, leaving a manual post-merge apply-and-re-smoke for someone to remember.
- **Reading "idempotent" as "safe".** A catalog-guarded `DO $$` block that no-ops on re-run is re-runnable, not compatible. It still reshapes the table the first time it runs, under code that is still using the old shape.
- **Applying the migration to the shared store to green your own live smoke.** The smoke goes green and every session on `main` starts failing — you have moved the breakage somewhere you cannot see it, which is strictly worse than a red smoke you can.
- **Contracting in the landing that expanded.** The overlap exists precisely so the old writers survive the gap between your merge and their death; dropping the old constraint in the same PR deletes the compatibility you just built.
- **Expecting the gate to catch it.** `pnpm gate` and CI are DB-free, and each code version's own suite is internally consistent and green. Only the COEXISTENCE of the two versions breaks, and nothing tests that.
verification: Nothing deterministic checks this ceremony, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight: `pnpm gate` and CI never touch a database, so no check sees a schema change at all; and both code versions' suites pass, because each is internally consistent — the failure lives only in their coexistence against one shared store, which no suite exercises. Every available signal is after the fact: a live `--pg` smoke red on your branch, or another session erroring on a write that worked yesterday. That is why step 1's question — what does the code on `main` infer? — is answered by reading `main` by hand BEFORE the DDL is written, and why this is a discipline rather than a gate.

why: A durable unit that records an owner's decision — an arc's intent, an ADR, a story — reliably preserves the WORDS and silently drops the THING. Prose survives a repull; a machine-local path does not, and the loss is invisible: the citation still reads like a reference, so the next session never learns it is missing anything and reconstructs a plausible DIFFERENT surface from the prose alone — which is worse than a blank, because it arrives looking finished. The measured case cost an owner interruption and a full rework: an owner-approved playable composition was passed only as a visualization path, the arc preserved its gauge semantics as prose, and the session that correctly repulled the canonical arc built a dashboard instead (`git ls-tree` at the pre-fix commit returned NO entries for the design directory — absence established at a named commit, not asserted; the fixing PR had to add the playback HTML, its image witness, and an explicit written anti-goal after the fact). The trap is that the corpus already tells an agent what must NOT go into the durable unit — implementation surface is banned from an arc body (ADR-0183 D4, `asset:anchor-implementation-surface`) — and says nothing about where the approved artifact must therefore live, so a correct "not in the arc" is silently completed as "nowhere".
title: An owner-approved reference is repo-resident
statement: An owner's approval is only as durable as the artifact it was given to: commit the approved reference — a mock, a render, a playable composition, a style bible, a captured witness — to a repo path in the same change that records the approval, and cite it BY that path from whatever durable unit carries the intent; a machine-local path, a scratchpad file, an attachment, or a live URL hands the next session a handle it cannot open, leaving prose to be reconstructed from.
howToApply: At any handoff where an owner has approved something you can render, replay, or look at, ask one question: could a session holding only this repo and this citation open the exact thing the owner approved? If the answer depends on your machine, your scratchpad, a session transcript, a chat attachment, or a running URL, it is no. Commit it — `docs/design/<arc-or-topic>/` is an allow-listed manifest directory for exactly this (owner-approved executable mocks and binary visual witnesses referenced by an arc or ADR; the entry itself is still governed by `asset:repo-surface-allowlist`) — and then replace the ephemeral handle with the repo path everywhere it is cited, including the durable unit's own body. Two fences keep this from over-reaching. The ban on implementation surface in a durable body is a ban on the PROSE, not on the artifact: the durable unit carries the pointer, the repo carries the thing, and nothing about the ban argues against committing it. And committing a reference is not approving it — the owner still signs the look (`asset:agent-never-self-exempts`); an uncommitted approval and an unapproved commit are different failures, and this principle only addresses the first.
provenance: Authored 2026-08-01 discharging `friction-visual-contract-lived-outside-arc-context` (the ADR-0168 guidance-routed friction drain). The item routed `edit-existing` against `asset:arc`, and its routeReason carried an explicit execution fence handing the tier call to guidance-curator; this landed as a PRINCIPLE instead, because the rule's subject is the owner's approval, not the arc — an arc is only one of several surfaces that cite an approved reference (a plan, an ADR, a story, an art-swarm style bible, an attestation handoff all can), so stating it on `asset:arc` would have left every other handoff uncovered and buried a general handoff rule inside a definition of what an arc IS (`asset:reference-dont-restate`). NOT a guardrail: nothing deterministic can observe an artifact nobody committed — `asset:repo-surface-allowlist` fences where a committed file may go, but no check can fire on an approval whose artifact was never written — so under the enforcer test the honest kind is a principle. `asset:arc` carries a one-clause pointer to this at the exact sentence where the wrong inference was made. Five-tier edit-first sweep (principle / guardrail / pattern / process / definition; 182 units) found no existing home — 'renderable', 'repo-resident', 'docs/design', 'approved mock', 'machine-local' and 'design reference' returned zero hits across all five tiers — and the named rejections were: `asset:render-and-witness-a-flag-guarded-surface` (committed harness over a per-run script — the witness TOOLING, not the approved artifact), `asset:art-asset-designer-swarm` (hands every designer a shared style bible but sets no residency rule for it), `asset:stage-the-attestation-experience` (stands the experience up for the owner, silent on what survives afterwards), `asset:a-handoff-claim-that-work-landed-is-unverified-state` (the truth of a handoff claim, not the durability of its referent), `asset:anchor-implementation-surface` (bans surface from durable bodies — the very inference that opened the gap) and `asset:repo-surface-allowlist` (the placement mechanism, not the discipline). Verified independently while authoring: `docs/design` is already an allow-listed directory in `repo-manifest.json`, justified as 'owner-approved executable HTML mocks and binary visual witnesses referenced by an arc or ADR' — so the mechanism existed in repo config and nothing in the Library pointed an agent at it.
description: An owner's approval is only as durable as the artifact it was given to: commit the approved reference and cite it by its repo path — a scratchpad path, an attachment, or a live URL leaves the next session only the prose.

why:
Two measured instances, both in this repo, and the shape only becomes recognisable with both.

AN ADR WRONG ABOUT ITS PREDECESSOR. At commit 4c7b5568 (PR #1051, 2026-07-31) ADR-0272 wrote "The three earlier failures were mechanisms that could not observe what they gated". At that same commit ADR-0240's Status block read "The first two named a guard that could not OBSERVE the thing it was meant to gate … The third named a treatment, 'defer', for a payload whose actual ROLE was never checked". Two, not three. THE DISCRIMINATOR, and the reason this is not simple carelessness: ADR-0272 QUOTED ADR-0240's root sentence verbatim two sentences earlier in the same paragraph — "prescribing a mechanism without first asking what it can SEE or what it is FOR" — and that quote carries the very disjunction that separates the third failure from the first two. The author had the file open far enough to copy a sentence out of it and still described the paragraph around it wrongly. Citation present, quote accurate, characterisation false; and because the citation was right there, a reviewer had every reason to believe the passage had been read. The cost is not the count. Under ADR-0139 every accepted ADR must be true in full, so this left two accepted records disagreeing with each other, and a reader routed from ADR-0272 to ADR-0240 to find three instances of one shape finds two and cannot tell which record is wrong. It then survived an intervening in-place correction pass that edited this very ADR (a346d23d, 2026-07-31) and was repaired only at a99fe246 (2026-08-01) — so a second reader opened the file, corrected other prose, and left the mischaracterisation standing. The lesson survives the repair.

A DECISION READ AS ITS OWN EXECUTION. In PR #1068 the friction item `tag-keyed-corpus-sweep-misses-untagged-legs` carried, inside its own adjudication (routeReason Q7), the claim "ADR-0247 D4 already supplies the mechanical fence for the witness case". D4 says `either` "**may** therefore be removed" and "This is a fail-closed tightening and lands as its own increment with its own red→green" — a permission and an explicit deferral, not a landing. The increment never landed: verified 2026-08-01, `either` is still in `UAT_TEST_CRITERION_WITNESSES` (`packages/library/src/uat-test-criteria.ts:29`) and `itemWitness` still returns it for an untagged leg (line 177). Two independent refutations exist here and they are NOT equally cheap — the code grep is the one that was actually run, but D4's own modal verb and its own deferral sentence refute "already supplies" without touching code at all. That is what makes it an instance rather than an ordinary doc-vs-code miss: the cheapest available check was to re-read the cited clause, and it was the one not run.

WHY IT RECURS BY CONSTRUCTION. ADR-0139 makes characterising a predecessor a REQUIRED move, not an optional flourish: an `amends` edge obliges the amender to say what of its target is now dead, and an in-place correction obliges an author to state what was overtaken. This corpus therefore manufactures these sentences by ceremony. And nothing checks them — `adr-health` validates that edge TARGETS exist and that statuses are consistent in both directions, never that one body's description of another body is faithful. The failure is silent on both sides: both records stay accepted, both stay green, and the contradiction surfaces only to a reader who follows the pointer.
title: Citing a document is not reading it
statement: A claim about what another document says — how many instances a predecessor named, whether a decision permitted or required something, what it concluded — is DERIVED from that document, and a citation is not a reading: the reference travels with the claim and makes it look checked, so nobody follows it. Open the passage you are characterising, before you write the sentence and before you rest a move on someone else's. This failure needs no staleness and no code — it lands the moment the sentence is written, and in a corpus whose accepted decisions are required to characterise each other it leaves two live records contradicting each other on the page.
howToApply:
The test is one question, asked of your own sentence: am I QUOTING this document or DESCRIBING it? A quote you verify by copying. A description — "ADR-N decided", "already supplies", "names three", "the spec requires", "that principle covers this" — you can verify only by reading around it, and the remedy is always the same and always cheap: open it, read the passage, and count or quote what is actually there. Do it before you write the sentence, and again before you rest a move on someone else's.

Two directions, both measured, both worth recognising by name. READ ENOUGH TO QUOTE, NOT ENOUGH TO CHARACTERISE — quoting is not exemption, because the summary you write is about the paragraph, not about the sentence you lifted from it; copy the line AND read what surrounds it. READ A DECISION AND DESCRIBE ITS EXECUTION — a decision's modal verbs are load-bearing, and "may be removed", "lands as its own increment", "is retired in scoped follow-ons" are permissions and deferrals. "Already supplies" is a claim about the world, not about the ADR, and the ADR cannot license it.

Where the corpus takes over. This rule is upstream of the two that repair what it fails to prevent: once you have opened the document and the disagreement is doc-versus-code, `asset:doc-vs-implementation-precedence` decides correct-the-doc against extend-the-code; once the overtaken claim is in your own accepted ADR, `asset:accepted-adrs-carry-no-stale-prose` supplies the operation — correct in place, or supersede-and-replace — which is exactly how the first instance was fixed. Neither tells you to go and look, and that is the whole of this rule.

FENCES. `asset:accepted-adrs-carry-no-stale-prose` is truth-maintenance for prose that WAS true and BECAME false; neither instance is staleness, since ADR-0240's Status block already read "the first two" on the day ADR-0272 was written — it owns the REPAIR where this owns the CHECK, and the corpus has already drawn that born-wrong-versus-stale line. `asset:prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` is the nearest neighbour and genuinely close on the first instance, which is an unchecked COUNT in its over-inclusive direction; it separates on remedy and on reach — there the members live somewhere in the code and the fix is to re-derive by sweeping with an idiom the author did not use, which costs minutes and can still miss, whereas here the source is one named passage in one named file, there is no idiom to vary and no sweep to run, and the fix cannot miss. The second instance is not a membership claim at all but a claim about a decision's FORCE, which no re-derivation of a set would reach. `asset:authoritative-source-beats-derived` arbitrates two KNOWN sources that disagree; here there is no second source to weigh, only the question of whether to go look, which its precedence chain leaves unasked — the same rejection `asset:a-handoff-claim-that-work-landed-is-unverified-state` recorded against the same artifact, for the same reason. `asset:no-claim-without-evidence` demands a citable path or verbatim output, and the first instance HAD one: a citation satisfies that bar and still carried the false claim, which is the line it does not draw. `asset:an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` governs instruments and measurements, and ADR-0240's own correction explicitly declined to rehome this residue to it, recording that the Library does not own it. `asset:friction-justification-bar` states the same epistemic core — cited is not supporting — but at the friction-graduation seat and as the adjudicator's duty, where this binds any author writing about any document. `asset:a-handoff-claim-that-work-landed-is-unverified-state` governs a claim about WORK STATE checked at the authoritative remote; the second instance sits near that seam and the two compose there. `asset:reference-dont-restate` is the affordance this fences: it rightly mandates citing over restating, which is what makes citations ubiquitous, and the missing half is that whoever DESCRIBES what is on the other end must follow the pointer at least once (`asset:pair-the-fence-with-the-affordance`).
provenance:
Authored 2026-08-02 by guidance-curator. SOURCE, named verbatim so a later sweep can read authoredness from this line rather than infer it: the lesson was surfaced by the pre-merge librarian pass on **PR #1068** (the 20-item guidance-routed friction drain, merged 2026-08-01) and deliberately NOT authored there, on the ground that it is guidance-curator's tier and should route through friction adjudication rather than a librarian queue drain. It has **no friction row of its own** — it was an observation the drain made about another item's adjudication — so there is no `routeReason` to carry the gate and the gate is recorded here instead. The two instances are `PR #1051` (ADR-0272 about ADR-0240) and `PR #1068` (the routeReason of `tag-keyed-corpus-sweep-misses-untagged-legs` about ADR-0247 D4). That friction item was deliberately NOT stamped `--discharged-by` for this write: its own route is `edit-existing` against `tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep`, a different remedy, and `friction route` overwrites `routeReason` wholesale.

ADJUDICATION (`asset:friction-adjudication`'s 7-question gate, run at this seat). Q1 EVIDENCE SUPPORTS, verified first-hand at the sources rather than taken from the drain's report — the differential `git show 4c7b5568:` on both ADR files is what establishes instance 1, and it establishes something stronger than the report claimed: ADR-0272 quoted ADR-0240's root sentence verbatim, so the citation was not merely present but correct, and the characterisation was still wrong. Instance 2's D4 text and the two code sites were read directly. Q2 NOT RECONSTRUCTIBLE in its sharp form: "read your sources" is generic craft, but the load-bearing twist is not — the citation is what makes the claim look checked, and the corpus's own ceremony (ADR-0139) requires the characterising sentence to exist. Q3 CLOSEST EXISTING ARTIFACT — see EDIT-FIRST below; an edit is not enough because the two candidate hosts separate on remedy and on trigger, not on wording. Q4 STATELESS: a property of how a claim about a document is produced, not of any ADR. Q5 DISCRIMINATORY: an author about to write "ADR-N decided X" opens ADR-N and reads the clause, instead of citing it. Q6 RECURRED — twice, in two different media (an ADR body; a friction adjudication), one week apart, and structurally certain to recur because `amends` edges and in-place corrections REQUIRE the characterising sentence while `adr-health` checks STRUCTURE only — its ten checks are enumerated at Q7, and not one of them reads a body for fidelity. Q7 CHEAPEST FIX is prose, unusually and provably: the `tool` route was considered and rejected because judging whether one body faithfully describes another is semantic, and the mechanical fence that does exist (`adr-health`) is structurally the wrong instrument. CORRECTED 2026-08-02 by the pre-merge librarian pass that landed this artifact, and recorded rather than quietly fixed because it is this rule biting its own adjudication: the original clause read “verified in source this pass — its six checks are …, none of which reads a body”, and it was neither six nor none. `adr-health` runs TEN checks (`packages/cli/src/adr-health.ts`, header comment 1 / 1b / 2 / 3 / 3b / 3c / 4 / 5 / 6 / 7 — the nine in `ADR_GATE_CHECKS` plus the WARN `enforced-by-anchors`): `adr-frontmatter`, `adr-number-unique`, `adr-edge-integrity`, `supersede-consistency`, `supersedes-in-part-retired`, `adr-link-integrity`, `story-decisions`, `green-flip`, `load-bearing-live`, `enforced-by-anchors`. Four were omitted, and one omission falsified the closing clause: `adr-link-integrity` DOES open a body — `loadDeadAdrLinks` reads every decision file and matches `](NNNN-slug.md)` against what is on disk. The corrected form is STRONGER than the wrong one, which is why the conclusion survives: the corpus already reads ADR bodies mechanically, and even then it only ever asks whether a POINTER resolves — never whether the sentence around the pointer is faithful. None of the ten keys on semantic fidelity and none could, so the prose route remains the cheapest fix.

KIND — principle, on the guidance-curator enforcer test. A guardrail must name a real deterministic mechanism that refuses, and none exists or could: deciding whether ADR A's sentence about ADR B is faithful requires reading both and judging semantic fidelity. `adr-health` was read in source rather than assumed (above) and validates structure only. Not a pattern either — this is a truth about what a citation can and cannot evidence, not an approach with tradeoffs. Same call and same reason as `asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted`, `asset:an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` and `asset:a-deferral-recorded-without-a-status-reads-as-pending-work`.

EDIT-FIRST (`asset:edit-first-curation`, under its 2026-08-01 five-tier amendment) — all five guidance-bearing tiers swept and NAMED: principle (72), guardrail (17), pattern (25), process (18), definition (52). The sweep scope was verified rather than asserted: live and seed were enumerated independently and agree exactly at 184 ids across those five kinds, zero live-only and zero seed-only, so the seed was a complete surface and not a stale one. Two instruments, per the PR #1068 finding that an id-grep alone under-reports: the title-and-statement pass above, plus a content grep over every artifact body in those tiers — `characteris*`, `characteriz*`, `mischaracter*` and `predecessor` return ZERO hits corpus-wide, with `summaris*` (3) and `citation` (10) as the positive control proving the instrument was live rather than dead (`asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted`). Verdict UNAUTHORED. Named rejections, each read in full: `accepted-adrs-carry-no-stale-prose` (principle — staleness axis; the corpus has already ruled born-wrong claims outside it, and it owns the repair this rule prevents needing); `prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` (principle — the nearest neighbour; an unchecked set re-derived AGAINST THE CODE by varying the search idiom, where here the source is one named passage and instance 2 is not a membership claim at all); `authoritative-source-beats-derived` (principle — precedence between two known sources, and its own chain leaves "should I go look" unasked, the identical rejection `a-handoff-claim-that-work-landed-is-unverified-state` recorded against it on 2026-08-01, which is the precedent this new-versus-edit call follows); `doc-vs-implementation-precedence` (principle — reactive and doc-versus-CODE, and in instance 2 the ADR and the code AGREE while the reader's sentence is false, so it has no gap to arbitrate); `no-claim-without-evidence` (principle — its bar is met by a citable path, which instance 1 had); `an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` (principle — instruments and measurements; ADR-0240's own correction explicitly declined to rehome this residue there, recording that the Library does not own it); `friction-justification-bar` (principle — same core at the friction-graduation seat, adjudicator-side); `unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted` (principle — a checker that could not RUN; no checker here); `reference-dont-restate` (principle — the affordance this fences, cited); `a-spec-body-describes-only-what-it-contracts` and `stale-prerequisite-links-are-phantoms` (principles — spec bodies read by a leaf, and dependency edges); `live-store-is-the-edit-surface`, `never-bypass-the-gate` and the remaining guardrails (write boundaries and gate discipline, silent on reading); `edit-first-curation` and `pair-the-fence-with-the-affordance` (patterns — curation and fence-pairing procedure, the latter cited); `library-edit-ceremony`, `friction-adjudication` and `verification-decay-detection` (processes — procedures, and the last is decay of VERIFICATION machinery, not fidelity of prose); the `definition` tier holds terminology only. Nothing in the corpus becomes redundant; this is a pure addition, and the id was checked free before minting.

NAMING — "document", "citation" and "reading" were each checked against the live `definition` tier and none is a live term, so the title carries no findability hazard (the `asset:boundary` trap `prose-names-a-set-it-never-checked` records).

TWO-CONSUMER-EXTRACTION cleared on two current, distinct consumers, one per instance: an author writing an ADR that amends or corrects another (librarian-curator, session-orchestrator, and any session landing a decision under ADR-0139), and an adjudicator writing a `routeReason` that rests on what an ADR decided (graduation-synthesist, guidance-curator). Both worked examples are carried with their discriminating rationale per `asset:example-carries-the-discriminator`: without the quoted-verbatim detail in the first and the modal-verb detail in the second, the rule degenerates into "read your sources", which has no discriminatory power.
description: A sentence describing what another document says — how many instances a predecessor named, whether a decision permitted or required something — is derived from that document, and the citation riding alongside it makes it look checked; open the passage you are characterising before you write the sentence.

title: Should the website expose a limited, live view of our REAL forest — and what does that open us to?
stakes: The website's Act 2 currently animates a MOCK forest. The owner's intent (2026-08-02) is that it grow OUR forest instead, and further, that a limited version of the forest UI be exposed publicly so people can watch the project being built live. That is a compelling product idea and a genuine attack-surface change in the same sentence, which is why it is a question and not a task. Nothing about it is settled, and the owner has explicitly deferred it: it gets its own arc AFTER `act2-intro-forest-regrow-arc` closes.
context:
Three facts frame it. (1) The Act 2 intro now regrows the whole forest app-native from the real story graph (ADR-0282/0283/0285), so the RENDERING half is built and proven at 40 islands — this question is not about whether it can be drawn. (2) Chapter 2 is a scripted mode of the real shared app and forbids a website-local reimplementation of product UI (ADR-0237), so the website would consume the same surface, not a copy. (3) Today every read of the live tier goes through Cloud SQL via the connector with keyless IAM (ADR-0021), and the members studio sits behind IAP (ADR-0042) — i.e. every existing reader is AUTHENTICATED. A public forest view has no such gate, which is the whole of the problem.

The exposure is not the map geometry; it is what the map is derived FROM. Story ids, titles, outcomes, capability names, dependency structure, build verdicts, session claims and in-flight work are all currently member-visible only. A public view has to decide, field by field, what a stranger may see — and a projection that leaks by accident is worse than no feature, because it looks deliberate. The transport shape matters too: ADR-0259 built an `HttpStore` + wire contract but wired it to no caller and no deployed server, so 'serve reads over HTTPS' is closer than it was but is still unbuilt, and pointing it at a public origin is a different decision from pointing it at an authenticated one.

Blocked until this lands: the website's Act 2 keeps animating a mock forest, and 'watch us build' does not exist.
options:
A — PUBLIC PROJECTION, BUILT AT PUBLISH TIME. A generated, redacted snapshot (ids + shape + status only) baked into the website at deploy, refreshed on a schedule. Pro: zero live attack surface, no new public endpoint, cannot leak what it never carries. Con: not live — 'watch us build' becomes 'watch what we built this morning', which may be most of the point lost.

B — LIVE READ-ONLY ENDPOINT WITH AN EXPLICIT ALLOW-LIST PROJECTION. A public HTTPS read of a deliberately narrow shape, served through the ADR-0259 wire contract. Pro: genuinely live, one surface, reuses built machinery. Con: a real public endpoint with real rate-limit, cache, cost and enumeration concerns, and every future field added to the story schema is a leak candidate unless the projection is allow-list rather than deny-list.

C — LIVE BUT ANONYMISED SHAPE ONLY. Stream the DAG's structure and activity — islands, edges, something is being built here — with no titles, ids or verdicts at all. Pro: the 'watch us build' feeling with almost nothing to leak. Con: an unreadable forest may be pretty and meaningless; the names are arguably what makes it interesting.

D — NOT YET. Close the arc, ship the app-native intro, and revisit when there is a reason beyond 'it would be cool'.
statement: What limited, public, read-only view of the live storytree forest can the website serve, and what is the security posture that makes it safe to open?
provenance: Owner, in conversation 2026-08-02, during the LOOK attestation of Act 2 intro increment 2 (PR #1078): "For Chapter 2 intro into i'm thinking we grow our forrest rather then a mock one, i'm actually thinking we expose our forrest ui onto the website just a limited version of it, then people can watch us while we build, this probably deserves its own separate arc after we done with this one as the security implications probably need a discussion - i dont want to open us up to attack." Captured so the intent survives outside chat; explicitly NOT started.
description: The owner wants visitors to watch the real storytree forest being built, not a mock. The blocker is not rendering — it is what a public read surface exposes.
recommendation: NON-BINDING, and deliberately not a technical pick: the first move is the owner's security conversation, not an implementation choice. The recommendation is that whichever option wins, the projection is defined as an ALLOW-LIST of fields with a test that fails when a new schema field is not explicitly classified — because the durable risk here is not the first release, it is the tenth field someone adds later. Option A is the cheapest way to learn whether the idea lands at all, and it can be replaced by B without changing the website's consumer. The owner named the security implications as needing discussion and deferred the whole thing to its own arc after `act2-intro-forest-regrow-arc` closes; nothing should start before that discussion.

risks: Low. The one behaviour change with any reach is that `loadLocalSecrets` now overwrites a BLANK env value, which a caller could in principle be using to mean "deliberately no credential". Nothing in the repo does — the SKIP paths test for absence, and a deliberate no-credential run simply leaves the variable unset — but the migration should grep for `STORYTREE_DB_USER=` with an empty right-hand side across `infra/` and the workflows before landing.
scope: Touches: `packages/drive/src/secrets.ts` (the hydrator's unset test), the `process.env["STORYTREE_DB_USER"] === undefined` guards in `packages/cli/src/check-corpus-content.ts` and `check-corpus-sync.ts`, and the studio server's store-selection path in `apps/studio/server/`. Leaves UNCHANGED: the keyless Cloud SQL IAM model (ADR-0021), env-always-wins precedence where the value is non-blank, the SKIP-on-absent-creds fail-open that keeps CI DB-free, and every message on the genuine unreachable path — a real connector failure must still say the database is unreachable, because there it is. Explicitly NOT a general env-var audit: this is the credential read path only.
title: An empty credential fails loudly at the boundary instead of being reported as an unreachable database
change: BEFORE: `STORYTREE_DB_USER` is read with an `=== undefined` test (`packages/cli/src/check-corpus-content.ts`, `check-corpus-sync.ts`, the studio server's store selection) or passed straight into the connector, so `""` reads as PRESENT and travels to the connector, which fails with a message about the database. `loadLocalSecrets` likewise only hydrates when the variable is `undefined`, so an empty export SUPPRESSES the hydration that would have fixed it. AFTER: one shared blank-is-unset predicate at every read site — an env value that trims to empty is treated exactly as unset. That has two consequences and both are wanted: `loadLocalSecrets` HYDRATES over a blank value from `~/.storytree/secrets.json` (so the mangled export self-heals), and any reader still left with nothing refuses with a message naming the VARIABLE and the hydration source, never the database.
summary: Every reader of STORYTREE_DB_USER treats a BLANK value as unset-and-refuse rather than as a credential, so a mangled export fails at the boundary naming the variable, instead of surfacing one process away as a live store that is perfectly healthy.
migration: 1. Add a `presentEnv(name)` helper beside `loadLocalSecrets` in `packages/drive/src/secrets.ts` returning the trimmed value or `undefined`, mirroring `resolveRepoRoot`'s `usable()`; unit-test that `""` and `"   "` both read as unset. 2. Make `loadLocalSecrets` hydrate when the variable is absent OR blank; test that a blank export is overwritten from the secrets file and a non-blank one is not (env-always-wins is preserved for real values). 3. Replace the `=== undefined` guards in the two checks with the helper; their existing SKIP paths then also cover the blank case, which is the correct classification (creds absent). 4. In the studio server, refuse a blank credential at startup with a message naming `STORYTREE_DB_USER` and `~/.storytree/secrets.json`, before any connector call. 5. Red proof for step 4: with `STORYTREE_DB_USER=` exported, the server must refuse naming the variable — today it starts and reports the store unreachable. Verified by `pnpm --filter @storytree/drive test`, `pnpm --filter @storytree/cli test`, and a manual blank-export run of the studio server.
readiness: No preconditions beyond a green gate. It touches no stored data, needs no DB, and is independent of any in-flight arc — `packages/drive/src/secrets.ts` is a small, rarely-edited surface, so the only real coordination cost is a session already editing the studio server's store selection. Safe to start at any time; a session should check `storytree noticeboard --pg` for a live claim on `studio` or `drive-machinery` first.
motivation: The failure this removes is not a wasted probe; it is a failure that manufactures exactly the evidence the house rule tells you to trust. `asset:probe-dont-assume-db-reachability` says never conclude the DB is down from your environment — PROBE it. Here the probe answers `{"store":"pg","db":"unreachable"}` and `/api/tree` 503s, which is the substrate speaking, and it is wrong: a direct connector `SELECT 1` answered `{"ok":1}` the whole time. Measured cost on the filing session (2026-08-02, branch claude/musing-hertz-44d3ee): ~25 minutes on a database that was never down, including a full 50-second connector probe to disprove it. The cost of NOT doing it is that the next session pays the same 25 minutes and reaches for `db:up` / `db:status` / the ADR-0250 remote-session fork — a whole diagnostic tree rooted at the wrong substrate. `resolveRepoRoot` already sets the house precedent for the exact same class: it treats a blank env value as UNSET rather than as the empty path, on the stated reasoning that `VAR=` is how a shell says "not configured" and reading it as a value would silently resolve every join against the filesystem root. This proposal applies that settled rule to credentials.
provenance: Written 2026-08-02 by the pre-merge friction drain (ADR-0168 D4) on branch claude/sleepy-northcutt-4d5383, as the `tool` route's emitted remedy for `asset:an-empty-env-var-from-a-shell-escape-reads-as-db-unreachable` (ADR-0287 D1: a `tool` routing that names a destination and stops is what let five items sit for five days with nothing built). The SCOPE and migration prose IS the adjudication's question-3/7 answer, moved here so it is listable and countable rather than buried in an archived routeReason. The `resolveRepoRoot` blank-is-unset precedent it leans on was read at ADR-0246's `packages/library/src/repo-root.ts` on the same day.
description: Refuse a blank STORYTREE_DB_USER at the point it is read, so a shell-mangled export cannot surface twenty seconds later as `db: unreachable`.

risks: Low, with one honest limit worth stating rather than discovering: a pid identifies a process on THIS machine, so the check is meaningful for a local dev server and meaningless against a remote or containerised one. The comparison must therefore be scoped to the localhost launcher path and must not become a general health assertion — a hosted `/api/health` carrying a pid nobody can compare is noise. The second limit is that this catches a foreign listener, not a foreign BUILD: the same session restarting a stale build on its own pid still measures the wrong code, which is the git-HEAD stamp's job and is already banner-covered.
scope: Touches: the `/api/health` handler in `apps/studio/server/serve.ts`, the `studio:up` / `studio:status` wrapper (pid capture, readiness assertion, `.studio.exit` truncation), and the desktop backend's mirrored health route IF it mirrors this one — mirrored routes are re-composed verbatim, never imported, so the mirror must be checked rather than assumed. Leaves UNCHANGED: the port-selection convention, the existing health fields (store reachability, the git-HEAD stamp that banners a moved checkout), the Cloud Run deployment's own health path, and every non-studio dev server. Explicitly NOT a port-allocation scheme — assigning unique ports per session is a larger, separate decision; this only makes the existing collision VISIBLE at the moment it matters.
title: A dev-server readiness probe answers "is it MINE", not merely "is something up"
change: BEFORE: `studio:up` writes `apps/studio/.studio.pid` and the readiness probe polls the port until something answers 200; `/api/health` reports store and git-HEAD state but nothing that identifies the PROCESS. On EADDRINUSE the server exits, the wrapper exits non-zero, and the probe — pointed at the port, not the process — still sees a healthy foreign listener. AFTER: `/api/health` includes `pid: process.pid`. The launcher records the pid it spawned and the readiness probe requires `health.pid` to equal it; a mismatch is reported as `port <n> is held by another process (pid <m>) — not this session's server`, naming `studio:down` or a different port. The stale-exit-file half is fixed alongside: the wrapper truncates `.studio.exit` before each launch, so an exit code can never belong to a previous run.
summary: The studio launcher records the pid it started and its readiness probe requires the health response to carry THAT pid, so a foreign process already listening on the chosen port is reported as a port collision instead of being silently measured as this session's build.
migration: 1. Add `pid` to the `/api/health` payload in `apps/studio/server/serve.ts`. 2. Have the `studio:up` wrapper capture the spawned pid, truncate `.studio.exit`, and after readiness fetch `/api/health` and compare pids; on mismatch exit non-zero with the foreign-pid message. 3. Make `studio:status` report the same comparison, so a session that did not start the server can still ask whether the listener is the one its pid file names. 4. Red proof: start a server on port N, then run `studio:up` again on port N from a second checkout — today the second run reports ready; after the change it must refuse naming the foreign pid. 5. Check whether the desktop backend mirrors `/api/health` and, if so, re-compose the field there too. Verified by `pnpm --filter studio test` plus the manual two-process red proof, which is the only place the defect is observable.
readiness: No preconditions beyond a green gate and no live claim on `studio` / `studio-build` (`storytree noticeboard --pg`). It changes no stored data and no deployed behaviour — `pid` is additive to a JSON response. Best run in a window where a second checkout is available, since step 4's red proof needs two concurrent servers to be observable at all.
motivation: This is `asset:an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` in its most expensive form: the probe observes "something on this port is healthy" and is read as "my server is healthy", and the two diverge precisely when a sibling session is running — the normal state of this shared dev box. Measured 2026-08-02 (branch claude/musing-hertz-44d3ee): `curl http://127.0.0.1:5199/` returned 200 and `/api/tree` returned 45 stories, the exact right shape, while the launch log carried `Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::5199` at `apps/studio/server/serve.ts:261` and the wrapper had exited 1. A stale `serve.exit` from a prior attempt further disguised which run the exit code belonged to. The cost was ~10 minutes and a near-miss on the increment's headline measurement — the run would have profiled a sibling's build and reported it as this branch's render change. That is a silent-wrong-answer, not a slowdown, and it is invisible to every check that asks "is it up?". The cost of NOT doing it scales with concurrency: the more sessions run, the more often a port answers for someone else, and nothing in the current path can tell.
provenance: Written 2026-08-02 by the pre-merge friction drain (ADR-0168 D4) on branch claude/sleepy-northcutt-4d5383, as the `tool` route's emitted remedy for `asset:a-foreign-dev-server-answers-200-on-the-port-you-picked` (ADR-0287 D1). The SCOPE and migration prose IS the adjudication's question-3/7 answer, moved here so the obligation outlives the routing rather than being archived with it. The mirrored-route caution in Scope is the house trap that a desktop route is re-composed verbatim and can silently lack a field the studio gained.
description: Stamp the studio server's health response with the pid the launcher started, so a sibling session's process on the same port cannot be measured as yours.

scope:
IN SCOPE. `listCategory` in `packages/cli/src/commands.ts` and its `orderedKinds` helper; the category-validation path and the two distinct answers it must now give; a red-green test that pins BOTH arms — a schema-defined kind with zero rows lists empty at exit 0, and a genuinely unknown string still errors with the available list at exit 1. The empty-tier arm is the red: it is the behaviour that does not exist today, and it must be provable without depending on which tiers happen to be empty at the moment the suite runs (stage the population, do not inherit it — `asset:an-inherited-precondition-holds-only-where-and-when-it-was-authored`, whose place/time face applies directly here since the natural test would otherwise assert a fact about today's corpus).

EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE, so this stays one small unit. No change to the `KindName` union or to `KIND_SPECS` — the schema is already correct and is the authority being adopted, not amended. No change to `SEED_SCOPE_KINDS`, the seed ceremonies, or any export path. No new CLI verb and no change to `storytree proposal list`, which reads the tier directly and was never affected. No attempt to backfill or create rows in any tier: the point is precisely that an empty tier must be reportable AS empty, so populating one would hide the defect rather than fix it. No change to the studio's category rendering — if the same population-derived pattern exists there it is a separate finding and belongs in its own item, not smuggled in here.

WHY THE `tool` ROUTE AND NOT GUIDANCE. The cheapest durable fix is a code fence, not prose an agent must remember (`asset:friction-justification-bar`, question 7). No amount of guidance would help: the failure is that a correct query returns a false denial, and the agent reading `unknown category` has no signal prompting it to distrust the answer. Fixing the derivation removes the trap for every future kind at once, where guidance would have to be re-read by every future session and would still leave the CLI asserting something untrue.
title: An artifact kind's listability comes from the schema, so an empty tier reports empty
change:
Make the category list SCHEMA-derived rather than population-derived, and give an empty tier its own honest answer.

1. In `listCategory` (`packages/cli/src/commands.ts`, currently line 355-358), stop deriving the valid-category set from `groupByKind(await store.queryDocs()).keys()`. Validate the requested category against the authoritative `KindName` union exported by `@storytree/library` (`packages/library/src/knowledge.ts`), so the set of listable categories is exactly the set of kinds the schema defines. `orderedKinds` keeps its ordering role; what changes is the set it orders.

2. Split the two answers that are currently conflated into one error. A category NOT in the schema stays `unknown category "<x>"` with the available list and a non-zero exit — that is a genuine user error. A category that IS in the schema but has zero rows returns a normal, exit-0 listing that says the tier is empty, in the same shape every populated tier uses (`<kind>  (0)`), so an empty tier reads as a fact about the population rather than a fault in the query.

3. Keep the `available categories:` line derived from the same schema union, so the error text can never again advertise a narrower world than the schema defines.
summary: `storytree library artifact list <kind>` derives its set of valid categories from the kinds that currently HAVE rows, never from the schema, so a real, schema-defined, seed-scope kind whose tier is empty answers `unknown category "<kind>"` and exits 1. Absence of rows is rendered as absence of the kind. Derive the category list from the `KindName` union instead, and report an empty tier as EMPTY rather than as unknown.
migration: No data migration and no schema change — the fix adopts an authority that already exists. One behavioural change to be aware of at the call sites: a query for a schema-defined kind with zero rows changes from exit 1 to exit 0. Any script or check that currently treats a non-zero exit from `artifact list <kind>` as "this kind is not a thing" would need to read the count instead; sweep for such callers before landing (`grep -rn "artifact list" packages/ scripts/ .github/`) rather than assuming there are none — `asset:tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep`. The change is strictly widening for human/agent readers: every invocation that works today keeps working and returns the same rows.
readiness:
READY TO BUILD. The defect is located to a single line that was re-verified in source at adjudication on 2026-08-03 (`packages/cli/src/commands.ts:356`), the authority to adopt already exists and is exported (`KindName` in `packages/library/src/knowledge.ts`), and the unit is small enough to prove in one red-green pass inside `packages/cli` with no cross-package sequencing.

The red is available without contriving anything: assert that a schema-defined kind with zero rows lists empty at exit 0. That fails today, for the right reason, against a staged population.

Nothing blocks this. It needs no DB (the in-memory seed store exercises both arms), no owner decision, and no ADR — the schema already decided which kinds exist; this only stops the CLI contradicting it. One caution for whoever takes it: the natural test would read whichever tier happens to be empty today, which is an inherited precondition that inverts the moment someone writes a row — stage the population in the test.
motivation:
Measured 2026-08-02 on branch claude/zen-chandrasekhar-e197f7 and re-verified at adjudication on 2026-08-03. `pnpm storytree library artifact list proposal --pg` returned:

    unknown category "proposal". available categories: definition, principle, pattern,
    guardrail, techstack, process, agent, arc, plan, open-question, friction, template,
    uat-criterion.

exit 1, with `proposal` absent from the list — while `proposal` was already a first-class kind in every sense that matters: a member of the `KindName` union (`packages/library/src/knowledge.ts`), holder of a full `KIND_SPECS` body table with a documented purpose, exported as a schema, and listed in `SEED_SCOPE_KINDS` so it is part of the committed seed's export scope. ADR-0168 D2 further names it a member of the Library's lifecycle tier, each with a mandatory drain.

The wrong reading is the attractive one. `unknown category` asserts that the kind does not exist, which is false, and points away from the real finding. The owner had asked why friction needing a build is not promoted into a `proposal`, observing there were no proposals in the Library; verifying that observation from the CLI was impossible, because the CLI's answer denied the tier rather than reporting it empty. Establishing that `proposal` was real took reading four separate places in `knowledge.ts`; establishing WHY it was unlistable took reading `listCategory`'s implementation. Roughly 15 minutes, spent to disprove the instrument rather than to learn anything.

The defect is one line. `listCategory` (`packages/cli/src/commands.ts:356`) reads:

    const kinds = orderedKinds(groupByKind(await store.queryDocs()).keys());

The category list is computed from DOCS PRESENT, never from the schema, so an empty tier erases itself. Confirmed at the time that the tier was genuinely empty rather than mis-queried (no `proposal` row in the seed either), with a positive control on the same instrument: `artifact list principle --pg` returned 78 rows.

WHY THIS IS NOT SPENT NOW THAT THE TIER HAS ROWS. As of 2026-08-03 the `proposal` tier holds two rows, so this exact invocation now succeeds. The defect is untouched, and it is structurally certain to recur on two independent paths. (1) A NEW KIND starts empty by definition — every kind added to the schema before its first row is written is unlistable for exactly as long as it takes someone to write one, which is precisely the window in which an agent orienting on the new kind most needs to see it. `proposal` itself is the worked example. (2) A LIFECYCLE TIER CAN DRAIN TO ZERO, and for the proposal tier that is the SUCCESS state, not a fault: `asset:retire-realized-proposal` exists to remove a proposal once it has been built. A fully-drained proposal tier — every parked remedy delivered — would make `storytree library artifact list proposal` report that the kind does not exist. An empty mandatory-drain tier is a FINDING, and the instrument that should report it currently denies it.
