scope:
IN SCOPE. The `gate` script in the root `package.json` and whatever small runner replaces the `&&` chain (a script under `scripts/`, or a CLI verb — the builder's call, but it must be testable without executing the real 25-minute gate). The per-step result table with its three distinct outcomes. The step reordering. A red-green test over the RUNNER, driven with stub steps: given a set of steps where step 2 fails, the runner must still execute steps 3..N, must report step 2 FAIL and the rest by their real outcomes, must exit non-zero, and must never print PASS for a step it did not run. The opt-in fail-fast flag.

EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE, so this stays one small unit and cannot become a gate rewrite.

No change to WHAT any check does, to any check's own exit semantics, or to any ceiling — in particular `check:declared`, whose lobby arm is correct, load-bearing and permanent under ADR-0284, is REORDERED and never weakened, never made a warning, and never given automatic remediation (ADR-0245 D5.2 D3 forbids that explicitly). If this unit ends up softening any check, it has gone wrong.

No change to CI. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `verify` job runs its own steps against the merge result and is the authoritative gate; it is deliberately untouched, and the local runner must not become a dependency of it in this unit.

No new check, no removed check, and no change to the set of 23 steps.

No attempt to parallelise the steps. Parallelism is a plausible next idea and a different unit with different risks (interleaved output, shared DB connections, and a `pnpm -r` step that already fans out internally); mixing it in would make the red-green proof about scheduling instead of about reporting.

WHY THE `tool` ROUTE AND NOT GUIDANCE. The cheapest durable fix is a code fence rather than prose an agent must remember (`asset:friction-justification-bar`, question 7). Guidance here would have to say "when the gate aborts early, reconstruct the remaining step list and re-run it by hand" — which is precisely the 25 minutes of manual work the friction measured, re-imposed on every future session and dependent on each one remembering. The runner does it once, for everyone, and turns an ambiguous abort into an explicit per-step verdict.
title: The gate runs every step and reports per-step, so one red never hides the rest
change:
Two changes, both to how the gate is SEQUENCED and REPORTED. Neither weakens what it enforces: every step still runs and any red still fails the gate.

1. RUN EVERY STEP, THEN REPORT. Replace the `&&` chain with a runner that executes each step, records its exit code, and continues; at the end it prints a per-step table — PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN — and exits non-zero if any step failed. `NOT RUN` must remain a distinct outcome from PASS and from FAIL, because a step that was skipped is unverified rather than green (`asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted`) and the current output cannot say so. This is strictly stronger than today: more steps actually execute, and the session learns the state of its own diff even when a shared-environment check is red.

2. ORDER BY WHO IS BEING JUDGED. Put the steps that judge THIS session's diff — `pnpm -r typecheck` and `pnpm -r test`, plus the cheap static checks over the session's own files — ahead of the steps that judge the shared environment or the shared checkout (`check:declared` in particular). Ordering is not correctness here, since every step runs either way; it is about which verdict arrives first when the run is long, and about not making the session's own answer wait behind a condition it is forbidden from remediating.

Keep one escape hatch for the fast inner loop: a flag (or a sibling script) that restores fail-fast for a session that wants the first red immediately rather than the full picture. Default is run-all; fail-fast is opt-in, not the other way round.
summary: `pnpm gate` is a 23-link `&&` chain, so the first red aborts it and leaves every later step UNRUN — reported as nothing at all, not as unverified. The steps that judge the session's own diff (`pnpm -r typecheck`, `pnpm -r test`) sit at links 11 and 12, behind nine environment and hygiene checks including `check:declared`, whose lobby arm reds on dirt another session left in the shared primary checkout. Make the gate run every step and report a per-step PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN summary, and order the steps so the ones judging this session's work run before the ones judging the shared environment.
migration:
No data or schema migration. One behavioural change with a real consequence to plan for: the gate's WALL CLOCK on a failing run goes UP, because a run that used to stop at link 10 now proceeds through typecheck and the full test suite. On this box that is roughly 25 minutes it previously skipped. That is the intended trade — the information is what the session was re-running by hand anyway — but it interacts with a known trap: `asset:merge-ceremony` step 2 already mandates invoking the gate BACKGROUNDED on the first attempt because a foreground run can exceed the harness's fixed tool-call ceiling and be killed with no verdict at all. Landing this makes that guidance more load-bearing, not less. If the ceremony's wording needs a companion note once the runner exists, that is a librarian edit in the same PR, not a separate item.

Consumers to sweep before landing (`asset:tightening-a-shared-contract-needs-a-full-sweep`): anything that shells `pnpm gate` and reads only its exit code keeps working unchanged, since the runner still exits non-zero on any failure. Anything that PARSES the gate's stdout would need to read the new summary table — check `scripts/`, `.github/workflows/`, and the desktop/studio backends for such a caller rather than assuming there is none.
readiness:
READY TO BUILD. The chain is a single line in the root `package.json`, re-read and confirmed at adjudication on 2026-08-03 (23 steps, `check:declared` at link 10, typecheck and test at 11 and 12). Nothing is blocked: no DB, no owner decision, no ADR — every step keeps its own semantics and any red still fails the gate, so this changes sequencing and reporting only, and does not touch what `asset:never-bypass-the-gate` protects.

The red is available cheaply and MUST be driven with stub steps rather than the real gate, or the unit becomes untestable: given a synthetic step list whose second entry fails, assert that the later entries still executed, that the summary distinguishes FAIL from NOT RUN, and that the process exits non-zero. That fails today because no runner exists.

One caution for whoever takes it. The obvious shortcut — keep the `&&` chain and simply move `check:declared` to the end — fixes only the instance in the evidence and leaves the general defect live: the NEXT early red (any of links 1 through 9) masks everything after it just as completely, and the output still cannot distinguish a step that failed from a step that never ran. Reordering alone is half the fix, and the half that does not generalise.
motivation:
Measured 2026-08-02 on branch claude/charming-elion-17944b, landing the ADR-0245 D5.2 lobby-arm scoping fix, and the chain re-verified in package.json at adjudication on 2026-08-03.

`pnpm gate` stopped at `check:declared` because the shared primary checkout carried four uncommitted paths authored by ANOTHER session (a modified docs/decisions/0253-*.md plus three untracked directories). The gate never ran typecheck, never ran the test suite, and never ran the eleven post-test checks. Verifying the change required re-running all fourteen remaining steps by hand across three invocations — typecheck plus `pnpm -r test` at roughly 25 minutes, then the post-test checks in two batches after a ten-minute tool timeout truncated the first. All fourteen were green: typecheck exit 0, tests exit 0 (packages/cli 1188/1188), every remaining check exit 0. Per the check's own message and ADR-0245 D5.2 D3 ("never automatic remediation"), the lobby was not that session's to clean, so NO in-session action could have produced one green gate run.

The chain is exactly as described. `package.json`'s `gate` script is 23 `&&`-joined steps:

    check:manifest, check:boundaries, check:mirror-conformance, check:claude, check:agents,
    check:process-graph, check:web-grounding, check:web-engine, check:web-experience,
    check:declared, typecheck, test, check:agents-sync, check:corpus-sync,
    check:corpus-content, check:friction-drain, check:verification-decay, check:coverage,
    check:surface-coverage, check:graduation-worklist, check:node-version,
    check:dist-drift, check:deploy-health

`check:declared` is link 10 of 23, and thirteen links follow it — including both steps that judge the session's own diff.

TWO THINGS MAKE THIS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN ENDURING.

First, the frequency changed and is not going back. The lobby arm is correct and load-bearing, and ADR-0284 makes the static write-authority wall permanent, so a red at link 10 on another session's dirt is now a ROUTINE outcome rather than a rare one — that branch found the lobby dirty on its first look. What fights is not the arm; it is the arm's POSITION in a fail-fast chain, ahead of the steps that judge the session's own work.

Second, the failure is silent in the direction that costs most. An aborted chain reports one red and says nothing about the other thirteen steps, but `asset:unrun-check-is-unverified-not-refuted` is explicit that a check which could not run is UNVERIFIED, not refuted — and the gate's output does not distinguish the two. A session that reads the abort as "the gate failed" and stops has learned nothing about its own diff. A session that reads it as "not my problem" may skip verification entirely. Both readings are available from the same output, and reconstructing the step list to re-run the remainder by hand is judgement the session has to supply itself.
description: `pnpm gate` is a 23-link `&&` chain, so the first red aborts it and leaves every later step UNRUN — reported as nothing at all, not as unverified.

scope:
IN SCOPE. The options table in `packages/cli/src/commands.ts` (lines 1953-2050, 71 entries), the new `FLAG_OWNERS` and `SHARED_FLAGS` declarations beside it, and a red-green test in `packages/cli` pinning the three-way agreement. Backfilling `FLAG_OWNERS` for all 71 existing flags is part of the unit — the declaration is worthless while it is partial, and the backfill is what surfaces any collision that already exists today (which is itself a finding worth having, and should be REPORTED rather than silently fixed if one turns up).

The red is the test running against a deliberately-unowned flag, or against a two-owner flag missing from `SHARED_FLAGS`.

EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE, so this stays one small unit.

No restructuring of the parser into per-area options tables. That is the structurally better answer and a much larger unit — `parseArgs` is called once because the area arrives as a positional, so splitting the table means restructuring the dispatch, and every area's parsing would need re-proving. If the declaration below later justifies that move, it is its own proposal. Doing it here would make the red-green proof about dispatch rather than about collision visibility.

No renaming of any existing flag, and no change to any area's current behaviour. In particular `storytree drift`'s `--change` keeps `multiple: true` and `storytree proposal`'s branch keeps joining the array; this unit makes the sharing VISIBLE, it does not adjudicate it.

No source scanning for `values.<key>` reads. It was considered and rejected: a scan is brittle against ordinary refactors and would fail in ways that name the scanner rather than the collision.

No attempt to verify that two readers of a shared flag mean the same thing by it. That is not machine-decidable and claiming it would be a false fence.

No change to `check:surface-coverage`, which governs the verb-to-process bijection and is a cited precedent here, not a target.

WHY THE `tool` ROUTE AND NOT GUIDANCE. The cheapest durable fix is a code fence over prose an agent must remember (`asset:friction-justification-bar`, question 7). The guidance alternative is literally "read all 71 entries before naming a flag", which is the exhaustive reading nothing prompts and everyone skips — and it would still be silent in the case that matters, since a session that skipped the read gets no signal at all. A declaration puts the existing owner one lookup from the author's cursor, and the test refuses the undeclared case.
title: A CLI flag's owning area is declared and machine-checked, so a collision is visible when the flag is named
change:
Make flag OWNERSHIP explicit and machine-checked, so the collision is visible at the moment a flag is named rather than discoverable only by exhaustive reading.

Recommended shape, chosen because it needs no source scanning and no restructuring of the parser:

1. Add a single declaration — `FLAG_OWNERS: Record<string, readonly string[]>` beside the options table in `packages/cli/src/commands.ts` — mapping each flag name to the area(s) that read it. This is the one place a reader or author looks to answer "who else uses `--change`?".

2. Add an explicit `SHARED_FLAGS` allow-list for the flags that are DELIBERATELY read by more than one area (`--file`, `--pg`, `--reason`, `--title`, `--node`, `--outcome` are the current population), each carrying a one-line note stating the single meaning all its readers agree on. Intentional sharing stays legal; it just has to be stated.

3. Add a test asserting the three-way agreement: every key in the options table appears in `FLAG_OWNERS`; every `FLAG_OWNERS` key appears in the options table; and any flag with two or more owners appears in `SHARED_FLAGS`. A new area declaring an existing flag name therefore cannot land without either adding itself as an owner — where the existing owner is sitting one line away, in view — or being refused by the test.

The mechanism is deliberately dumb: it compares declarations to declarations, so it cannot rot the way a source-scanning heuristic would. It does not attempt to prove that two readers of a shared flag interpret it the same way — that remains a judgement — but it does force the sharing to be written down, which is the step that makes the judgement possible at all.
summary: `storytree` parses every area's flags from ONE global `parseArgs` options table, so a flag name that is natural for a new area may already be declared for a different one. When the two declarations disagree on arity the collision surfaces at `tsc`; when they agree, two areas silently share one flag whose help text describes a single meaning, and the failure is a wrong VALUE rather than an error. Make each flag's consuming area an explicit, machine-checked declaration, so a collision is visible to the author of the next flag instead of discoverable only by reading the whole table.
migration:
No data migration, no schema change, and no user-visible CLI behaviour change — every existing invocation parses exactly as it does today. The whole unit is a declaration plus a test over it.

One thing to expect during the backfill: enumerating the owners of all 71 flags may surface an ALREADY-LIVE accidental sharing — two areas reading one flag with different intended meanings, currently silent because their arities happen to agree. If one turns up, report it as a finding and file it rather than folding a behaviour change into this unit; renaming a live flag is a back-compat question that `asset:cli-relocations-keep-an-alias` governs, and it does not belong in the same change as the fence that found it.
readiness:
READY TO BUILD, with one honest caveat about size. The surface is located and measured: one `parseArgs` call at `packages/cli/src/commands.ts:1952`, one options table at lines 1953-2050 holding 71 entries, all re-verified at adjudication on 2026-08-03. No DB, no owner decision, no ADR — this adds a declaration and a test and changes no behaviour.

The red is trivially available and does not depend on the corpus or the environment: assert the three-way agreement against a table entry with no declared owner. That fails today because no declaration exists.

THE CAVEAT: the mechanism is small but the BACKFILL is 71 entries of judgement, since each flag's owning area must be read off the code rather than guessed. That is the bulk of the unit and it is unglamorous. It should not be skipped or sampled — a partial `FLAG_OWNERS` is worse than none, because it reads as authoritative while being silent about exactly the flags nobody got to. If the backfill turns up an already-live accidental sharing, report it; do not fold the fix into this unit.
motivation:
Measured 2026-08-03 on branch claude/sad-borg-39ce40 while adding the `proposal` area (ADR-0287 D1), and re-verified in source at adjudication the same day.

The `proposal` kind's `KIND_SPECS` body table has a required field literally named `change`. `packages/cli/src/commands.ts` already declared `change: { type: "string", multiple: true }` for `storytree drift` (confirmed at line 2006), so `values.change` arrived in the proposal branch as `string[]` and had to be joined into paragraphs. The five sibling fields — `--summary`, `--motivation`, `--scope`, `--migration`, `--readiness` — were all free, so nothing signalled that one of the six was different.

THE LOUD CASE IS THE LUCKY ONE. That collision cost about five minutes, and only because the ARITY happened to clash: a `string[]` where a `string` was expected is a type error, so `tsc --noEmit` caught it. Had `drift`'s flag been a plain `{ type: "string" }`, the proposal branch would have compiled and run with two areas sharing one flag and no error anywhere. The cost that matters is that silent case, and it is a wrong VALUE rather than a crash.

THE STRUCTURE MAKES IT INEVITABLE, and it is measured, not hypothesised. There is exactly ONE `parseArgs` call in `packages/cli/src/commands.ts` (line 1952) with a single options table spanning lines 1953-2050 — 71 flag entries — serving every area of the CLI. Several flags are already read by multiple areas: `values.file` is read at 8 sites, `values.reason` at 4, `values.title` at 3, `values.outcome` at 3, `values.node` at 2, `values.change` at 3. Those sharings are mostly intentional today, but nothing in the code says so and nothing distinguishes an intentional sharing from an accidental one.

WHAT NOTHING PROMPTS. Avoiding this today requires reading all 71 entries before naming any new flag, and no step in authoring a CLI area asks a session to do that. The next person to add an area — or simply the next field on an existing one — meets the same trap, and meets it silently unless they are lucky enough to clash on arity. The house already has the right precedent for this shape: `check:surface-coverage` makes the CLI verb surface a DECLARED, machine-checked projection rather than something a reader must reconstruct (ADR-0154). Flags have no equivalent.

why:
A plausible physical story arrives first and arrives free, and it will fit a pure processing artefact perfectly well — so nothing about the defect itself flags the misattribution, and the mechanism you build on the story looks like progress the whole time it is failing.

Measured in `docs/research/chapter2-code-only-art-2026-08-01/blender-hero-v1/`. The mature crown of a rendered tree carried a scatter of bright bark-coloured flecks, measured at 3.8% of the crown, all landing on the brightest bark band (152,106,60). The story was immediate and, in general, physically true: bark and canopy are separate surfaces, so an outer twig pokes a fraction through the lobe meant to hide it, and at 128 px that reads as orange specks. A geometry mechanism was built on it — twigs taper away under their own canopy weight, `WOOD_HIDE = 0.32` in `blender_tree.py`, keyed on the same cloud weight that placed the lobe so the two surfaces agree by construction. That mechanism shipped, and its docstring still stands today, unmodified, stating that diagnosis.

The flecks were not twigs. They were a classification bug one stage downstream: Cycles anti-aliases its own band edges, so the raw frame carries a fringe of intermediate values at every boundary, and the pixeliser's ABSOLUTE foliage-membership threshold dropped those fringes out of the foliage family and snapped them to the nearest brown — which is exactly (152,106,60), the band the flecks were measured on. `pixelise.py` now classifies by NEAREST FAMILY instead, `ffol = df.min(axis=2) <= db.min(axis=2)`, with the comment "A nearest-family test has no threshold to miss", and that removed the colour completely. Both the code and the write-up attribute the fix entirely to the classification change and never to the taper; the README concedes it directly — the wood taper written first to "stop twigs poking through" was treating a symptom.

Three costs, and the third is why this is a rule rather than a note. (1) The mechanism did not MOVE the defect, and the response to that was to tune it — the taper was lowered more than once, which is the trap and not the fix. (2) It regressed a second axis while it ran: the crown went from 29% bark by area, where the limbs running through the canopy are much of what makes it read as a tree, down to 17% and closer to a solid mass — and the README records that lowering the taper "moved this less than expected, because the twigs are geometrically *inside* the clouds rather than hidden by a parameter". (3) An untraced hypothesis is not merely unproven, it is unfalsifiable in practice: a mechanism with a continuous knob converts every failure to move the defect into "not enough yet" rather than "wrong cause", so the cost is unbounded in the tuning direction and the wrong answer never announces itself.

That shape recurs, which is the case for stating it once rather than a fourth time in a fourth domain. Three instances in three days by three unrelated mechanisms: ADR-0240 attributed a reported symptom (choppy pan when zoomed out) to re-computation and re-mounting without ever measuring a pan frame, and four stages of an arc were sequenced against that untraced cause before ADR-0272 measured one and found ~99.8% of the frame in rasterisation; `asset:frontend-perf-measured-on-the-vite-dev-server-misattributes-the-cost` gave a correctly-observed slow frame a plausible-but-wrong causal story because the measurement was taken at a layer the shipped bundle does not have; and this one.
title: Trace a defect to its producing stage before building against it
statement: A defect observed in a downstream artifact must be traced back to the stage that PRODUCED it — the specific pass, buffer or layer the offending values actually came out of — BEFORE any mechanism is built to prevent it. Until that trace exists you hold a plausible story, not a cause; and a mechanism standing on a story cannot be falsified by the tuning you will then spend on it.
howToApply:
Before authoring any mechanism against a defect, produce the TRACE: name the stage the defective values actually came out of, and show the mapping from the defect you can see back to the input that produced it. Concretely — for a bad pixel in a pixelised output, which 3x3 source block in the raw frame; for a slow frame, which of script / paint / rasterise / composite; for a wrong value in a projection, which write produced the row; for a wrong colour in a composited sprite, which layer carried it in. The instrument is almost always cheap and already available: read the INTERMEDIATE at each stage and find the first one where the defect is present. The bar is that the trace RULES OUT the upstream stages — not that it is consistent with the story you already have, which a plausible story always is.

The tell that closes it, and the most useful thing on this page: **a mechanism aimed at a cause that does not MOVE the defect has falsified its own hypothesis.** Not "needs more tuning". When the parameter has gone from high to middling to low and the artefact is still sitting there, the loop you are in is not convergence — it is a wrong cause with a continuous knob attached, and the knob will absorb any amount of effort while the defect stays exactly where it was. Stop and trace. Treat a SECOND-AXIS regression as corroboration of the same thing: a mechanism working against the wrong cause is still doing something, and what it does usually shows up somewhere you were not looking.

Two neighbours sit close and neither covers this. `asset:an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes` governs the INSTRUMENT — an observable that is wrong-but-correlated, or a figure generalised past what it measured. Here the observation was sound: the flecks were real, correctly measured, correctly located on the bark band. What was wrong was a causal HYPOTHESIS about a correct observation, and the remedy differs accordingly — there you replace the observable or re-measure, here you ORDER THE WORK. `asset:dogfood-fix-the-source` says fix tooling AT its source rather than working around it downstream, which presupposes the source is already KNOWN; finding it is the entire content of this rule. `asset:frontend-perf-measured-on-the-vite-dev-server-misattributes-the-cost` is the third member of the family and the discriminator is worth holding: that one is about INSTRUMENT choice a-priori, before measuring; this is about diagnostic ORDERING, before building. Adjacent, not the same.

The fence, so this does not read as a bar on acting under uncertainty. Ship a probe, a spike, an experiment, anything that READS an intermediate — those are how a trace gets made, and none of them is what this refuses. What it refuses is a MECHANISM: something built into the artifact and then tuned, standing on a hypothesis that a short read of an intermediate buffer would have confirmed or killed. No mechanical check can decide whether a causal hypothesis has been traced to its producing stage, which is why this is a principle rather than a guardrail and why it has to be asked by hand, at the moment the plausible story arrives and before the first line of the mechanism is written.
provenance: Authored 2026-08-03 by guidance-curator in the ADR-0168 D4 board drain, graduating friction `built-a-mechanism-for-a-defect-i-had-not-traced-to-its-source-buffer` (routed `principle` by graduation-synthesist, with corpus-investigator verification treated as mandatory rather than optional because behavioural-floor content carries the highest blast radius). EVIDENCE, confirmed in committed sources — the location is `docs/research/chapter2-code-only-art-2026-08-01/blender-hero-v1/`, not the earlier blender spike: the flecks measured 3.8% of the mature crown at (152,106,60), stated verbatim in three independent committed places (blender_tree.py, README.md, pixelise.py); the twigs-poking-through diagnosis and the geometry mechanism built on it, whose docstring still stands unmodified in blender_tree.py while the README concedes it was treating a symptom; `WOOD_HIDE = 0.32`, committed and absent from the prior commit; the second-axis regression, "exp-16's crown is 29% bark by area... This one is 17%"; and the nearest-family classifier read from the current logic rather than its prose, `ffol = df.min(axis=2) <= db.min(axis=2)` with the comment "A nearest-family test has no threshold to miss", which both the code and the README attribute the fix to entirely, never to the taper. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED as unverifiable in committed history, and named here so a later editor does not re-admit them: (i) the 0.92 -> 0.55 -> 0.32 taper progression — only 0.32 was ever committed, the intermediate tuning happened inside one working session, so git cannot confirm the two earlier values; nothing contradicts them and the README's "Lowering the wood taper twice" is consistent, which is why the text says the taper was lowered more than once without naming figures. (ii) The literal classifier formula `min |raw - FOLIAGE_BANDS| < 24` and the raw fringe pixel value — the prior COMMITTED foliage test was a different and simpler hue heuristic with no FOLIAGE_BANDS array and no constant 24 anywhere, and the specific fringe pixel the item reports is not in committed history. The CONCEPT (an absolute membership threshold dropping anti-aliased fringes into the bark family) is in pixelise.py's own comment and is what the text states. The rule depends on neither. A NEW UNIT AND NOT AN EDIT: all five guidance-bearing tiers were swept TWICE at adjudication, offline and live with identical ids and counts so there is no seed/live drift — principle (73), guardrail (17), pattern (25), process (18), definition (52) = 185 artifacts by title, 14 read in full, plus a full-text grep of the seed for `root cause|trace.*back|traced to|producing buffer|source buffer|downstream|misdiagnos|wrong (layer|stage|buffer)`. Verdict UNAUTHORED, and the investigator's tell for genuinely new content held: the candidate wording traces to the item's own closing sentence rather than paraphrasing anything in the corpus. WHY NOT FOLDED INTO `an-observable-is-evidence-only-for-what-it-observes`, the obvious consolidation candidate, which this same pass ALSO edited (adding its temporal-window face): that artifact's own provenance states the corpus's consolidation test as whether the REMEDY is one, and here it is not. Its design-time face REPLACES a mis-chosen observable, its inference-time face RE-MEASURES or narrows the claim, its new temporal face BRACKETS the interval — and this rule's remedy is to ORDER THE WORK, trace before you build, on an observation that was entirely sound. Three remedies is three artifacts, and loading a fourth unrelated face onto that principle in the same pass would blunt all of them. Named rejections with discriminators: `dogfood-fix-the-source` (fix tooling AT its source once the source is KNOWN — it does not prescribe finding the source first, which is this rule's entire content); `a-green-positional-oracle-is-necessary-not-sufficient` (a checker blind to a defect class — the opposite shape, since here the defect was plainly visible and merely misattributed); `observability-first` (studio event typing); `no-claim-without-evidence` (admissibility of claims, silent on diagnostic ordering); `verification-decay-detection` (decay of proof surfaces); `implementer-shortcut-patterns` (hollow implementations gaming a test's shape); `assess-tradeoffs-by-naming-both-sides` (decision communication); `deterministic-parameterised-geometry` (how to author geometry); `art-asset-designer-swarm` (nearest thematic cousin — a screenshot blind to a CSS cascade — but scoped to that swarm's self-verification step); `verification-wins`, `authoritative-source-beats-derived`, `evidence`, `probe` (unrelated axes). RECURRENCE, which is what takes this past the one-off bar: three instances in three days by three unrelated mechanisms — ADR-0240's untraced attribution of a reported pan symptom, corrected only when ADR-0272 measured an actual pan frame after four stages of an arc had been sequenced against the wrong cause; `frontend-perf-measured-on-the-vite-dev-server-misattributes-the-cost`, archived and routed edit-existing one day before this item was filed; and this one. The family has now surfaced three times without converging, and the third instance's discriminator is carried in the text so the members do not blur: instance two is INSTRUMENT choice before measuring (a-priori), this is diagnostic ORDERING before building (procedural). KIND — principle, not guardrail, on the standing enforcer test: no deterministic mechanism can decide whether a causal hypothesis has been traced to its producing stage, and a guardrail must name its enforcer. Not a pattern either — this is a truth about the epistemic status of an untraced hypothesis, not an approach with tradeoffs. THE OPERATIONAL TELL is stated prominently and on purpose, because it is the only part of this rule that fires AFTER the mistake has been made and is therefore the one an agent can still be saved by: a mechanism that does not MOVE the defect has falsified its own hypothesis. A FENCE is paired with it so the rule is not read as a bar on acting under uncertainty — probes, spikes and experiments that read an intermediate are how the trace gets made and are explicitly permitted; what is refused is a tuned mechanism standing on an untraced story. Consumers: any agent building against a defect it can see in a downstream artifact — frontend-builder, the art and geometry swarms, planner, session-orchestrator, and any session that reaches for a parameter after a symptom report.
description: A defect seen in a downstream artifact must be traced to the stage that PRODUCED it before any mechanism is built to prevent it — a plausible physical story fits a pure processing artefact perfectly well, survives rounds of tuning without moving the defect, and can regress a second axis while it does.

title: The gate asserts behaviour, never wall-clock time
change:
Today: `packages/forest-world/src/routing.test.ts:710` measures `performance.now()` around a 30-island / 60-edge routing run and asserts the elapsed wall-clock is under 2000ms.

After: the same test asserts something the diff can actually change and the machine cannot. Two acceptable shapes, executor's choice:

- Or DELETE the assertion and keep the correctness half of the test. A deleted flaky assertion is strictly better than a retained one that is believed at random.

Whichever is chosen, no wall-clock threshold survives in a gate-run test.

title: One canonical DB-reachability probe serves both db:up and the CLI

title: A backgrounded gate exits with the gate's own status
change:
Today: each session invents its own backgrounding wrapper, and every shape that also captures the exit code destroys it.

After: `pnpm gate:bg` (a script in the repo, e.g. `scripts/gate-bg.sh` plus a `package.json` entry) that
- runs `pnpm gate`,
- tees combined output to a known per-session log path (NOT a fixed `/tmp` path — that collides across concurrent worktrees, and a sibling's log has already been read as this session's result),
- writes the gate's exit code to a sibling `.exit` file, and
- EXITS with the gate's own status, so any wrapper, notification, or `$?` read above it reports the gate.

The verification instruction collapses from "remember that notifications lie, and remember which capture shapes force zero" to "run `pnpm gate:bg`". That is the whole point: prose is what already failed here, twice, including when it was in the task brief.
summary: Ship a repo script that backgrounds `pnpm gate`, tees to a log, and EXITS WITH THE GATE'S OWN STATUS — so a red gate can never be announced as a clean completion, and no session has to decide whether to trust a completion notification.
migration:
1. Reproduce the red honestly, because it is a shell property and not a code path: assert that the current documented backgrounding shapes (`{ cmd; echo $?; }`, `cmd | tail`) return 0 for a command that exited 1. That is a real, checkable test over a trivial failing command — no gate run needed.
2. Write the script. The exit-code propagation is the load-bearing line and needs its own assertion: wrap a command that exits 1, and assert the WRAPPER exits 1.
3. Make the log path session-unique and assert THAT too — the fixed-path collision is a distinct trap (a sibling worktree has clobbered a shared `gate.log` and its red was read as this session's).
4. Assert the `.exit` file contains the same status the wrapper exited with, so the two ways of reading the result cannot disagree.
5. Use it for this unit's own gate run. If the script cannot report its own build honestly it is not finished.
readiness: Ready now. No dependency, no decision outstanding, and the whole change is one script plus its test. It is also the cheapest guard in the tier against the highest-consequence failure — reporting a false green to the owner.
motivation:
A backgrounded command's completion notification reports the outer shell's exit code, not the wrapped command's. Measured: `pnpm gate` was backgrounded as `{ pnpm gate; echo "GATE_EXIT=$?"; } > gate3.log 2>&1`. The gate FAILED — the log's last line reads `GATE_EXIT=1` and `pnpm -r test` aborted on `apps/studio test: Failed`. The completion notification for that same task read `Background command "Run the gate" completed (exit code 0)`: true of the wrapper, false of the gate. Acting on the notification, the session reported the gate as GREEN TO THE OWNER and had to correct it one turn later.

The generic shell fact (a `{ cmd; echo $?; }` group exits with the echo's status) is reconstructible. The actual failure is not that rule — it is that the harness completion notification LOOKS authoritative and was believed. The item records that the task brief warned about this in advance and it happened anyway. That is the guidance-quality signal (`asset:guidance-quality`): when guidance is not followed, fix the structure, not the emphasis.

Reinforced 2026-07-28, and it recurs with a second face — `| tail` and a trailing `; echo "EXIT=$?"` both force a zero status the same way. Structurally certain to recur, because backgrounding the gate is the standard move for a run that outlives one foreground tool call, and the gate takes ~25 minutes.

The consequence is the worst-shaped one available: a session reports green to the owner when the gate was red. Every other cost in the friction worklist is time; this one is a false statement to the human.

title: library artifact can read one raw stored field
change:
Today: two read paths, neither raw. `library artifact <id>` renders; `--json` is an input flag on that verb and cannot be used as an output switch.

After: `storytree library artifact <id> --raw <field> [--pg]` writes the field's EXACT stored value to stdout and nothing else — no heading, no `next:` block, no trailing newline beyond the value's own. That makes it composable with the existing `--set field=@path` write, so the read→edit→write round trip becomes two supported commands instead of a store script.

Behaviour at the edges, so the executor does not have to invent it: an absent field exits non-zero naming the field and listing the ones the doc has; a non-string field emits its JSON; the flag is read-only and offline-capable against the seed like every other read.

The flag name is `--raw <field>` rather than reusing `--json`, deliberately: `--json` already means something else on this verb, and overloading it would reproduce the exact confusion the item reports. That collision is itself a parked proposal (`a-cli-flags-owning-area-is-declared-and-checked`).
summary: Add a raw-field read to `storytree library artifact` (for example `--raw <field>`) that emits one stored field's exact value with no rendering — so a partial edit to a long prose or structured field can round-trip the untouched parts instead of being skipped or hand-rolled through a store script.
migration:
1. Confirm the gap is still open: `pnpm storytree library artifact merge-ceremony --pg --raw statement` should be an unknown flag today.
2. Red first, and make it a ROUND-TRIP assertion rather than a string comparison — write a known multi-line value to a test doc, read it back with `--raw`, and assert the bytes are identical. A test that only checks "some output appeared" would pass on the lossy render.
3. Implement, including the absent-field and non-string-field cases with their own assertions.
4. Prove it against a REAL long field, not only a fixture: read `routeReason` off a friction item with a multi-KB reason and diff it against the stored value. That is the use case the item was filed from.
5. Confirm stdout carries the value ALONE — no envelope, no `next:` — since anything else defeats piping it to a file.
readiness: Ready now. No dependency, no decision outstanding, one dispatch site. Sequence it EARLY relative to the rest of this tier: several other parked remedies involve rewriting long Library fields, and each of them currently pays the same hand-rolled-script tax this removes.
motivation:
The write side is fine and the read side has no path at all. `storytree library artifact edit --set field=@path` writes a long field from a file; nothing reads one back. `storytree library artifact <id> --pg` emits a formatted render, which is lossy for round-tripping, and `--json` on that verb is an INPUT option that takes a value — `npx tsx packages/cli/src/main.ts library artifact <id> --pg --json` returns `bad arguments: Option '--json <value>' argument missing`. Re-verified live 2026-07-28 from worktree gracious-rubin-dce071.

The concrete cost, measured: correcting ONE bullet of `process:verification-decay-detection`'s 2748-character `failureModes` field needed the exact stored string to round-trip the other eight bullets unchanged. Two sessions hit it on the same artifact within one day (2026-07-27), and it BLOCKED a librarian pass, which declined the edit and left known-stale guidance live. That is the load-bearing consequence: the gap does not merely cost time, it silently converts "correct this artifact" into "leave it wrong".

Reproduced first-hand again 2026-08-03 by the session filing this proposal: extracting `routeReason` from fourteen friction items — a mandatory step, because `friction route` overwrites `routeReason` wholesale and `--reason` is required on every call — required writing a throwaway `PgLibraryStore` script, exactly the fragile path CLAUDE.md steers sessions away from. Each of those reasons is 0.5–8 KB of multi-layer adjudication that only exists in the live row.

No prose makes a read verb exist, which is why this is a tool rather than an edit to `process:library-edit-ceremony`.

title: check:corpus-sync classifies an absence before prescribing its remedy
change:
`check:corpus-sync` today: compares the working-tree seed's non-agent artifacts against the live `library_artifact` projection, and reports every seed-only id as "absent from live, past the ceiling (M=0)" with the single remedy `sync-corpus --pg`.

`check:corpus-sync` after: classifies each seed-only id before printing anything, on the ADR-0290 D3 precedent of one label per cause.
- NEVER MIGRATED — no create event for the id in `events.library_event`. Remedy unchanged: `sync-corpus --pg`.
- BEHIND MAIN — `origin/main`'s seed no longer carries the row. Remedy: `git merge origin/main`, and explicitly NOT `sync-corpus`, which on a stale base re-authors a row main has already dropped.
- RETIRED LIVE — the event log shows create-then-delete for the id. Reported with the retiring event and NOT drained: re-creating it reverses an owner decision.

Charging follows ADR-0290 D3 as well: only NEVER MIGRATED is charged against the ceiling. The other two are reported in full with their cause and their own remedy, never counted.

Attribution failure follows ADR-0290 D7 exactly: if the git or event signal cannot be read once the check is running, fall back to today's behaviour (charge everything, print the unconditional remedy) with the reason printed — a wrongly-charged red costs a merge, a wrongly-excused one lands a one-sided edit no later gate catches.
summary: Give `check:corpus-sync` the two signals ADR-0290 gave `check:corpus-content` — the merge-base seed and the live event log — so it distinguishes "never migrated" from "behind main" and from "deliberately RETIRED live", and prints the remedy that matches the cause it actually found.
migration:
1. Verify the premise still holds before starting: `grep -c "origin/main\|merge-base\|library_event" packages/cli/src/check-corpus-sync.ts packages/cli/src/sync-drain.ts` must still be 0. If ADR-0290's attribution has since been extended to this check, this proposal is already delivered — stamp the two source friction items `--discharged-by` instead of building.
2. Read `corpus-content-attribution.ts` and extract the reusable half (merge-base seed read + latest-live-writer lookup) rather than copying it.
3. Add the three-way classification to the pure core in `sync-drain.ts`, with the red→green test proving each label independently: a never-migrated id charges, a behind-main id does not, a retired-live id does not.
4. Wire the labels into `check-corpus-sync.ts`'s report, one remedy per label, on the ADR-0290 D3 print shape.
5. Prove the retirement case over real data, not only fixtures: the `oq-diff-view-altitude` event sequence in the live log is the worked example and is still readable.
6. Add the ADR-0290 D7 fallback and assert it: signals unreadable ⇒ today's behaviour plus a printed reason.
readiness:
Ready now. Every dependency has landed: ADR-0290 is accepted and its code is on main (PR #1090, merged 2026-08-02T16:02Z), so the attribution helper this reuses exists; the live event log retains the superseded versions the classification reads; and the ceiling this reports against is unchanged.

The one precondition is a branch cut fresh from `origin/main` — the executor will be editing a check that reads its own branch's staleness, and a stale branch makes the red→green proof ambiguous.
motivation:
ADR-0290 (PR #1090, landed 2026-08-02) fixed exactly this class of defect on the corpus-CONTENT side: drift is now charged by authorship and labelled YOURS / BEHIND MAIN / ANOTHER WRITER, with a per-label remedy. `check:corpus-sync` was not part of that change and remains blind to both signals. Measured 2026-08-03: `grep -c "origin/main\|merge-base\|library_event"` returns 15 matches in `check-corpus-content.ts`, 11 in `corpus-content-attribution.ts` and 4 in `corpus-content-drain.ts`, but ZERO in both `check-corpus-sync.ts` and `sync-drain.ts`.

The cost is not symmetric with corpus-content's, and it is worse. corpus-content's wrong remedy publishes a stranger's prose; corpus-sync's wrong remedy REVERSES AN OWNER DECISION. Its zero ceiling (ADR-0252 D3) prints one unconditional instruction — "DRAIN it — `pnpm storytree library sync-corpus --pg`. Never raise the ceiling." — and on a branch cut before an owner-directed live retirement that instruction resurrects the retired artifact. Measured on `oq-diff-view-altitude` (retired live under ADR-0267 D5, seed row already dropped from `origin/main` in 583dbd27): a session on a 17-commit-stale branch obeyed the printed remedy, `sync-corpus` reported `created (1)`, a ~25 min gate reported the same id missing again, and a second sync reported `created (1)` a second time. `events.library_event` records the oscillation directly — 2694 deleted, 2695 created, 2696 deleted, 2698 created, 2702 deleted. A third resurrection was averted only because a librarian pass read the event log instead of the CLI projection.

The failure mode is a session correctly obeying a correct-looking instruction from the gate itself, which is the one place prose cannot reach: guidance cannot outrank a gate's own printed output at the moment of failure.

title: A gate check's self-description is asserted against its own exit code
change:
Today: each check's report prose and its exit code are produced in different places and asserted separately, if at all. A test can pass while the two contradict each other.

After: one shared assertion helper, used by every gate-check test suite, that RUNS the check's own report+exit path over a given state and asserts they agree —
- exit 0 ⇒ the printed preamble does not claim to have blocked;
- exit non-zero ⇒ the printed preamble does not claim to be advisory / never-a-block.

The helper asserts the RELATIONSHIP, not the wording, so it survives every prose edit and does not become a second place to keep sentences in sync.

Applied at minimum to the five checks with this split shape: `check:surface-coverage` (whose specific instance is already closed — the 2026-07-28 header of `check-surface-coverage.ts` records that the RED block always follows the WARN lines so reader and exit code agree), plus `check:agents-sync`, `check:corpus-sync`, `check:corpus-content`, `check:coverage`. `check:friction-drain` and `check:proposal-drain` share the shape and should be included.
summary: Add a shared assertion that binds each gate check's printed self-description to the exit code that same run actually sets — so a check can never tell the reader "advisory only, never a block" in the same breath as exiting 1, and the next check to gain a ceiling inherits the guard automatically.
migration:
1. Confirm the general assertion is still absent (the specific `check:surface-coverage` instance is already closed, so do NOT re-fix that one — grep its header for the 2026-07-28 note first).
2. Write the helper, and prove it works by pointing it at a DELIBERATELY contradictory fixture: a check state that exits 1 while printing an advisory preamble. That fixture failing is the red.
3. Adopt it check by check. Each adoption is independently green, so this can land as one unit or several.
4. Where a check's prose is caught contradicting its exit code, fix the PROSE — the exit code is the behaviour and is not up for revision here.
5. Record in the PR which checks were caught, because that list is the evidence the assertion was worth adding.
readiness:
Ready now. Every check named exists and has a test file; the helper depends on nothing new; and no decision is outstanding.

Measured immediately after wiring the drain ceiling into `packages/cli/src/check-surface-coverage.ts`: a control run of the real binary printed "[check:surface-coverage] WARN — the process↔entrypoint bijection has gaps (ADR-0154). Advisory only — this is the process-tier backfill worklist, never a block." — at a moment when the same shell had already been proven to set `process.exitCode = 1`. All 19 tests across `check-surface-coverage.test.ts` and `surface-coverage-drain.test.ts` PASSED against exactly that state, because their assertions match the gap-list headings and the OK line and never the WARN preamble that carries the self-description.

That is a demonstrated hole in the assertions, not a narrative. The mechanism is structural and repo-wide: the self-describing prose lives in a pure formatter, the exit code is set in a separate shell, and a fixture-only proof cannot see the two halves disagree. The item names the four remaining worklists that would be bounded the same way and carry the identical split shape — `check:agents-sync`, `check:corpus-sync`, `check:corpus-content`, `check:coverage` — so the exposure is a queue, not an incident. Reinforced 2026-08-02 on claude/exciting-dewdney-481b87, during exactly such a bounding.

Why this matters more than a stale sentence: a check's WARN preamble is what a session reads at the moment it decides whether a red is a landing blocker. A check that says "never a block" while blocking teaches sessions to distrust gate output, which is the one thing they must be able to trust.

title: friction route refuses to overwrite another branch's adjudication
change:
Today: `routeFriction` (`packages/cli/src/friction.ts`) performs an unguarded upsert of `route` and `routeReason`. The second write silently replaces the first, taking its entire seven-question audit record with it.

After: before writing, compare against the stored doc. If it already carries a route AND the last route write came from a different branch, REFUSE — naming the existing route, the branch that set it, and when — unless an explicit re-route flag is passed. The writer identity is already available: CLI library writes stamp `cli@<branch>` (ADR-0290 D2), and `events.library_event` carries the timestamp.

Deliberately the NARROW fix. It kills the load-bearing harm the item names — "two adjudicators can route the SAME item with DIFFERENT routes and the second write simply overwrites the first, taking its justification with it" — and nothing more. Duplicated READ effort survives and is ACCEPTED: that is wasted tokens, not lost audit.
summary: Make `storytree friction route` stop being a bare last-write-wins upsert: refuse — or require an explicit override — when the item ALREADY carries a route set by another branch, and say who set it and when.
migration:
1. Confirm the gap: `routeFriction` still upserts without comparing the stored `route`.
2. Red first, over the real shape: route an item as branch A, then route it as branch B, and assert B's write is REFUSED and A's `routeReason` survives byte-for-byte. The byte-for-byte assertion is the one that matters — a test that only checks the route enum would pass while the justification is still destroyed.
3. Implement the compare-and-refuse using the `cli@<branch>` actor already stamped by ADR-0290 D2, so no new attribution mechanism is invented.
4. Add the explicit override flag, and assert that WITH it the write succeeds — a refusal with no override would wall off the legitimate re-adjudication path (including `--discharged-by` re-runs).
5. Assert the SAME branch re-routing its own item is never refused: a session correcting its own adjudication is the normal case and must stay frictionless.
readiness:
Ready now, and its dependency has already landed: ADR-0290 D2 made CLI library writes stamp `cli@<branch>`, which is exactly the signal the guard needs and did not exist when this item was adjudicated. Before that, the check would have had to invent an attribution mechanism.

Sequence it before the next board drain rather than after — the exposure is a function of concurrent drains, and the ADR-0168 D4 ceiling keeps spawning them.
motivation:
Friction routing has no claim, mutex or compare-and-refuse of any kind, and the noticeboard claims a STORY rather than the queue (ADR-0200 grades claims per story node, and the friction queue is not one). So two adjudicator seats drain the same items in parallel with nothing refusing, queueing, or even warning.

MEASURED, and the numbers are the argument. On 2026-07-30 a board-drain chair ran five concurrent graduation-synthesist seats fenced only by a hand-assigned disjoint split, while TWO other sessions were draining the same queue:
- FOUR items were routed twice within ~13 minutes (`events.library_event` seq 2731/2735, 2732/2737, 2733/2739+2740, 2738/2741).
- TWO of those overwrites CHANGED THE ROUTE ENUM, and both changed whether the owner is involved: `story-work-claim-refuses-disjoint-file-concurrency` went `adr` → `tool`, silently cancelling an owner escalation; `adr-awaiting-an-owner-signature-looks-exactly-like-an-unfinished-draft` went `nothing` → `adr`, escalating over a peer's reasoned tombstone.
- Roughly 22,000 characters of verified peer justification were overwritten with no conflict surfaced at either seat.
- Three of the five seats declined to write only because they had been BRIEFED to re-read first — hand discipline the tool does not require.
- One seat reproduced the mechanism on ITSELF, overwriting its own `routeReason` after a correction.

This item's own `routeReason` was overwritten and then restored verbatim from the event log; recovery was possible ONLY because `events.library_event` retains superseded versions. A reader of the `library_artifact` projection would have seen no trace.

The exposure is rising by design: ADR-0168 D4's ceiling SPAWNS board-drain sessions, so concurrent adjudication is a designed-in condition. Prose cannot fix it — an adjudicator would have to hand-roll a six-call "is another drain in flight?" probe on every pass, forever.

title: Every CLI store write path is checked to carry branch attribution
change: Add a mechanical check that fails when a CLI store-write call site supplies an event actor that does not resolve through `defaultCliActor()`. The shape that fits this repo's existing checks is a source-level scan over the CLI write paths asserting that any `actor:` property in a store-write options object is either `defaultCliActor()` or a caller-supplied `deps.actor` that falls back to it — with a literal string refused. It belongs beside the existing `check:*` family and inside `pnpm gate`; unlike its DB-reading siblings it needs no store and no credentials, so unlike `check:corpus-content` it can run in CI as well as locally. Test fixtures are the legitimate exception and must be excluded by path rather than by pattern (there is one today, `corpus-content-attribution.test.ts:189`, which deliberately constructs a bare `cli` row).
summary: Every store write path in the CLI must carry branch attribution, and nothing forces it to. The convention lives in a shared helper (`defaultCliActor()`, `packages/cli/src/cli-actor.ts`) that a new write path is free not to call; opting out is invisible because an unattributed write still succeeds, still typechecks, and still passes its own tests. Add a mechanical check that every store-writing call site in the CLI resolves its event actor through that helper rather than a literal.
migration: None required. The one known offender is already fixed and a sweep on 2026-08-03 found no other live holdout: `grep -rn 'actor: *"cli"' packages/cli/src packages/drive/src` returns exactly one hit, and it is the deliberate test fixture named in Change. So the check is expected to land GREEN, with a zero drain ceiling from the first commit in the ADR-0252 D3 shape its sibling checks already use — there is no backlog to drain and therefore no headroom to grant. If the sweep is re-run at build time and finds a holdout that appeared in the interim, that holdout is fixed in the same PR rather than admitted as a ceiling.
readiness: Ready to author. The defect is diagnosed to a single line, its fix is landed and proven, the enforcement gap is confirmed by direct inspection (nothing in `packages/cli/src/check-*.ts` reads the actor convention), the exception set is exactly one known test fixture, and the check needs no DB and no credentials so it carries none of the SKIP-when-offline complexity its store-reading siblings do. NOT ready in one respect, recorded rather than hidden: no one has yet judged whether a source-level scan is the right instrument versus a runtime assertion in the store-write boundary itself, which would catch a call site the scan's pattern misses. That is an implementation fork for the authoring session, not a blocker on the decision to build.
motivation:
ADR-0290 made `check:corpus-content` charge seed-live drift BY AUTHORSHIP, which turned the event `actor` column into a load-bearing signal: the check reads the latest live writer per artifact and labels each drift YOURS, BEHIND MAIN, or ANOTHER WRITER, and a session is instructed to act differently on each.

On 2026-08-03, the FIRST pass that used ADR-0287's `tool` route hit the gap. `storytree proposal new --pg` wrote `actor: deps.actor ?? "cli"` while every sibling write path passed `defaultCliActor()` (arc.ts, friction.ts, commands.ts). `pnpm check:corpus-content` then told the authoring session that its own three brand-new proposals were `not yours` — and the printed remedy for a not-yours row is "route it back, or leave it". A session obeying its own gate would never have exported the proposals it had just authored, so they would have stayed live-only and the delivery signal ADR-0287 built the proposal tier to carry would have been destroyed on its first use.

`packages/cli/src/cli-actor.ts` already documents the exact consequence: `branchOfActor` returns null for the bare `cli`, and that null "means UNATTRIBUTED, never 'not yours'". The check nonetheless charges it as not-this-branch's. So the failure was foreseen at the helper and unenforced at the call sites.

It was caught only by luck of arithmetic — the count (3) exactly matched what that session had authored minutes earlier. With a single sibling proposal in the same list it would have read as ordinary sibling drift and gone unnoticed.
description: Every store write path in the CLI must carry branch attribution, and nothing forces it to.
